lines.text: I heard about the old woman. At the farm. I could go. I'm quick. I've gone first on worse.
You'll do what you're told. That was the word.
You'll do what you're told. Your gran sent you with me for that.
I know. I'm only saying I could.
Nobody's told me not to. That's not the same as being told to, is it. I'll do the ropes.

talks.label: Ask Rue how the Wold walks a column

lines.text: Roped. Everyone. A child between two grown people. Nobody unties for anything, not to drink, not to help. If you untie, you are gone.
And someone at the back who says the names, all day, down the rope, so the front knows who is still on it. In Thrum that is the oldest. Here they will want it to be you.
If someone goes back for anyone, they go off the rope. Alone. And they come after us in the white, with whoever they find. Sometimes they come. It is written when they do.

talks.label: Ask Nessa where she wants to be

lines.text: Front. Always. Except I've got the end house's three behind me, and the littlest won't walk unless she can hold my hand, so I'm not really first, am I. I'm second, with a child.
And there's a woman out at a farm on her own and her son's standing at the end of the road looking at it. Nobody's said a word about her. I've noticed.

b4-sheddon.clue: The white will close the Orme road by dark. Sedge's farm is an hour out and an hour back, from the cairn where the farm track leaves the road.

investigate.label: Read the white on the Orme road, and how long the day is

success.narrate: {You walk|@ walks} out to the first bend of the Orme road and {read|reads} the white the way Rue reads it: the grey line on the posts where it lay last night, and the line under it, and how far it came between. By dark it will be over the road at the low ford, two hours short of Orme.

A column of two hundred, roped, with children, walks at the pace of the slowest child. If it stops for nothing it is past the ford at dusk. The cairn where the farm track leaves the road is at noon. The farm is an hour out from the cairn, and an hour back.

failure.narrate: {You try|@ tries} to read the white on the Orme road, but the posts are written over with a hundred winters' lines and {you cannot|@ cannot} tell last night's from any other. All {they} can be sure of is that it will be over the road by dark.

route.label: Go house to house and count who is in the column before it moves

success.narrate: {You go|@ goes} down the column house by house before it moves, and {chalk|chalks} each house's count on the shoulder of whoever is at its front. Two hundred and three. Everyone in Sheddon is in the road, except one old woman at a farm at the edge.

failure.narrate: {You go|@ goes} down the column house by house before it moves, but the houses keep changing places in the line, and the count comes out different each time {you make|@ makes} it. By the time {you give|@ gives} up, the front has started walking.

peaceful.label: Keep the column moving, every child roped, all the way to the ford

success.narrate: {You know|@ knows} what the posts said: past the ford at dusk, or not at all. {You do|@ does} not let the column stop for anything.
Every house knows its count, chalked on the shoulder of whoever is at its front, and calls it down the rope at every post.
{You call|@ calls} the names down the rope at every post, as near as {they} can remember them.
Orin walks at the front, and sets the pace, and does not look back, because the people behind him are looking at him.
{You walk|@ walks} at the front, and {set|sets} the pace, and {do|does} not look back.
Davin walks the rope from end to end all morning, re-tying the children's knots where they have pulled loose.

When the white comes across the road in a long arm from the low fields, the column does not stop. It walks into it, roped, saying its names, and out of the other side, and every name that went in comes out.
By noon the column is at the cairn where the farm track goes off east. Sedge stops.

failure.narrate: {You try|@ tries} to keep the column moving, but the white comes across the road in a long arm from the low fields, and the front stops dead in it, and the rope goes slack all the way back, and in the white beside the road things begin to stand up.

direct.label: Go down the valley to Sheddon
direct.text: You go down the valley from Lantry to Sheddon, walking through the night.

approach.narrate: The column moves at first light. Two hundred and some, roped, a child between every two grown people, with Sheddon's eldest in a cart in the middle and the rope cart at the back.
The Orme road goes north out of the valley between low walls, with the white lying in the fields on both sides of it, flat and still, like snow that has not decided to be snow.
Behind the column, Sheddon goes under. Nobody looks back. It is on their doors where they are going.

crisis.narrate: Mid-morning, the white comes across the road. Not all of it: one long arm, out of the fields on the east side, lying across the Orme road a hundred paces deep and moving.

crisis.text: Do not stop. If the front stops in it, the back walks into the front, and someone unties to see why.
Nobody stops. Nobody unties. Names, down the rope. Now.

crisis.narrate: Sedge is at the back of the column, roped, walking. Every few paces he turns round and looks east.

objective.name: Through the white
objective.label: Get the column through the white across the road, everyone on the rope
objective.description: Four successful actions get two hundred people, roped, through the arm of white across the Orme road without the column stopping or anyone untying.
objective.failText: The column comes out of the white in the end, every name on the rope, but it stopped in the middle, and it has lost an hour it did not have, and two of the children cannot remember the house they walked out of.
objective.successText: The column comes out of the white on the far side, roped, still walking, and every name that went in comes out.

b4-sheddon.foeName: The White on the Orme Road

oneOf.narrate: Noon, at the cairn where the farm track leaves the Orme road. The column has not stopped since dawn, and nobody is hurt.
Noon, at the cairn where the farm track leaves the Orme road. The road behind the column is trampled grey where the fight was, and the column has been walking again since, faster than it wants to.

after.narrate: Sedge stops at the cairn. He does not untie. He stands there, roped, with the column going on past him, looking down the farm track into the white.

after.text: An hour out. An hour back. I'm not asking. I said I wouldn't.
Whoever goes, goes off the rope, and comes after us alone, in the white, with her. The column cannot wait. It has two hundred on it.

after.narrate: Orin has stopped, too, at the front, and turned round, and everyone behind him has stopped because he has. He looks at Sedge, and then at the track, and then at you.

after.text: This is mine, isn't it. They gave it me at the head of the road. It's mine.

decisions.label: Let Orin give the order: the column goes on
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Orin orders the column on. Nobody goes back for Sedge's mother.

told.ballad: At the farm-track cairn Orin Stoneward said 'on', and two hundred went on, and one old woman stayed in the white.
told.tally: Sheddon. At the farm-track cairn the southern soldier ordered the column on. Sedge's mother was not fetched. Written: he said it himself, and he asked who she was.

text.text: Column moves. Now. Nobody unties. Sedge, you're on the rope. You stay on it.
Yes.

text.narrate: Sedge goes on with the column. He walks the rest of the day with his face to the north, and does not look east again. He does not have to. The farm is on his arm, in his own hand, and he can read it without looking.

text.text: Her name. What was her name.
Mother. At the edge farm. She hasn't a name of her own now. She gave it, the winter my father died.
Sedge's mother, at the edge farm. I gave the order. Write that. Not 'the column went on'. I said it.
Somebody could have gone. Somebody always can.
I know. That's why it was mine to say.

text.narrate: The column comes past the ford at dusk, and into Orme after dark, two hundred and three.

decisions.label: Let Orin go back for her, and take the column yourself
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Orin goes off the rope, down the farm track into the white, for Sedge's mother. You take the front.

told.ballad: At the farm-track cairn Orin Stoneward untied, and went into the white for an old woman, and came out of it carrying her, and lighter by a name.
told.tally: Sheddon. At the farm-track cairn the southern soldier went off the rope for Sedge's mother, and brought her in after dark. Written: he gave a name to the white for her.

text.text: No. Not this time. Not again. You take the front. Names down the rope. Past the ford at dusk. Don't wait for me. That's an order too.

oneOf.text: Davin. Rear of the column. You hold it. Nobody falls off the back. That's your order. Your gran sent you with me for this. Keep it.
Davin. Rear of the column. You hold it. Nobody falls off the back. That's your order, and it's the word, and you keep it.
Somebody take the rear. Somebody who'll not untie for anyone.

text.text: Yes. The rear. Yes.

text.narrate: Davin holds the rear of the column all afternoon, saying the names down the rope, and does not once look back for Orin. It is the hardest thing you have seen anyone do today.
Orin unties at the cairn and goes down the farm track into the white, alone, without a lamp, and is gone in ten paces.
You take the front. The column comes past the ford at dusk. In the last of the light, behind it, a shape comes out of the white on the road, carrying another on its back.

It is Orin, with an old woman on his back who keeps asking him, politely, who he is. He tells her. Then, at the gates of Orme, he stops, and frowns, and asks you what Varn's company was called. There was a name. They painted it on the carts. He cannot find it.

text.text: Forty of us. I'd have told you yesterday. It's gone. The white had it. Fair price, I suppose. I never liked it.

decisions.label: Go back for her yourself
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. You go off the rope, down the farm track into the white, for Sedge's mother.

told.ballad: At the farm-track cairn the stranger from the south untied, and went into the white for an old woman, and came out with her, and with a day gone.
told.tally: Sheddon. At the farm-track cairn a southerner went off the rope for Sedge's mother and brought her in. Written: they gave a whole day to the white for her, and did not ask which.

text.narrate: You untie at the cairn before anyone can say anything.

text.text: You took it off me. I'd made my mind up. I was going to say it. You took it off me.
Go on, then. I've got them. Past the ford at dusk.

text.narrate: You go down the farm track into the white, alone. It is an hour to the farm. The old woman is sitting at her kitchen table with her coat on, reading the inside of her door, and she is very glad to see you, and has no idea who you are.

It is more than an hour back. You carry her the last of it. In the last of the light you come out onto the Orme road behind the column, past the ford, and walk into Orme after dark with Sedge's mother asleep on your back.

At the gate Rue asks you, gently, what you did on the day of the vote at Highpass. You know there was a vote. You know how it went, because she has it written down, and reads it to you. You cannot remember the hall, or the day, or anything in it. A whole day of your own, given, on the farm track, without your asking which.

decisions.label: Go back for her yourself
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. You go off the rope, down the farm track into the white, for Sedge's mother.

told.ballad: At the farm-track cairn the stranger from the south untied, and went into the white for an old woman, and came out with her, and with a day gone.
told.tally: Sheddon. At the farm-track cairn a southerner went off the rope for Sedge's mother and brought her in. Written: they gave a whole day to the white for her, and did not ask which.

text.narrate: You untie at the cairn before anyone can say anything.
Rue takes the front of the column, with her book in her coat, and calls the names down the rope herself.

You go down the farm track into the white, alone. It is an hour to the farm. The old woman is sitting at her kitchen table with her coat on, reading the inside of her door, and she is very glad to see you, and has no idea who you are.

It is more than an hour back. You carry her the last of it. In the last of the light you come out onto the Orme road behind the column, past the ford, and walk into Orme after dark with Sedge's mother asleep on your back.

At the gate Rue asks you, gently, what you did on the day of the vote at Highpass. You know there was a vote. You know how it went, because she has it written down, and reads it to you. You cannot remember the hall, or the day, or anything in it. A whole day of your own, given, on the farm track, without your asking which.

decisions.label: Order the column on yourself
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. You give the order. The column goes on, and nobody goes back for Sedge's mother.

told.ballad: At the farm-track cairn the stranger from the south said 'on', and two hundred went on, and one old woman stayed in the white.
told.tally: Sheddon. At the farm-track cairn a southerner ordered the column on. Sedge's mother was not fetched.

text.narrate: You tell the column to go on. Nobody unties. Sedge's mouth goes tight, and he goes on with it, and walks the rest of the day with his face to the north.

text.text: Somebody could have gone. Somebody always can.

text.narrate: The column comes past the ford at dusk, and into Orme after dark, two hundred and three. Sedge writes something on his arm at the gate, and shows it to nobody.

b4-orme.name: The Long Tally
b4-orme.region: Orme, the Wold's chief town, and the Long Hall, where nine hundred years of the Long Tally are kept
b4-orme.threat: The Reckoner's tally-guard mean to hold the party in the Long Hall as surety for whatever the bell-country answers.
b4-orme.brief: Orme's Long Hall holds the Long Tally, nine hundred years of it. Burdock keeps it, and Sloe the Reckoner does its sums. She sent Rue south to find out who sends the white, and Rue has come back with you.

told.ballad: In Orme they keep a tally nine hundred years long, and they wrote the strangers from the south into it, and asked them what to write about the south.
told.tally: Orme, the Long Hall. Southerners came, with Rue of Thrum, who went south to ask. Burdock wrote them in.

opening.narrate: Orme is low stone houses banked with snow round one long building, the Long Hall, with lamps in every window. Inside, the walls are cut with writing from the floor to the roof-beams, and the books stand in stacks to the roof-beams too, nine hundred years of them, and the lamps burn all night.

Burdock of the Long Hall has kept the tally for forty years. He is seventy, small, and very clean, with ink to the second knuckle of every finger. He remembers none of it. He reads it every morning, from wherever he left off, and believes every word.

Sloe of Orme, the Reckoner, has a table at the far end of the Hall, under the oldest wall, covered in slates, and she is doing a sum on them. She has been doing it, the clerks say, for a month. She does not look up when you come in. Then she does.

By the lamp nearest her table a man sits on a bench with his back to the wall, in a southern coat gone grey with the road, with a lamp on the floor between his boots: the lamp they sent him down Vell's stair with. It is Hesk.

Pinned to the wall above Sloe's table, at the end of the newest line of the tally, there is a sheet of paper in a southern hand, pebble-marked at one corner. It is your letter, from the floor of given things. You do not remember writing a word of it. Sloe has read it. It is the first letter from the south in nine hundred years of tally.

talks.label: Let Burdock write you in

lines.text: From the south? No. Nobody has come from the south. It is not in the tally. I have read the tally. If they had come, it would say so.

oneOf.text: One came. In the spring, with a lamp, out of the marked way, and is written. One. It does not say any more came after him.
Wagons came. In the summer, forty, with a map, and asked the way to the empty land, and went on down the valley road. Wagons that ask the way are not people who come to a door.
Carts came, to Lantry, with grain, and they are standing at the well. Carts are not people. Nobody came to the door.
A letter came. From the floor. A letter is not a person. It says 'we are coming'. It does not say you came.

lines.narrate: Rue opens her book and shows him a page. Burdock reads it, and then reads it again, and then puts on a second pair of spectacles over the first and reads it a third time.

lines.text: Rue of Thrum went south, and came back with these, from the south. In her hand. Then it is true.

oneOf.text: And Lantry has sent a slate ahead of you by the carter: 'The southerners gave at our well.' Givers. Well. Givers are written in.
And Lantry has sent a slate ahead of you by the carter: 'The southerners rang. The white went to Sheddon.' I do not know what rang means. Sloe does.
And Lantry has sent a slate ahead of you by the carter: 'The southerners went in, as guests do. The smith gave for them.' Guests, then.

lines.narrate: He takes down the newest book, and opens it, and writes you in, carefully, in the square hand, and blots it, and reads it back aloud. Then he looks up at you with complete and delighted belief, as if you had just walked in.

oneOf.text: From the south! Sit down. You must be very tired. Nobody but the man with the lamp has ever come from the south. Well. You have. It is written.
From the south! Sit down. You must be very tired. Nobody has ever come from the south to stay and be written. Well. You have. It is written.

talks.label: Sit down at the Reckoner's table

lines.text: Rue says you can do sums. Good. Look.

lines.narrate: She turns a slate round. On it, in columns, is every winter in the tally since the bells went south: how deep the white lay, how often Orme gave, and how much.

lines.text: Every winter since the bells, doubled. You can do the arithmetic yourself. I have done it every way there is. It comes out the same.

oneOf.text: And then last winter. The lightest in the tally. In nine hundred years, the lightest. Somebody in the south did something. I would like to know who, and what, and whether they will do it again, or undo it.
And then last winter. Bad. Worse than the one before. Less bad than the sum says it should have been, by about a third. Somebody in the south made more bells, and fewer than they meant to.
And then last winter. The worst in the tally. Something in the south got louder. I would like to know what.
And then last winter, worse again, as every winter is. And in the spring a man came out of the marked way with a lamp, and told me why. I did not need him to. I had the sum.

lines.text: And this. 'The night of the great note, the white came down on Orme and Lantry and did not lift until the giving.' The tally dates it to a midwinter. Rue wrote me down your midwinter, the night your Mother Bell was rung. They are the same night.
So I know where it comes from. I know it can be sent harder, because it was. Then it can be sent softer. Somebody down there chose. I want them to choose again.
I am not angry. Write that down, Burdock. I want it written that I was not angry. I want one winter back for my people, and I will pay for it with whatever it costs.

talks.label: Talk to Hesk

lines.narrate: Hesk does not get up. He looks at you for a long time, and moves his lamp an inch with his boot, so that it is between you.

lines.text: They sent me down a stair alone, with that, to carry the free wards on my own back. I came out the other end. These people fed me before they asked my name. Then they asked, and wrote it down.

I told them what bells are. What they cost and who pays. I told them the free wards will never stop ringing, because I wouldn't, in their place. Strangers are a luxury, and nobody south of those peaks can afford them.
I told them the truth. They wrote it down. That's more than you did.

talks.label: Ask Rue what she will tell the Reckoner

lines.text: She sent me to find out who sends the white. I found out. It is everybody. It is the bells. Every bell. And they did not know.
I will tell her both. She will write the first. She will not write the second, because the second does not change the sum.

oneOf.text: I read her my book this morning. All of it. She listened to every page, and at the end she said, 'So you were kind to them,' as if it was a figure that would not add up.
I told her my book burned. She asked who burned it. I told her. She wrote it down, and did not say anything, and that was worse.

talks.label: Ask Maren what she hears in the Long Hall

lines.text: Sloe isn't lying. About anything. Not the numbers, not the winters, not that she isn't angry. She means every word, and every word is true.
Burdock believes us now, completely. Ten minutes ago he believed the opposite, completely. Both times, true. He's not lying either way. He's reading.
Hesk believes what he says. He always did. That was never the trouble with him.

b4-orme.clue: Two lines on the oldest wall: the year the bells went south, and, three hundred years ago, 'the bell-country asked us once to come south; we wrote it down, and forgot'.

investigate.label: Read the Long Hall's oldest wall by Burdock's lamp

success.narrate: {You take|@ takes} Burdock's lamp along the oldest wall, where the cutting is worn so shallow that the letters show only when the light is held sideways, and {read|reads} it back to the line every child copies: 'The year the bells went south, the white doubled.'

Then forward, six hundred years, to a line nobody reads, because it is in the middle: 'The bell-country asked us once to come south. We wrote it down, and forgot.' Under it, smaller, in another hand: 'Who asked? Not written.'

failure.narrate: {You take|@ takes} Burdock's lamp along the oldest wall, but the cutting is worn so shallow that the letters come and go with the flame, and all {they} can be sure of is the line every child copies: 'The year the bells went south, the white doubled.'

route.label: Find out where the Reckoner's tally-guard are mustering

success.narrate: {You watch|@ watches} the Long Hall's doors through the afternoon, and {see|sees} the tally-guard come in by the clerks' door at the back, one at a time, with their slates under their arms and their spears wrapped in sacking, and stand along the oldest wall where Sloe can see them.

failure.narrate: {You watch|@ watches} the Long Hall's doors through the afternoon, but Orme comes and goes through every one of them, to read and to be written, and {you cannot|@ cannot} tell a tally-guard from a clerk until it is dark.

peaceful.label: Ask Burdock to read what the tally says about guests

success.narrate: {You remember|@ remembers} the line in the middle of the oldest wall, and that the bell-country asked once, and {say|says} so, loud enough for the guard to hear.
{You have|@ has} seen the guard come in by the clerks' door, and {you are|@ is} standing between them and Burdock's desk before they are across the Hall.
{You go|@ goes} to Burdock's desk, past the guard, and {put|puts} the oldest book in front of him.
{You ask|@ asks} Burdock to read what the tally says about guests. Not about the south. About guests.
Burdock finds it in four minutes, because nobody has ever asked him for it, and so it is in exactly the place it was put. He reads it aloud in the voice he uses for the oldest lines.
'A guest at Orme is written in on the day they come. What is written in is not held. A guest is not surety. Whoever holds a guest writes their own name under it.'
The tally-guard look at Sloe. Sloe looks at the line for a long time. Then she takes her own pen out of her sleeve, and does not write her name under it, and puts the pen away.

success.text: Very well. You are guests. Then answer me as guests.

failure.narrate: {You ask|@ asks} Burdock to read what the tally says about guests, but he cannot find it, because there are nine hundred years of it and he does not know what he is looking for, and while he looks the tally-guard put down their slates and unwrap their spears.

direct.label: Go to the Long Hall
direct.text: You go up through Orme to the Long Hall, where the Long Tally is kept.

approach.narrate: At dusk the Long Hall fills. Orme comes in to read what happened to it today, and to be written, and the clerks go up and down the ladders with lamps.
Sheddon comes in too, two hundred of them, to be written into Orme's tally as Orme's now, one at a time, at Burdock's desk.

oneOf.narrate: Sedge comes in with his mother on his arm. She gives Burdock her name as 'Sedge's mother, of the edge farm', and he writes it that way, and she watches him do it as if it was a kindness.
Sedge comes in on his own, and gives Burdock his name, and his farm, and then, after a long time, his mother's farm, so that it is written somewhere that she lived there.

approach.narrate: Sloe has stopped doing her sum. She is watching the door.

crisis.narrate: The tally-guard come in by the clerks' door at the back of the Hall: a dozen of them, in long grey coats with the tally's square hand stitched down the front, each with a slate under one arm and a spear in the other hand.

crisis.text: The bell-country owes the Wold nine hundred years. It has sent you. Until it answers, you stay here, in the Hall, written, and fed. You are surety for the answer.
Nobody will hurt you. Nobody here hurts anybody. But you will stay.
Stay where you are. They want us sitting down, not hurt. So do I.

crisis.narrate: The tally-guard spread out along the oldest wall, between you and the doors, with their spears down and their slates up.
Behind them the clerks' door stands open on the night, and the white comes in off the snow along the floor of the Hall, ankle-deep, as cold as the street.

objective.name: The doors of the Long Hall
objective.label: Get to the Long Hall's doors without hurting anyone who keeps the tally
objective.description: Four successful actions get the party past the tally-guard to the doors of the Long Hall, without a clerk or a book harmed.
objective.failText: You reach the doors in the end, but a stack of the tally went over in the fight, two hundred years of it on the floor, and the clerks are on their knees picking it up in order, crying.
objective.successText: You are at the doors of the Long Hall, and the tally-guard have stepped back from them, and not a book is out of its place.

oneOf.narrate: Midnight in the Long Hall. The tally-guard have gone back out by the clerks' door with their spears wrapped up again. Nobody is hurt, and nobody is held.

Midnight in the Long Hall. The tally-guard are sitting along the oldest wall with their heads in their hands and their slates in their laps, and the clerks are going round them with bandages and lamps, and writing down who was hurt, and by whom.

after.narrate: Burdock has the newest book open on his desk, at a clean page, with his pen wet.

after.text: Now. The south. It has to be written. What is to be written about the south? I will write whatever you say. I always do. Whatever I write, they will believe, after a season. That is how it works.

after.narrate: Sloe sits at her table with her hands flat on her slates, and waits.

after.text: Before I write anything, I read what is already written. This is yours. 'To whoever is on the other side of the bells. This is the south. We did not know you were there. We are sorry it took nine hundred years to ask. We are coming north, to ask properly.'

decisions.label: The whole truth: the bells, the Mother Bell, all of it
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Burdock writes everything you know: what the bells do, where the white goes, and that the free wards rang it.

told.ballad: In Orme they asked what to write of the south, and the strangers told them all of it, the bells and the great note and the nine, and it was written.
told.tally: Written, at the southerners' word: the bell-country rings the white north. It always has. The great note was theirs. They told us themselves.

text.narrate: You tell Burdock all of it, and he writes it down as you say it: the bells, and the lanes, and the nine on the lid at Cinder Fold, and the founders who cast them, and the Mother Bell that Elske rang at midwinter, and that every bell in the free wards rings the white north and always has.

text.text: Thank you.

text.narrate: She does not say anything else. She turns one of her slates over and starts a new sum on the back of it.

text.text: That is what I would have written. All of it. That is the first time anyone from the south has said it, in nine hundred years. It is written that you said it.

decisions.label: The truth, and the free wards' reasons with it
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Burdock writes what the bells do, and beside it why the free wards ring them: their children, their lanes, and that they did not know.

told.ballad: In Orme they asked what to write of the south, and the strangers told them the truth, and why, and Burdock wrote both sides of the page.
told.tally: Written, at the southerners' word: the bell-country rings the white north, to keep its children out of it. Written beside it: they did not know where it went.

text.narrate: You tell Burdock what the bells do, and where the white goes. Then you tell him why: that the free wards ring them because the white takes their children too, out of the lanes, the way it takes Lantry's; that the founders did it, nine hundred years ago, to save the people in front of them; and that nobody in the south knew where it went, until a girl from Thrum walked down the old north road and asked.
Burdock writes it in two columns, on facing pages: what the bells do, and why. Then he reads both columns aloud, across the page, line by line.

text.text: The second column does not change the sum.
No. But it is written. That is what a tally is. Both columns, Sloe.
She means it. It doesn't change the sum. She means that too.

decisions.label: Nothing, until the free wards answer for themselves
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Nothing is written about the south until the council answers. The Reckoner will not forget that you asked her to wait.

told.ballad: In Orme they asked what to write of the south, and the strangers said, not yet, not until the south can answer for itself.
told.tally: Asked what to write of the south, the southerners said: nothing, until the bell-country answers. Written by the Reckoner: they asked us to wait. We have waited nine hundred years.

text.narrate: You tell Burdock that it is not yours to write. The council at Highpass has to answer for the free wards, in its own words, and until it does, nothing should go in the tally about the south that the south did not say itself.
Burdock writes: 'The south: not yet.' And underlines it, and blots it.

text.text: You carry their seal on a cord round your neck. Then they have answered, and you will not say what.

text.narrate: Sloe takes her own pen out of her sleeve, and reaches across his desk, and writes under it, in a smaller and squarer hand: 'They asked us to wait. We have waited nine hundred years.' Then she goes back to her table, and her slates, and does not look at you again tonight.

text.text: That's the free wards. Every time. I told her you'd say that.

b4-greve.name: The House of Letting Go
b4-greve.region: Greve, a day up the valley from Orme, and Yarrow's house, where the Wold's grieving come to give their grief to the white
b4-greve.threat: A surge of the white on Greve's giving night, with Yarrow's house full of the grieving.
b4-greve.brief: Yarrow of Greve keeps the house where the Wold's grieving come to give their grief to the white, so that they can go home and work. Maren has spent her life on lists of names.

told.ballad: At Greve they give their grief to the white, and the strangers from the south stood in the house of letting go on the giving night.
told.tally: Greve, the giving night. Southerners came to Yarrow's house, and the white came over the wall. Written: what they did with the names.

opening.narrate: Greve is a day up the valley from Orme: a mill on the river, a street of twenty doors, and at the top of the street a long low house with its door standing open and a lamp in every window.
The doors in Greve are written like every door in the Wold, except that on some of them a line near the bottom has been rubbed out, carefully, with a wet cloth, and nothing has been written over it.

That is Yarrow's house. The Wold's grieving come to it from every valley and sit in its long room, and on the giving night they give their grief to the white, and go home, and work. Nobody in the Wold remembers its dead past a season. Most of them never try.
Yarrow meets you at the door: a broad grey woman in an apron with flour on it, and a censer on a chain in one hand, not lit.

opening.text: Rue sent word you were coming. Come in, all of you. Wipe your feet. There's soup. It's the giving tomorrow night and I've forty in, so you'll have to sit where you can.

opening.narrate: Maren stops on the step and reads the rubbed-out lines on the doors, one after another, all the way down the street.

talks.label: Ask Yarrow what her house is for

lines.text: A woman loses her husband in the white in the autumn. She can't get up in the morning. She reads him on her door and on her arm, every day, and every day it happens to her again, and the children don't get fed.
So she comes here, and sits with the others, and on the giving night she gives it. Not him. He's still on her door, and on her arm. Just what it does to her. And she goes home and makes the bread.
Nobody's made to. They come because they can't work. I can't stop the white taking. I can make it take the right thing. That's all this house is.

oneOf.text: Rue says your Sister keeps names. All of them, for ever. I'd like to hear how she gets anything done.
Rue says in the south you keep your dead. All of them, for ever. I can't think how you get anything done.

talks.label: Sit with the woman by the fire who has come to give her son

lines.narrate: She is sitting by the fire with her sleeve rolled up, reading her own arm. Her son's name is written there, and under it the day: the day the white came over the top field.

lines.text: Comfrey. He was eleven. He went up for the ewes. I've read it every morning since, and every morning it happens again. I can't get the bread made.
Tomorrow I give it. I'll still have him on my arm. I just won't mind. Yarrow says it's like reading about somebody else's boy. I'd like to read about somebody else's boy. I'd like to make the bread.

oneOf.text: What was he like? Not what happened to him. What was he like?

oneOf.narrate: You ask her what he was like. Not what happened to him: what he was like.

lines.text: I don't know. I've only got the day written. Nobody writes down what they were like. What would you write it for?

talks.label: Ask Maren what she makes of the house

lines.text: Yarrow isn't lying. Not about any of it. They all believe every word they say in here. I can't hear a thing, and I've never been in a room where I wanted to more.

oneOf.text: I carry a list of yeses in my coat, for the seal. Every town that said yes. I could read it in my sleep. I can't think of anything that would make me give it to the white.
I gave a day once, in the deep. The day my gift woke. I don't miss it. I don't know what I would miss. That's what frightens me about this house.
I kept a list once. Every shrine keeper lost in the Gloam's years, and how each one ended. I put it down, in the end, and I was right to. I didn't forget one of them. That's the difference.

lines.text: Anwen used to say a name said aloud in a room is a person in the room. I'd like to see what the white does with that.

talks.label: Ask Rue whether Thrum sends its grieving here

lines.text: Every town sends people to Greve. Most people come once. I have not. I have it written that I never will.
I do not know if that is brave, or only something I wrote down once and have read every morning since.
Thrum is three days down the valley from Orme. If my mother has been, it will be on her door. I will know when I see the door.

b4-greve.clue: Those who keep their griefs live shorter. Those who give them forget the dead entirely. The Long Tally keeps no names of the dead, only numbers: nine hundred years of 'lost: four'.

investigate.label: Read Yarrow's house-book, where every giving is written

success.narrate: {You read|@ reads} Yarrow's house-book by the fire. It has three columns: who came, what they gave, and when they came back. The ones who came once, and gave, and went home, are written old. The ones who would not give, and kept it, are written dead young, of the cold and the not eating.
At the back is the tally Greve sends to Orme each spring, copied out year after year: 'Greve. Lost: four.' 'Lost: two.' 'Lost: eleven.' Three hundred years of it, and not one name.

failure.narrate: {You read|@ reads} Yarrow's house-book by the fire, but it is in forty hands over three hundred years, and all {they} can follow is the column of numbers at the back: lost: four, lost: two, lost: eleven.

route.label: Walk Greve's yard wall before dark and find where the white comes over

success.narrate: {You walk|@ walks} the yard wall in the last of the light and {find|finds} the low place by the mill-race where the frost on the stones is thickest. That is where the white comes over first. {You set|@ sets} a row of Yarrow's lamps along it.

failure.narrate: {You walk|@ walks} the yard wall as the light goes, and the cold off the mill-race gets into {their} hands and feet, and the white is over the low place by the water before {you are|@ is} back at the door.

direct.label: Go up the valley to Greve
direct.text: You go up the valley from Orme to Greve, a day's walk, and come to Yarrow's house at dusk the day before the giving.

approach.narrate: The giving night. The long room is full: forty of the grieving on the benches with their sleeves rolled back, and Yarrow going between them with the censer lit, slowly, so that the smoke goes up into the roof.
Outside, the white is coming down the valley the way it comes on a giving night, low and slow, to be given to.

crisis.narrate: It does not come slowly. It comes over the yard wall all at once, thick as fleece and higher than the door, and it does not stop at the step.

crisis.text: That's not a giving. That's too much. Shut the... no. You never shut the door on a giving night. I don't know what to do. I've always known.

crisis.narrate: On the benches the grieving have begun to stand up, one by one, and walk towards the door with their arms held out, the way people walk to the giving. Madder is first.

oneOf.text: It is taking all of it. Not what they came to give. All of it.
They'll give everything. Not the grief. All of it. It's taking whatever is held out.

peaceful.label: Read the names aloud, every name said, so that the room holds them

success.narrate: {You know|@ knows} from the house-book whose names are in the room tonight, every one, and {you start|@ starts} with the oldest.
The lamps along the low place by the mill-race hold the white back from the yard for as long as it takes to get up onto the end bench.
{You get|@ gets} up onto the end bench with the white already in the doorway.

{You read|@ reads} the names aloud off the grieving's own arms, one at a time: the name, and the day, and then one true thing about them, whatever the one who wrote it can remember. After each name {you wait|@ waits}, and somebody in the room says it back.
Maren takes the other end of the room and does the same, Anwen's way, and nobody on her benches gets up.

Madder stops on the step with her arm held out, and looks at it, and says: 'Comfrey. He was eleven. He could whistle with two fingers. He taught the dog to come to it.' Then she sits down on the step, and does not go out.
The white comes to the door and stops there. It lies in the yard all night, as high as the sill, and takes nothing from a room where every name has been said.

success.text: Thirty years I've kept this house. I've never seen it stop at a door.

failure.narrate: {You read|@ reads} the names aloud from the end bench, but the room is standing and moving and nobody hears them over the cold, and Madder is through the door, and in the yard the white is standing up into shapes.

objective.name: Yarrow's door
objective.label: Hold Yarrow's door until the surge passes, and keep the grieving inside
objective.description: Four successful actions hold the house's door against the white's shapes and keep the grieving from walking out into it.
objective.failText: The door holds in the end, but six of the grieving walked out into the yard before it did. They come back in at dawn on their own, and sit down on the benches, and do not know why they came to Greve. Yarrow writes them in the house-book: gave everything.
objective.successText: The door is held, and the surge goes on down the valley, and nobody in the house walked out into it.

oneOf.narrate: Dawn at Greve. The white has gone back down the valley without its giving. The grieving are asleep on the benches, still holding their own arms.
Dawn at Greve. The yard is trampled to the stones, and the white has gone on down the valley. Yarrow is going along the benches with tea, and the grieving are holding their own arms.

oneOf.text: Nobody gave last night. Not one of them. They'll give at the next, or go home with it. I don't know which is kinder. I used to know.
Nobody gave what they came to give last night. They'll give at the next, or go home with it. I don't know which is kinder. I used to know.

oneOf.narrate: Madder is at the fire with the house-book open on her knee, writing under her son's name, in her own hand, the thing about the whistle.
Madder is at the fire with the house-book open on her knee, writing under her son's name, in her own hand, one true thing about him: that he could whistle with two fingers.

after.text: You came in at my door and changed my house in a night. So tell me what to do with it. I'll listen. I don't promise more.

decisions.label: Teach Greve to keep its names, and the grief with them
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Yarrow's house stops taking griefs. The grieving keep their dead, and their grief, and their anger with them.

told.ballad: At Greve the strangers said, keep them, and the grieving went home with their dead, and with the grief, and with the anger.
told.tally: Greve. The southerners said: keep the names. Yarrow put her censer on the shelf. Written: the grieving went home angry, and two went down to the Reckoner's table.

text.narrate: You tell Yarrow to stop taking griefs. To keep the names, and say them, and let the grief come home with them.

text.text: They'll be angry. Grieving people are. They'll be angry at the white, and at whoever sends it, and they'll know who that is, because you'll have told them.

oneOf.text: Let them be angry. They'll be angry with their sons' names in their mouths. That's better than calm with nothing.

oneOf.narrate: You tell her that angry with a name is better than calm with nothing.

text.narrate: Yarrow puts the censer on the shelf over the fire, and does not light it. That afternoon the grieving go home with their names and their griefs, and something hard in their faces that was not there yesterday. Two of them go down the valley road to Orme instead, to the Reckoner's table.

decisions.label: Write the names in the tally, and let the griefs go
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Every name goes to Orme, to be written in the Long Tally for the first time. The griefs go to the white at the next giving, as they always have.

told.ballad: At Greve the strangers said, write the names, and give the grief, and the Long Tally opened its first page of names in nine hundred years.
told.tally: Greve. The southerners said: write the names, then give. Written in the Long Tally, a new page: names, for the first time. Comfrey of Greve, eleven, who could whistle with two fingers.

text.narrate: You tell Yarrow to give the griefs, as her house always has, but to write the names first: every name, and the day, and one true thing. And to send them to Orme.

Madder carries them herself, down the valley to Orme, forty slates in a basket, and puts them on Burdock's desk. Burdock reads the first one aloud: 'Comfrey of Greve, eleven. He could whistle with two fingers.' Then he takes down a new book and opens it at the first page.

text.text: Names. Nine hundred years and nobody has sent me names. I shall need more ink.

oneOf.text: I don't need to hear them to believe them. I never did. I just didn't know it.

oneOf.narrate: The first page of names in the Long Tally is in Burdock's square hand, forty lines long, and every line has one true thing on it.

decisions.label: Leave Greve's custom as it is
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Yarrow's house goes on as it has for three hundred years. At the next giving, the grieving give.

told.ballad: At Greve the strangers said, it is your house, and the grieving gave at the next giving, as they always had.
told.tally: Greve. The southerners said the house was Yarrow's. Written: at the next giving, the grieving gave.

text.narrate: You tell Yarrow it is her house, and her people's custom, and three hundred years of it, and that you came here as guests.

text.text: Thank you. I didn't want to be told I was wrong. I'd have listened, mind.

oneOf.text: It's their grief. I know it is. I'd have liked them to keep the names.

oneOf.narrate: The house-book goes back on its shelf by the fire.

text.narrate: Madder will give at the next giving. She says so, and rolls her sleeve down, and goes to help with the bread.

b4-thrum.name: Rue's Mother
b4-thrum.region: Thrum, three days down the long valley east of Orme, and the lane of twelve doors where Rue was born
b4-thrum.threat: The white comes up Thrum's lane past the fourth door, and Rue will not leave her mother's step.
b4-thrum.brief: Rue comes home to Thrum after a spring, a summer and an autumn away. Her mother, Heath, gave her grief for a lost daughter to the white at Greve, and does not know her. The lines about Rue on Heath's door have been scrubbed off.

told.ballad: Rue of Thrum came home over the peaks and down the long valley, and her mother opened the door to her, kindly, as to a stranger.
told.tally: Thrum. Rue of Thrum came home, who went south to ask. Written: her mother did not know her.

opening.narrate: Thrum is a lane of twelve doors at the end of the long valley, three days east of Orme. Most winters the white lies in the lane as far as the third door. This winter it is already at the third, and it is early yet.
Rue walks up the lane in front of you, reading the doors aloud, the way she has read every door since Lantry. At the seventh she stops.
It is her mother's door. Heath's name is on it, and today's weather, and the bread. Halfway down, where Rue's lines were, the wood has been scrubbed pale, and nothing has been written over it.
Heath opens the door before Rue can knock: a thin, tidy woman with flour to the elbow. She looks at Rue the way you look at a stranger on your step, kindly, and waiting to be told.

opening.text: Yes? You'll be the southerners. The carter said there were southerners on the road. Come in, there's bread. Who's this, your guide?

oneOf.narrate: Rue does not say anything. She pushes back her left sleeve, without looking down, as if to be sure the word is still there: 'Heath'.
Rue does not say anything. She has her book open in both hands at the first page, the new one, with today first.
Rue does not say anything. She has her book open in both hands at the oldest page, where her mother's name is, in the first hand she ever wrote.

talks.label: Sit with Rue on the wall at the end of the lane

lines.text: She gave me. At Greve, I think, in the spring, after I went. She will have read her door every morning, 'Rue, my daughter, went south', and every morning it happened to her again, and she could not make the bread.

oneOf.text: I have one word of her. On my arm. I wrote it at Highpass, after the fire, because it was the only thing I knew was mine. I do not know what she was like. I know her name. That is what she has of me now. We are even.
My book starts with today now, and with who sat with me. Everything about my mother is further in, behind it. I could read it to her. I do not know if she would want to hear it from a stranger.

I have all of it. Every page. Her bread, her hands, the winter the lane went under to the fourth door and she carried me up it on her back. I could read it to her. It would be like reading her a story about somebody else's girl.

lines.text: I do not know what I want. That is not in my book either.

talks.label: Talk to Heath at her table

lines.text: Sit down. Eat. You've come a long way, the carter said. Over the peaks. Nobody does that.

I gave something at Greve, in the spring. I don't know what. Yarrow writes it down, but she doesn't tell you unless you ask, and I didn't ask. I came home and made the bread. I've made it every day since. Before that I couldn't. That's all I know.

lines.narrate: She looks across the table at Rue, kindly, the way she looks at all of you.

lines.text: You've a look of somebody. I can't think who.

talks.label: Talk to the boy who writes Heath's door

lines.narrate: Furze is ten, with chalk on both hands to the wrist. He writes his mother's door every morning, because her hand shakes in the cold.

lines.text: I scrubbed it. Mother said to. After Greve. She said there was a line on it she didn't know, and a door's not for things you don't know.
I didn't know it either. I can read, though. It said 'Rue'. Is that her?
Yes.
Oh. Hello.

talks.label: Ask Nessa what she thinks Rue should do

lines.text: I was the kid somebody went back for. Wren came and got me, and then she was stuck with me. I used to think she'd have been better off leaving me.
I asked her once. She said no. Just no, and went back to the lamp. That's Wren.

oneOf.text: I gave one thing about her, in the deep. I don't know what. There's a gap where it goes. I'd have it back tomorrow if I could. Every day I would.
I kept all of it. Everything. The bad nights too. Some nights I'd give the lot. I never have.

lines.text: I'm not going first on this one. It's hers. I'm just going to sit there.

talks.label: Talk to Davin on Heath's step

lines.narrate: Davin is up on Heath's step, trimming the lamp over the door.

lines.text: She lights it every night. I asked her what for. She said she doesn't know. She just does.
In Saltwick we put a lamp in the window for whoever's out. You light it whether they're coming back or not. You don't stop.

b4-thrum.clue: Under the new chalk on Heath's door the old chalk still shows. Heath kept one line: 'Leave the lamp.'

investigate.label: Read Heath's door in the low sun, under the new chalk

success.narrate: {You stand|@ stands} at Heath's door with the sun low across the lane, so that the old chalk shows up through the scrubbing like frost on a window, and {read|reads} what was there.
Most of it is gone. One line is not. It has been gone over every morning in a hand that shakes, over and over, so that the scrubbing never took it: 'Leave the lamp.'

failure.narrate: {You stand|@ stands} at Heath's door with the sun going, but the scrubbing has taken it down to the wood, and in the dusk {you cannot|@ cannot} tell the old chalk from the new.

route.label: Find where the white comes into the lane

success.narrate: {You walk|@ walks} the end of the lane at dusk and {find|finds} the gap in the field wall below the first door, where the white comes in first, with the frost already grey on the stones.

failure.narrate: {You go|@ goes} out below the first door at dusk, and the white is over the field wall before {you are|@ is} back, and {you come|@ comes} up the lane cold to the bone.

direct.label: Go down the long valley to Thrum
direct.text: You go east down the long valley from Orme to Thrum, three days, and come into Rue's lane at noon.

approach.narrate: Dusk in Thrum. The lane gathers at its top end, the way it does when the white is coming, with its giving in its hands: a smell, a tune, the colour of a coat.
Heath's lamp is lit over her door.

crisis.narrate: The white comes up the lane past the first door and the second, faster than it should, and past the third, and the fourth, and goes on coming.

Thrum goes up the lane in front of it with the children carried. Heath goes with them, with Furze by the hand. Rue does not. She is standing on her mother's step with her back to the door and her book in both hands, and she will not move.

crisis.text: If it takes this door, it takes the last of me in this town. I am not leaving it.

oneOf.text: Rue. Rue, come on. Rue.

oneOf.narrate: Nobody can make her move.

peaceful.label: Hold the lane at Heath's door with Thrum's giving, and stay with Rue

success.narrate: {You know|@ knows} the line under the chalk, and {you take|@ takes} Heath's lamp down off its hook and {set|sets} it in the middle of the lane, lit.
{You know|@ knows} where the white comes in over the field wall, and Thrum's givers go down to meet it there first, with their giving held out.
Thrum's givers go down the lane in front of the white with their giving held out, as far as they dare.
Nessa does not go first. She sits down on the step beside Rue, with her shoulder against Rue's, and stays there.
{You stand|@ stands} in the lane between the givers and Heath's door and {call|calls} them on, one door at a time, until there is a giver on every step from the fourth door to the seventh.
The white comes up to the fourth door and is given to, and to the fifth, and the sixth. At the seventh it stops, a hand's breadth from Heath's step, and lies down in the lane.
By morning it has gone back to the third door, where it lies most winters.

failure.narrate: {You call|@ calls} the givers down the lane, but the white is past the fourth door before they reach it, and the givers break and run, and in the lane the white stands up into shapes and comes on towards Heath's step.

objective.name: Heath's step
objective.label: Hold the lane at Heath's step until the white goes back
objective.description: Four successful actions keep the white's shapes off Heath's step, where Rue will not move.
objective.failText: The step is held in the end, but the white was in at the door first, for a moment, and Heath's kitchen is as cold as the lane, with frost on the bread.
objective.successText: The step is held, and the white goes back down the lane to the third door, and nothing in Heath's house is touched.

oneOf.narrate: Morning in Thrum. The white is back at the third door, where it lies most winters. Rue is still on her mother's step, asleep sitting up, with her book on her knees.

Morning in Thrum. The lane is trampled to the stones from the fourth door to the seventh, and the white is back at the third. Rue is on her mother's step, asleep sitting up, with her book on her knees.

after.narrate: Heath opens the door, and finds a stranger asleep on her step, and puts a blanket round her without waking her, and goes in to make the bread.
When Rue wakes she reads the blanket, which has nothing written on it, for a long time. Then she looks at you.

after.text: Tell me what to do. I have never asked anybody that. I would like it written that I asked.

decisions.label: Tell Rue to give her memory of her mother, so that it stops hurting
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. At Thrum's giving, Rue gives what she remembers of Heath. She will still have it written. She will not mind.

told.ballad: Rue of Thrum gave her mother to the white, as her mother had given her, and they sat at the one table as two kind strangers.
told.tally: Thrum. Rue of Thrum gave at the third door what she had of her mother. Written: she ate the bread, and said it was good bread.

text.narrate: You tell her to give it. Not her mother: her mother will still be written, on the door, if Furze writes it. Only what it does to her.

text.text: Yes. That is what she did. Then we will be the same. Two strangers who are kind to each other at a table.

text.narrate: At the giving that night, at the third door, Rue holds out her hands and gives.

oneOf.narrate: In the morning she reads the word on her wrist at Heath's table, 'Heath', the way you would read the name of somebody you have heard of, and eats the bread, and says it is good bread.
In the morning she reads the page with her mother on it at Heath's table, the way you would read about somebody else's mother, and eats the bread, and says it is good bread.

text.text: That's all right. It is. It's hers.

decisions.label: Tell her to keep it, and start again with her mother as a stranger
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Rue keeps what she remembers, and the hurt with it. She writes herself onto her mother's door again, as a stranger, and starts again.

told.ballad: Rue of Thrum kept her mother, and wrote herself on her mother's door as a stranger, and was asked in to the bread.
told.tally: Thrum. Rue of Thrum kept what she had of her mother. Written on Heath's door: a stranger, who brought the southerners, who would like to come to the bread.

text.narrate: You tell her to keep it. All of it, and the hurt with it, and to start again from the door.

Rue takes Furze's chalk. She stands at her mother's door with it for a long time, and then writes, small, under the scrubbed place: 'Rue of Thrum. A stranger. She brought the southerners. She would like to come to the bread.'
Nessa takes the chalk off her and writes the next line, in capitals, under Rue's: 'SHE IS MY FRIEND. NESSA.' It is the first thing Nessa has ever written on a door.
In the morning Furze reads the door to his mother, aloud, as he does every morning. Heath listens to the new lines, and goes to the step, and asks the stranger in.

decisions.label: Ask Nessa to answer her
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Nessa answers Rue from her own past, and Rue does as she says.

told.ballad: Rue of Thrum asked the girl from Cinder Fold, who was the one somebody went back for, and did as she said.
told.tally: Thrum. Rue of Thrum asked Nessa of Cinder Fold what to do with her mother, and did what Nessa said. Written: it was Nessa's to say.

text.text: Me? Why me?
Because you were the one somebody went back for.

oneOf.text: Keep it. I gave one of mine, in the deep, a thing about Wren, and I'd have it back tomorrow. Keep it. Every bit.
It's yours. I kept all of mine, and some nights I'd give anything. Give it. I'd not blame you. Nobody would.

oneOf.narrate: Rue takes Furze's chalk and writes, under the scrubbed place on her mother's door: 'Rue of Thrum. A stranger. She would like to come to the bread.' Nessa writes the next line under it in capitals: 'SHE IS MY FRIEND. NESSA.' It is the first thing Nessa has ever written on a door.
At the giving that night, at the third door, Rue holds out her hands and gives, and Nessa stands next to her the whole time, and holds the book.

b4-reckoning.name: The Reckoner's Sum
b4-reckoning.region: Orme's Long Hall, with the tally towns come in to vote by their door-boards
b4-reckoning.threat: The Reckoner means to ring the Parting Bell backward at midwinter, and the tally towns are come to Orme to vote on it.
b4-reckoning.brief: Sloe has called the tally towns to Orme. She has read the Parting Bell's line, and done her sum: share the winter with us, or at midwinter she rings the Parting Bell backward, and every bell in the bell-country goes quiet for one winter. Whoever rings it forgets everything. She will.

told.ballad: In the Long Hall the Reckoner did her sum before all the towns of the Wold, and it came out right, and the strangers from the south had to answer it.
told.tally: Orme, the Long Hall. The tally towns came in with their door-boards. The Reckoner read her sum. Written: it was right.

opening.narrate: The Long Hall is full of doors. Every tally town has carried one in on a cart, its own door-board, written over with its name and its winters: Lantry's, and Greve's, and Thrum's, and Dunnet's and Wem's, and forty more, stood up along the oldest wall like people waiting to be written.
Sloe stands in front of them at her table, with one slate. She has finished her sum.

oneOf.text: The line on the Parting Bell: 'Rung once, to part. Ring it again and all will answer.' The founders cut it round the bell's shoulder. Our side of the Hall has it too, worn almost smooth, on the stone under our nine. Rue copied it for me off the stone. And in the first snow, somebody rang it, and I heard every bell in the south answer it, from here.

The line on the Parting Bell: 'Rung once, to part. Ring it again and all will answer.' The founders cut it round the bell's shoulder. Our side of the Hall has it too, worn almost smooth, on the stone under our nine. Rue copied it for me off the stone.

opening.text: Rung forward, the founders' way, it rings the white north, all of it, every bell at once. Rung backward, it is the other note. Every bell answers it, and goes quiet. For one winter, every bell in the bell-country is a pot. And the white lies where it falls.
Whoever rings it forgets everything. Everything, not a season. I have done that sum too. I will ring it. At midwinter, unless the south shares the winter with us. That is my sum. It is right.

talks.label: Ask Sloe what share of the winter she means

lines.text: Half. Not all. I am not asking the south to take our winters. I am asking it to stop sending us its own. Ring your bells half the nights. Let the white lie where it falls the other half. Be cold. Give. Write it down. We will show you how.

oneOf.text: Burdock wrote what you told him. All of it: the bells, the great note, the nine. Every town in this hall has read it. That is why they came. That is also why they will listen to you.
Burdock wrote your reasons beside it. Both columns. Every town in this hall has read both. Some of them have read the second column twice. It does not change the sum. It changes who is in the hall.
You asked us to wait. The towns have read that too. 'The south: not yet.' I wrote under it. They have read what I wrote under it.
And Greve's grieving came to my table with their sons' names, angry. I did not ask them to. They are the first in nine hundred years to know what they are angry about.
And Burdock has a page of names now, from Greve. I have read it. I did not know you could feel a sum.

lines.text: I am not angry. I want it written that I was not angry.

talks.label: Ask Burdock what the tally says about a vote

lines.text: A vote is a door-board, laid down. Each town lays its door face up for yes, face down for no, in front of the Reckoner. Then I write which. I have never written one. The tally has eleven. The last was two hundred years ago.
I do not know what they were about. I have read them every morning. I believe they were very important.

oneOf.text: I have Greve's names on a new page. Forty. I read them every morning now, before the winters. It takes longer. I do not mind.
I would like it to be a short vote. I have a great deal to write today.

talks.label: Listen to Dunnet's and Wem's door-bearers quarrelling

lines.narrate: Dunnet's and Wem's door-boards stand next to each other at the end of the row, because the carts came in together, and their bearers have been arguing since dawn.

lines.text: Dunnet rings a pot. Every night. And every night the white comes down on Wem, a mile down the valley, and lies in our street to the eaves.
We ring it so it doesn't come down on Dunnet. It worked. It's in the tally. Dunnet: lost none, since the pot. First time in the tally.
And under it, Wem: lost seven. Read the whole line.
They are both right. That is the sum. That is Sloe's whole sum, a mile wide.

talks.label: Ask Hesk what a casting does

lines.text: She's right. I've told her she's right. A casting is a note you make the metal remember. The founders made every bell in the south remember one note, the parting note, and ring the white away from it.

Ring the Parting Bell the wrong way and every bell remembers the other note at once. They'll ring like pots for a winter. Then they'll remember the right one again. One winter. She's done the sum. I checked it.
I'm going south with her, when she goes. Somebody has to tell the council it's right, in a voice they'll listen to. They never listened to mine either. They'll listen to the sum.

talks.label: Ask Rue what she thinks of the sum

lines.text: She sent me south to find out who sends the white. I found out. Now she has the answer, and she is doing exactly what I would do with it, and I would like her to stop.

oneOf.text: I kept my mother. It hurts every morning. Sloe will not have a morning after midwinter. She will not have a mother either, or a name. I would not wish that on anyone. She is wishing it on herself, carefully.
I gave my mother. It does not hurt. Sloe will give everything at once, and nothing will hurt her ever again. I know what that is like now. It is not nothing. It is not enough.

b4-reckoning.clue: The note is real. Rung backward, the Parting Bell's other note silences every bell that answers it for one winter, and the ringer forgets everything. Sloe has it right.

investigate.label: Check the Reckoner's sum against the oldest wall and the bell's line

success.narrate: {You take|@ takes} Sloe's slate to the oldest wall and {check|checks} it line by line against the tally, and against the bell's line as Rue copied it, and against what the founders' page said about casting the nine.

It comes out the same every way. There is another note. Rung backward, the Parting Bell would make every bell that answers it a pot for one winter. Whoever rings it gives everything at once, not a season. Sloe has made no mistake.

failure.narrate: {You take|@ takes} Sloe's slate to the oldest wall, but the sum runs back nine hundred years in four hands, and {you cannot|@ cannot} find the place where it could be wrong. That is not the same as knowing it is right.

route.label: Find out which door-boards will lie face up before the vote

success.narrate: {You go|@ goes} along the row of door-boards through the morning and {talk|talks} to every bearer, and by noon {you know|@ knows} which towns have come to vote for the sum and which have come to be told something else first.

failure.narrate: {You go|@ goes} along the row of door-boards, but every bearer says what their door says, and their door says their winters, and by noon {you know|@ knows} no more than {they} did at dawn.

direct.label: Go to the Long Hall for the vote
direct.text: You go up through Orme to the Long Hall at dusk, for the vote.

approach.narrate: At dusk Burdock rings the vote three times. The vote is a small brass hand-bell that came over the old road from the south two hundred years ago, with somebody nobody remembers, and the Long Hall has kept it on the desk ever since, for calling votes, because nobody knew what else it was for. Nobody in Orme calls it a bell. The bearers stand by their door-boards along the oldest wall.
Sloe reads her sum aloud, once, from the slate. It takes four minutes.

crisis.narrate: Then the door-boards begin to come down, one at a time, in front of Sloe's table: Thrum's face up, and Greve's, and Lantry's, and the next, and the next.

crisis.text: Every door that lies face up says: send the sum south as the Wold's, and if the south will not share, I ring the bell at midwinter. Every door that lies face down says: wait.

crisis.narrate: The tally-guard stand along the walls in their grey coats with their spears wrapped and their slates under their arms. If the vote is Sloe's, they will hold the southerners in the Hall until midwinter, as surety for the answer.

crisis.text: Count them. We've a dozen doors to turn, maybe less. Say it now, whatever you're going to say.

peaceful.label: Ask the door-boards to wait for the free wards' own answer

easierWith.reason: Burdock wrote the truth about the south into the tally, and every town has read it

harderWith.reason: The towns have read 'The south: not yet', or Greve's grieving are in the Hall, angry

success.narrate: {You know|@ knows} that the sum is right, and {you say|@ says} so first, to the whole Hall, before anything else.
{You know|@ knows} which bearers came to be told something first, and {you go|@ goes} to those doors.
{You stand|@ stands} in front of Sloe's table, between her and the door-boards still standing, and {speak|speaks} to the Hall.

{You tell|@ tells} them that the free wards have never been asked. That the council at Highpass has never heard the sum, and that a sum nobody has been told cannot be answered. That if the Wold waits until midwinter for the south's own word, it will have lost nothing it has not lost already, and Sloe will still have her bell.
Dunnet's door-bearer turns Dunnet's door face down, because Wem's has just gone face up. Then Wem's bearer turns Wem's over, because Dunnet's did. Then Greve's. Then, one at a time, the rest.

success.text: Face down. Then the Wold waits for the south's answer until midwinter. I will be at the bell at midwinter whatever it is. Burdock, write that the vote was against me, and that I asked for it.
Written. Against. Asked for. It is the first vote in the tally where I know what it was about.

failure.narrate: {You speak|@ speaks} to the Hall in front of Sloe's table, but the door-boards keep coming down face up while {you speak|@ speaks}, Wem's and then Dunnet's to spite it, and when the last is down the tally-guard unwrap their spears and come off the walls to close the doors.

objective.name: Burdock's desk
objective.label: Get to Burdock's desk and have the vote written as it fell, before the guard close the Hall
objective.description: Four successful actions get the party through the tally-guard to Burdock's desk, so that the vote is written as it fell and nobody is held.
objective.failText: You reach Burdock's desk in the end, but three door-boards were knocked over in the fight, and nobody can say now which way they fell, and Burdock writes them as fallen.
objective.successText: You are at Burdock's desk, and he has the vote written as it fell, and the tally-guard have stopped at the edge of the lamplight.

oneOf.narrate: Midnight in the Long Hall. The door-boards lie where they fell, face down, along the oldest wall. Nobody has been held, and nobody is hurt.

Midnight in the Long Hall. The door-boards lie where they fell, face up, along the oldest wall, and the tally-guard sit under them with the clerks bandaging their hands. Nobody is held. Sloe told them to stop, in the end. Her sum stands.

after.narrate: Sloe sits at her table with her one slate in front of her and her hands flat either side of it.

after.text: So. You have to answer it. Not the council: you. You are the south that came. What do you do with my sum?

decisions.label: Carry her demand south as hers, word for word
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. You carry the Reckoner's sum south to the council at Highpass, in her words, and promise nothing yourself.

told.ballad: The strangers took the Reckoner's sum on a slate, in her own hand, to carry over the peaks, and promised nothing but to carry it.
told.tally: Orme. The southerners took the Reckoner's sum to carry south, in her hand. Written: they promised to carry it, and nothing else.

text.narrate: You tell her you will carry it. Her sum, in her hand, to the council at Highpass, every word, and that you will promise nothing about the answer, because the answer is not yours.

text.text: Good. That is honest. I can do a sum with honest.

text.narrate: She copies the sum onto a clean slate, in her square small hand, and signs it at the bottom with her name and her town, and gives it to you, and Burdock writes that she did.

text.text: That's a load I know how to carry. Somebody else's words, all the way, and set them down where they're meant.

decisions.label: Promise the Wold a share of the winter, under the council's seal
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. You promise the Wold half the winter, in the council's name, with the council's seal on a cord round your neck.

told.ballad: The strangers promised the Wold half the winter, with the council's seal, and the Reckoner wrote it down, and waited to see.
told.tally: Orme. The southerners promised half the winter, under their council's seal. Written: we will see.

text.narrate: You take the council's seal off its cord and press it into the wax at the foot of Sloe's slate, under a line in your own hand: the free wards will share the winter, half the nights.
You can hear Iona as if she were in the Hall: whatever you promise with that, I pay for.

text.text: That is the council's seal. Then it is the council's promise, and I will hold the council to it. Burdock, write that the south promised, sealed.
Written. Sealed. I have never written that before either.

decisions.label: Promise the Wold a share of the winter, on your own word
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. You promise the Wold half the winter, on your own word, for a council that has not said it will.

told.ballad: The strangers promised the Wold half the winter, on their own word, for a south that had not said it would.
told.tally: Orme. A southerner promised half the winter, on their own word. Written: their council has not.

text.narrate: You write it at the foot of Sloe's slate, in your own hand: the free wards will share the winter, half the nights. Then you press the seal on your cord into the wax under it.

oneOf.narrate: It has only the free wards' bell on it. It is yours, not the council's, and everybody in the Hall can see that it is.
It has the free wards' bell on it, with an open door under the bell. Iona costed that door at ten thousand. Nobody costed this.
It is your own seal, not the council's, and everybody in the Hall can see that it is.

text.text: That is your word. I believe it. I do not believe the south will keep it, and neither do you. Burdock, write that the south promised, and who.
That's a promise nobody can keep yet. Not you. Not the council. I've carried a few of those. They get heavier.

decisions.label: Ask Sloe to come south and make her demand herself
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. When you go south over the peaks, the Reckoner comes with you, to put her sum to the council herself.

told.ballad: The strangers asked the Reckoner to come south and ask the south herself, and she put her slate under her arm and said she would.
told.tally: Orme. The southerners asked the Reckoner to come south and say her sum herself. Written: she will go.

text.narrate: You tell her that you can carry a slate, but the council at Highpass has never heard anybody from the Wold say anything, and it should hear this from her.

text.text: Over the peaks. In winter. To a hall of people who ring bells.

text.narrate: She thinks about it for as long as it takes her to do a sum, and then puts the slate under her arm.

text.text: Burdock. Write that the Reckoner will go south to ask, as Rue did, when the southerners go. I will wait for them at the Hall.
Then I will read the doors to her, all the way down.

b4-potbells.name: The Bells of Dunnet
b4-potbells.region: Dunnet and Wem, two villages a mile apart a day down the valley road from Orme, and the boundary stones between them
b4-potbells.threat: Dunnet rings a bell it cast from pots and nails, and the white it rings away falls on Wem. The two villages are at the boundary stones with axes.
b4-potbells.brief: Dunnet has cast a bell from its pots and nails, and rings it every night. The white it rings away comes down on Wem, a mile down the valley. The two villages are at the boundary stones with axes.

told.ballad: At Dunnet they cast a bell out of their own pots, and rang it, and the white went down the valley onto Wem, and the strangers from the south knew that sum by heart.
told.tally: Dunnet and Wem. Dunnet rang a pot-bell, and the white fell on Wem. The southerners came to the boundary stones.

opening.narrate: Dunnet is thirty doors on a shelf above the valley road, a day down the valley from Orme. In the middle of its street there is a frame of green timber, and in the frame there is a bell: lumpy, dark, the size of a water-butt, with the handle of a pan still sticking out of its shoulder where it did not melt.

A mile below, at the foot of the shelf, Wem is under the white to the eaves. Its people are standing in the snow at the boundary stones between the two villages, with axes, and Dunnet's are standing on the other side of the stones with axes, and nobody has swung one yet.

oneOf.narrate: Dunnet learned it from a southern man with a lamp, who came up the valley road in the spring and told them what bells are for. They listened very carefully.

Dunnet learned it from the Company. Forty wagons came down the valley road in the summer, asking the way to the empty land, with a bell on wagon one to keep the white off the road. They camped a night in Dunnet's street and rang it. Dunnet watched the white go.

Dunnet learned it from Lantry. The carters brought the news up the valley: the southerners rang Lantry's pots in the street, and the white went off Lantry onto Sheddon. Dunnet thought about it, and then melted down its pots.
Dunnet learned it from the tally. Sloe read the bell-country's line aloud in the Long Hall, and Dunnet's door-bearer listened, and went home, and melted down every pot in the village.

talks.label: Talk to the girl who rings the pot-bell

lines.narrate: Campion of Dunnet is fifteen, with burnt hands and her hair tied back with string. She rings the bell at dusk every night, forty strokes, and she has rung it every night since it was cast.

lines.text: We melted down every pot we had. Every nail. The smith's anvil-horn. My mother's good pan, that's the handle there. It took a week to get it hot enough. I worked the bellows.
And it works. You ring it, and the white goes. Dunnet, lost none. That's in the tally now. First time ever.
Nobody said where it goes. I asked. Everybody said, away. Where's away?

talks.label: Go down to the stones and talk to Wem's elder

lines.text: Every night at dusk we hear it, up there. Forty strokes. And every night the white comes down the shelf and lies in our street. Seven of ours are gone since that bell was hung. Seven. Before that bell, the worst winter in the tally was three.
Vetch's house went down to give in the summer, at the floor, and never came back up. We have him on the stones. Vetch, Clary, Burnet, gone to give.

lines.narrate: You know where they came up: in the casting hall at Cinder Fold, by the forge fire, under the free wards' bells.
