She does a sum. You can see her do it.

oneOf.text: Then the bell is in a town of rope families, in the south, and nobody in your council knows. My ringers are on this road. I could take them there. I am not going to.
Then the bell is in a town of rope families, in the south, and nobody in your council knows. I could send to the Hall for my ringers. I am not going to.
Then the bell is in a town of rope families, in the south, and nobody in your council knows. I could send to Orme for my ringers. I am not going to.

text.text: You are going to bring it back. I am going to trust you to. In the Wold, when you trust somebody to do a thing, you write it on their door. I will not write on yours. You will know it is there.

b4-invoice.name: Nine Hundred Years, Itemised
b4-invoice.region: Highpass Watch: the council hall under the gatehouse, the gatehouse yard, and Iona's office
b4-invoice.threat: The council is hearing the Wold's winters read aloud, all nine hundred of them, and there are men in Highpass who would rather the free wards never heard them.
b4-invoice.brief: The council hears the Wold. Its winters are read into the free wards' minutes, the Reckoner puts her sum, and Quartermaster Iona stands up with an invoice. Before anybody goes home, the council has to be asked for something.

told.ballad: The council at Highpass heard nine hundred winters read, one line each, and Iona the quartermaster costed them, and the hero held the door while it was done.
told.tally: Highpass. The bell-country heard the tally read, every winter. Written: the south listened to the end.

opening.narrate: Two days after the white came over the upper gate, the council hears the Wold, in the hall under the gatehouse, with the doors open to the yard and the yard full.

oneOf.narrate: Elske has the chair, with the papers in four neat piles. She has had a stool put out for Sloe in front of the benches. Sloe has not sat on it.
Brannagh has the chair, because nobody else would take it. She has had a stool put out for Sloe in front of the benches. Sloe has not sat on it.
Outside, on the road below the lower watch and in the pass's lower fields, three thousand people are waiting on their ropes to hear what the hall decides about them.
Up in the Hall of Legends, three thousand people are waiting along the walls for Sloe to come back up with the answer.
Down in Orme, three thousand people are waiting for their envoys to come home.

Burdock has had the sledges of the Long Tally dragged up into the gatehouse yard, under Highpass's bell, with their hides off. He stands at the clerk's table with the book of winters open and reads it to the council: nine hundred winters, one line each, the first and then the next.
Burdock stands at the clerk's table with the book of winters open, and reads it to the council: nine hundred winters, one line each, the first and then the next.

Burdock is in Orme with the tally. Rue stands at the clerk's table with the copy of her old book that Sister Ilse made at Ashford, and reads the council the winters in it, in the founders' spellings, the first and then the next.
Burdock is in Orme with the tally. Rue stands at the clerk's table with her book open, and reads the council the winters in it, in the founders' spellings, the first and then the next.

opening.narrate: 'The year the bells went south, the white doubled.' Then the next winter. Then the next. It takes all morning, and the afternoon.

oneOf.narrate: The line for last winter is the one Burdock wrote at Orme about the south: what the bells do, and where the white goes, and that the free wards rang it. Nobody in the hall moves.

The line for last winter is the one Burdock wrote at Orme about the south, in two columns: what the bells do, and beside it why the free wards ring them, their children, their lanes, and that they did not know. Somebody on the benches starts to cry, and stops.
The line for last winter says only 'The south: not yet.' Under it, in Sloe's smaller and squarer hand: 'They asked us to wait. We have waited nine hundred years.'

oneOf.text: You have my sum. It was carried to you. I will say it myself, once. Ring your bells half the nights. Let the white lie where it falls the other half. Give. Or at midwinter the bell is rung the other way. I have not said by whom. That is not a threat. It is arithmetic.

I was promised half the winter by the one who stands at your door. I have come to hear whether the south keeps it. If it does not, at midwinter the bell is rung the other way. I have not said by whom. That is not a threat. It is arithmetic.

I said I would put my sum to you myself. Ring your bells half the nights. Let the white lie where it falls the other half. Give. Or at midwinter the bell is rung the other way. I have not said by whom. That is not a threat. It is arithmetic.

opening.narrate: Then Quartermaster Iona stands up at the end of the front bench, with a sheaf of paper ruled in columns, and reads it.

opening.text: An invoice. The Wold's winters, as they've been read to this hall. Against each one: the lives lost, at what this council pays a widow. The doors given up. The fields. The memories given at a door, at what it would cost to keep a clerk to write them down instead. What I could cost, I've costed. The rest has a column of its own.

opening.narrate: Nobody on the benches says anything. At the back of the hall a delegate from Fenmere stands up, and opens his mouth, and sits down again.

opening.text: I know what it sounds like. It's also an invoice. Somebody has to be sent it. I've made it out to us.

talks.label: Go down to Iona's office and look at the invoice

lines.narrate: Iona has the invoice on her desk in her office under the gatehouse, with the last page turned face down.

lines.text: I said it at the vote, to anybody who'd listen. The bill for nine hundred years of weather, and nobody had sent it. So I wrote it.
I can't pay it. Nobody can. That's not what an invoice is for. It's so that it's written, and has a name at the top, and the name is ours.

oneOf.text: And you promised them half the winter up there with the council's seal round your neck. I've a column for that too. It's the shortest. It's the dearest.
And you went up there with the council's seal round your neck. Whatever you said, we said. I've a column for that too. It's the shortest.
I costed the refuge at ten thousand. It's three thousand. I can count three thousand. I've started.
You went as yourself, so the council owes the Wold nothing in writing. I've put that on the invoice too. It's the only line with nothing in it.

lines.text: Burdock found me a winter that was forty for three hundred years and is fourteen now. I've costed fourteen, and put the other twenty-six in a column of their own. Somebody believed in them.
Burdock has a winter that says forty or fourteen. I've costed both. I'm not choosing.

talks.label: Ask Brannagh what the hall will do

lines.text: Fenmere's for whatever's decent. I'm Fenmere. I'd like it written down that I said so before it was popular. Again.
Sloe hasn't sat on that stool. It's been out for her two mornings. She stands, because in her country you stand at a door until somebody answers. I'm going to answer her if it kills me.
And whatever they ask us for, Iona will have costed it before they've finished asking. She's been doing that to me for years. I've stopped minding. Mostly.

talks.label: Hear what Elske has to say

oneOf.narrate: Elske comes down from the chair at the noon recess and talks to you on the hall steps, with her papers under her arm.
Elske has written from the Sallows hospice, which the council sentenced her to keep open. Iona reads you the letter on the hall steps.
Elske has written from the harbour hospice in Merrowgate, where she works. Iona reads you the letter on the hall steps.

oneOf.text: At Hollin's Reach I argued for waiting, and the town burned while I argued. I've known since that night what a slow council costs. I didn't know until this week who else had been paying for it.

oneOf.narrate: 'I rang the Mother Bell, and it saved us, and I never asked where the white went. Now I know. Whatever the council sends north, put my name first on it. Elske.'

talks.label: Find Hesk

oneOf.narrate: Hesk is in his cell under the gatehouse. He has heard the reading through the floor all day, and he has written the first winter on his wall in charcoal.
Hesk sits on the front bench in a good coat with the council's medal on it, which he wears as if it itches.
Hesk sits at the end of the Wold's bench, behind Sloe, with his lamp between his boots. The council has still not decided what he is, and has given him a bench while it decides.

oneOf.text: I bought every yes in my ring and never once costed the white. She has. I'd like to have been the one. I wasn't.
My ring held the towns in it this winter. Iona has my ring on her invoice, a line of its own. She was right to put it there.
My ring held this winter. The mildest in memory, they tell me, and they gave me a dinner. Iona has my ring on her invoice, a line of its own. She was right to put it there.
I went north with a lamp to see what I'd been sending them. I've seen it. They want to know what I am, in this hall. I'm the line on her invoice that walked.

talks.label: Look at Cinder Fold's empty chair

lines.narrate: Cinder Fold's chair is at the end of the front bench, under the window, with nobody in it.

oneOf.narrate: Since the cut rope went on the clerk's table, the whole hall looks at it when it thinks nobody is looking. The letter to Cinder Fold went down the road the morning after the white. There is no answer yet.
Sloe looks at it every time she comes into the hall. Nobody else does.
Nobody in the hall looks at it but you. The clerk has written 'kept at home by the thaw' in the minutes, and the council has moved on.

lines.text: In Orme, when a town is not at the vote, its door-board is carried in anyway and stood against the wall, so that the vote can see who is not there. You do not do that here. I think you should.

b4-invoice.clue: Where every town in the hall stands, and why: what each has heard of the founders, the letters from the floor and the embassy, what Briarwatch has learned of quiet nights, and what the hall knows about Cinder Fold.

investigate.label: Find out where each town stands, before anybody asks it for anything

success.narrate: {You go|@ goes} round the benches at the noon recess, and the inn, and the yard, and {ask|asks} every delegate who will talk what their town will vote for, and why.

oneOf.narrate: Briarwatch has kept one quiet night a month since last summer. Its delegate will vote to share, and says the Briarwood edge has learned what it costs, house by house, and can say so.
Briarwatch's delegate still has Pim's rule in her pocket, and his summer nights, one a month. She will vote to share, and to go slowly.
Briarwatch keeps its watch every night. Its delegate will vote for whatever is slowest, and says so, and is not ashamed of it.
Every town has had the founders' page off a door since last summer, and the towns are ahead of their delegates again.
The delegates had the founders' page first and sat on it, and their towns know they did. They will vote for something, to be seen to.
Cinder Fold heard the founders' page in Ailith's own voice. With Cinder Fold's chair empty, nobody knows how Cinder Fold would vote, and everybody guesses.
The towns that heard the letters from the floor read in their squares want to share. 'Tell us what we did' has been read in every square, and now somebody has.
Fennick's copies of the letters from the floor are on the clerk's table in a box. Three delegates have read them since the Wold came down, and two of those have changed their vote.
Some delegates are still angry that the first letter north was not the council's. They will vote to take the Wold in, so that the next thing sent north is.
The embassy went under the council's seal, and some delegates have worked out this week what that means: whatever was promised in the Wold, the council has promised.
The embassy carried an offer of refuge, and the hall voted for it in the autumn. The delegates who voted for it will vote to take the Wold in again.
The embassy went on its own word, and the council owes the Wold nothing in writing. Half the hall says so with relief, and the other half with shame.
And every delegate asks about the rope. Half of them want Cinder Fold made to answer before anything is voted; the other half want the vote taken without it, and quickly.
Nobody mentions Cinder Fold, except Sloe, who asks once, quietly, whether the promise at the end of the street still stands. It does.
Nobody mentions Cinder Fold at all.

failure.narrate: {You go|@ goes} round the benches at the noon recess, but every delegate says the same thing, that something will pass, and none of them will say what. By the night sitting all {you know|@ knows} is that somebody has been asking in the yard where the Wold's books are kept.

route.label: Sit in the inn yard at dusk, and find out who has been asking where the books are kept

success.narrate: {You sit|@ sits} in the inn yard at dusk with a cup, and {hear|hears} them: carters off the Highpass road, and townsmen, and four of the lower watch out of their coats, saying that the free wards' minutes are no place for nine hundred years of somebody else's winters, and that a thing nobody has read cannot be voted on. Sorrel lends {you|@} two of the watch she trusts, and the key to the hall's back stair.

failure.narrate: {You sit|@ sits} in the inn yard at dusk, but whoever was asking has stopped asking, and {you come|@ comes} back to the hall with nothing but the faces of the men who stopped talking when {you sat|@ sat} down.

direct.label: Go back to the hall for the night sitting
direct.text: You go back to the hall under the gatehouse for the night sitting, where the reading is to go on by lamplight until it is finished.

approach.narrate: The night sitting. The hall is lit with every lamp the gatehouse has, and the doors are open on the yard, and the reading goes on: the next winter, and the next, the year and the town and the count.
Somewhere past the middle of it, the yard goes quiet in the wrong way.

oneOf.narrate: Men come into the gatehouse yard out of the dark, twenty or so, carters and townsmen and some of the lower watch out of their coats, with cudgels, and put their shoulders to the Long Tally's sledges, and start to drag them out of the yard towards the road gate, hides and books and all.

Men come in at the hall doors out of the dark, twenty or so, carters and townsmen and some of the lower watch out of their coats, with cudgels, and come up between the benches for the clerk's table: for the book, and whoever is reading it, and the Wold's envoys on the bench beside it.

crisis.text: Nobody's going to get hurt. We're taking them up to the gate, that's all. The free wards don't have to sit and listen to this. It's not ours. We didn't do it.

oneOf.narrate: Burdock does not stop reading. He turns the page.
Rue does not stop reading. She turns the page.

crisis.text: In the Wold, nobody stops a reading. Not for weather. Not for anything.
They mean it. Every word. They think if nobody reads it out, it didn't happen. I can hear them believing it.

peaceful.label: Hold the hall door, and keep the reading going to the last winter

success.narrate: {You know|@ knows} which towns in this hall want the reading stopped and which want it finished, and {you say|@ says} so in the doorway, by name, so that every man with a cudgel knows whose town he is standing in front of.
Sorrel's two men are on the back stair already, and the back door is barred, and there is only the one way in.
{You get|@ gets} to the hall doors ahead of them, through the benches, as the first of them reach the steps.
{You go|@ goes} out into the yard and {stand|stands} on the first sledge, on the hide, and the men with their shoulders to it stop, because {you are|@ is} on it.

{You do|@ does} not shout. {You call|@ calls} each winter out after the reader, word for word, out into the yard, in a voice that carries: the year, and the town, and the count. 'Lantry. Lost: six.' 'Orme. Lost: eleven.' The next. The next.
To get past {them} the men have to hear it, and they stop to hear it, one at a time, the way people stop in a doorway in the rain. One of them sets his cudgel against the wall. Then the next.
It takes until the small hours. The last winter is read. Nobody has been carried anywhere.

failure.narrate: {You get|@ gets} to the doorway, but the first of the men are through it before {you are|@ is} set, and somebody on the benches shouts, and somebody in the yard swings a cudgel at the shout, and the hall comes up off its benches.

objective.name: The reading
objective.label: Keep the hall door until the last winter is read
objective.description: Four successful actions keep the men with cudgels off the tally and away from the Wold's bench until the reading is finished.
objective.failText: The reading is finished in the end, by lamplight, but the men had their hands on the book once before they were stopped, and one winter is torn through, and nobody can say which.
objective.successText: The last winter is read, in the small hours, to a hall that nobody has left.

oneOf.narrate: Morning. The cudgels are stacked against the hall wall where the men left them, and the men have gone home to bed, and the hall has not.

Morning. The watch has eight of the men from the yard in the cells under the gatehouse, with their heads bound, and the benches are back on their feet, and one of the clerks has a black eye he is proud of.

The council sits on into the morning with the reading done and Iona's invoice on the clerk's table, and nobody goes home. The cut rope is on the same table. Somebody in the south has the Parting Bell, and everybody in the hall knows it now.

The council sits on into the morning with the reading done and Iona's invoice on the clerk's table, and nobody goes home. Nobody in the hall but you, and Sloe, knows that the hook in the Hall is empty.

oneOf.text: So. You've been north, and you've brought the north back with you. Tell us what to ask for. We'll argue about it afterwards.
So. You've been north, and you've brought the north back with you. Tell us what to ask for. We'll argue about it afterwards. We always do.

decisions.label: Ask for a vote to share the winter, now
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. The council votes today on sharing the winter with the Wold: quiet nights by rota in every town that votes for it. The vote is counted town by town.

told.ballad: The council at Highpass voted to share the winter with the Wold, town by town, and the first shared night was set for midsummer.
told.tally: Highpass. The bell-country voted to take its share. Written: the towns, by name, and the night.

text.narrate: You ask for the vote, now, today, before anybody goes home to think about it: that the free wards share the winter with the Wold, quiet nights by rota in every town, and give, as the Wold gives.
Fenmere votes for it first, with Brannagh on her feet before the question is finished.

oneOf.narrate: Briarwatch votes for it, and its delegate reads the hall what quiet nights have cost the Briarwood edge, house by house, and votes for it anyway.
Briarwatch votes for it, slowly, because its delegate wants it written that the Briarwood edge was asked.
Ashford votes for it, and the Merrowgate dockers, and Saltwick, whose delegate says Mags Peller told her to.
Saltwick votes for it, because its delegate says Mags Peller told her to. Ashford's delegate votes against, and says Ashford has given enough for one year. Merrowgate's two delegates split.
Cinder Fold's chair is empty and its vote is not cast. The clerk writes 'absent' against it, and under it, at the chair's word, 'the rope'.
Cinder Fold's chair is empty and its vote is not cast.

text.narrate: It passes. Not by much. The first shared night is set for midsummer.

text.text: Midsummer. Then I will tell the Wold midsummer, and we will count the days. We are good at that.

decisions.label: Ask for a rota: each town chooses its own quiet nights
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Each town in the free wards chooses its own quiet nights, when it is ready, and says so in this hall. It is slower, and no town is made to.

told.ballad: The council at Highpass asked every town to choose its own quiet nights, and Briarwatch chose first.
told.tally: Highpass. The bell-country said: each town when it is ready. Written: four towns were ready.

text.narrate: You ask for a rota, not a vote: every town to choose its own quiet nights, and how many, and to say so in this hall when it is ready. Nobody made to. Nobody let off.

oneOf.narrate: Briarwatch's delegate stands up before you have sat down, and puts Briarwatch first. It has kept one quiet night a month since last summer; it will keep midsummer night as well, and the council can come and see what it costs.
Briarwatch's delegate stands up when nobody else will, and puts Briarwatch first, for midsummer night, and asks the council to come and see what it costs.

text.narrate: By the end of the day four towns have written a night against their names. The rest have written 'later'.

text.text: Slower. Cheaper this year. Dearer every year after it. I'll cost it.
Four. I will tell the Wold four. Four is a number. It is not nothing.

decisions.label: Ask the council to take the Wold in
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. The council votes to take in anyone from the Wold who wants to come south, shared out among the towns. Nobody votes to share the winter.

told.ballad: The council at Highpass voted to open the free wards to the Wold, a door in every town, and did not vote to share the winter.
told.tally: Highpass. The bell-country said: come south, all who want to. Written: the door, and not the winter.

text.narrate: You ask the council to take them in: anyone from the Wold who wants to come south, shared out among the towns, fed and housed for as long as it takes.

oneOf.narrate: It passes easily, because the hall voted it once already in the autumn, under the seal round your neck, and a vote is harder to take back than to make.
It passes by four votes. Iona votes for it, and then sits with her head in her hands.

text.text: Three thousand. I can count three thousand. It's the winter after this one I can't count.
You will take in the people. You will not take the winter. Some of us will come. I will not. Somebody has to stay and be the Wold.

b4-quietnight.name: The Quiet Night
b4-quietnight.region: Briarwatch at midsummer: the square, the bell tower, and the lanes down to the Briarwood edge
b4-quietnight.threat: On midsummer night Briarwatch will keep no watch on purpose, and the white will come up out of the Briarwood into lanes that have been emptied for it.
b4-quietnight.brief: Briarwatch keeps a quiet night at midsummer, and lets the white into its lanes on purpose. In the tower, somebody would like, for once, to be asked what Briarwatch's bell is for.

told.ballad: Briarwatch kept a quiet night at midsummer, and let the white lie in its lanes, and asked its own bell what it wanted, for the first time.
told.tally: Briarwatch. A town in the bell-country kept a night quiet on purpose. Written: the night, and the bell asked.

opening.narrate: Midsummer in Briarwatch. The hay is in on the near fields and half in on the far ones, and the square smells of it, and of Dera's forge, the way it did the summer Linus Pardew stood on the well and sang about you.

oneOf.narrate: Along the far fields by the Briarwood road there are tents: Wold families from Lantry and Orme, who came down from Highpass in the spring, a few to each town, helping with the hay because nobody told them not to. They have chalked their names on the tent-poles.
Two of the Wold's door-bearers have come down from Highpass with you, with their door-boards on their backs, to see a quiet night kept in the south and carry word of it back.
Tonight is midsummer night, the first night the council voted to share. In every town that voted for it, the watch will not ring tonight, and the white will go where it goes.
Tonight is midsummer night, and Briarwatch's: the first night on the council's rota, because Briarwatch asked to go first.

Tonight is midsummer night. The council voted to take the Wold in, and not to share its winter. Briarwatch is keeping the night quiet anyway, by its own vote at Aveline's table, to find out what it would have cost.
Briarwatch has kept a quiet night at the dark of the moon every month since last summer. This is the first one anybody outside Briarwatch has asked it to keep.
Briarwatch has kept Pim's summer nights, one a month, by his rule, since last summer. This one is not his. He says he does not mind.
Briarwatch has kept its watch every night since last summer, as it always has. Tonight will be its first quiet night on purpose.

opening.narrate: Over the peaks to the north, in the evenings, there is a white on the snow-line where there has never been a white in summer. Sorrel has written from Highpass that it lies on the north road above the last watch-fire every evening and goes back up at dawn, and the Wold's people at Highpass say it is Dunnet's: a pot-bell, rung every night in an empty valley. It is the first white anybody in the south has seen come from the north.
Linus Pardew is on the well again with his fiddle, and a new verse, which he says is about the Wold, and which he will not sing until tonight.

oneOf.narrate: Up in the tower Tovin rings the hour by hand with Pim, a breath behind him, on a bell that is bronze only.
Up in the tower Tovin rings the hour with Pim, a breath behind him, and inside the bell Aster Vey rings with them, a little late, as she always has.

talks.label: Climb the tower and speak to Aster in the bell

lines.narrate: In the bell-room, between the hours, Aster Vey's voice comes out of the bronze, quietly, so as not to carry down to the square.

lines.text: Every time I ring, I feel where it goes. I've felt it since last summer. North, over the peaks, the way water goes downhill. Now there are people from there in Briarwatch, and I can hear them talking at the well.

I'm not the only one in a bell. Everyone who was ever put in one, wherever they are. If anybody rings the bell from the Hall again, it moves all of us at once. Nobody has asked us. Nobody ever asks the bell.
Sable's in Highpass's bell, arguing with it. He'd want to be asked first, and he'd want it in writing.
Wren's in the tenth bell at Cinder Fold. Nobody has asked her anything since.

oneOf.text: And Hesk's ring, the ones who stayed in the circle. They're tired. I can hear it.
And Hesk's ring, all of them. They're tired. I can hear it.

lines.text: I'd like to be asked. Before midwinter. By somebody who'll listen to the answer.

talks.label: Climb the tower to Tovin

lines.narrate: Tovin is in the bell-room with the ropes tied off between the hours, on the bench under the window, where Pim sits when he is up here.

lines.text: Since she went, there's nobody in this bell but me on the end of a rope. If anybody's going to be asked what it wants, it'll have to be the keeper. So ask me. I've had a while to think.

oneOf.text: She's at rest. She went to rest from Vell's great bell at the end of the winter before last, and she's not coming back to answer anybody. I'll say it for her, since I'm asked: she'd have wanted to be asked. She always did.

She's in Vell's great bell. When I ring the hour, sometimes this one answers a breath late, from a long way off, and it's her. The bells are joined, under. You can ask her through it, if you're patient.

lines.text: If anybody rings the bell from the Hall again, every voice in a bell in the free wards moves. Nobody's asked them either.

talks.label: Find Pim

lines.narrate: Pim is in the square with a lantern, though it is not dark yet, helping Aveline count the houses on the Briarwood edge.

oneOf.text: I asked where away was. Now everybody knows. Some of them are in the far fields, making hay.
I asked where away was. Now everybody knows. Two of them are at the well.
We've done this every month since the song. It doesn't get easier. It gets known.
My rule was one summer night a month. Tonight isn't one of mine. I said I don't mind. I mind a bit.
We've never done it on purpose. Only the once, and that was me, and nobody asked me to.
Tonight nobody lights the fire at the stream. I'm going to sit by it and not light it. I've done that before. I'd like to do it right this time.
Tonight nobody rings. I'm going to sit with the rope in my lap and not ring it. I've done that before. I'd like to do it right this time.

talks.label: Go into the forge

oneOf.narrate: Dera has your gear on the bench, and shows you again, without being asked, which side of the fire is the hot side.
Dera has your gear on the bench before you have finished saying hello.

lines.text: Linus has a new verse. He sang it to me in the forge to see if I'd cross it out. I didn't. That's twice now. He's getting worse at lying.
And the Briarwood edge houses are up in the hall tonight, all of them, with their bedding. I've seen Briarwatch frightened before. I've not seen it frightened on purpose.

talks.label: Ask Linus Pardew about his new verse

lines.narrate: Linus Pardew is on the well step, tuning, with his writing case at his feet.

lines.text: I sang the first true verse here at midwinter. Nobody threw anything. Then they asked for the old one, with the sword of light, and I sang that too, and they sang it louder. I'm not proud.

oneOf.text: The new one's about three thousand people coming down a mountain on ropes. I wasn't there. I had it off a carter. I'm going to sing it anyway, and afterwards you can tell me what I got wrong.
The new one's about a hall on a mountain with a town in it, waiting. I wasn't there. I had it off a carter. I'm going to sing it anyway, and afterwards you can tell me what I got wrong.

The new one's about a country that went back down its mountain and sent its voices instead. I wasn't there. I had it off a carter. I'm going to sing it anyway, and afterwards you can tell me what I got wrong.
The third verse is still Dera's, the boy who asked where away is. They want it every night. He hates it.
The third verse is still Tovin's, with the end left off. Everybody still notices. That's still the point.
The third verse is still everybody's, forty lines, and it doesn't scan, and nobody will let me cut a line.

talks.label: Ask Reeve Aveline about the night

lines.text: I've a list. Every house on the Briarwood edge, and who's in it, and where they're sleeping tonight, which is my hall. I've never had a list for a night we chose before.
If it goes wrong, it's my list that was wrong. I'd like you on the edge tonight. Not because the song says you rang it away. Because you know what it does.

b4-quietnight.clue: Every bound voice in the free wards can hear the joined bells, and can be asked what it wants rung through it, before anybody rings the Parting Bell again.

investigate.label: Sit in the bell-room through the hour, and listen past the bell

success.narrate: {You sit|@ sits} in the bell-room through the hour, and {listen|listens} past the bronze, down into the ground, where the bells are joined.
{You sit|@ sits} in the bell-room through the hour with Tovin, and {listen|listens} past the bronze, down into the ground, where the bells are joined, the way Aster used to say she could.

success.text: Hear that? Every bell with somebody in it, all the way to Cinder Fold, ringing the same hour. I can't move them. I can ask them, through the bells, all at once. Nobody ever has.

success.narrate: At the end of the hour the bronze answers a breath late, faint, from a long way off, and it is Aster's voice, from Vell's great bell.

success.text: I can hear them all from here. Every bell with somebody in it. I can't move them. I can ask them, through the bells, all at once. Nobody ever has.
She could have asked them all, through the bells, at once. She told me so, the last winter she was anywhere. She's at rest. If they're asked now it'll be by letter, slowly, by people like me.

failure.narrate: {You sit|@ sits} in the bell-room through the hour, but all {you hear|@ hears} is the bell, and the square below, and the swifts under the eaves.

route.label: Walk the Briarwood edge before dusk, and set the watch line

success.narrate: {You walk|@ walks} the lanes down to the Briarwood edge before dusk with Pim and Aveline's list, and {find|finds} where the white came to on the night of the song, and on every hard frost since: the stream, and the third hedge, and the bottom of the mill lane. {You set|@ sets} the watch line above the highest of them, with a lamp at every gate.

failure.narrate: {You walk|@ walks} the lanes down to the Briarwood edge at dusk, but the hedges are high with summer and every lane looks like the next, and {you come|@ comes} back up with the watch line where Aveline's list says it should be, and no surer of it.

direct.label: Wait in the square for the hour that will not be rung
direct.text: You wait in the square for the hour that is not going to be rung, with Briarwatch round you, and the Briarwood edge empty below.

approach.narrate: Dusk on midsummer night, and then the dark, which comes late and does not last.

oneOf.narrate: The hour comes, and nobody lights the fire at the stream. Pim sits beside the cold fire-pit with his knees up.
The hour comes, and the bell in the tower does not ring. Tovin and Pim sit under it with the ropes in their laps.

approach.narrate: Linus Pardew sings his new verse from the well, quietly, and the square listens, and then nobody sings anything.
At midnight the white comes up out of the Briarwood.

crisis.narrate: It comes up out of the wood under a sky that is barely dark, and it is not thin, for summer. It comes over the stream and up the lanes between the hedges, knee-deep and then waist-deep, cold enough to stop the breath, and the lamps at the gates of the empty houses go out one by one.
There are shapes in it: frost standing up in the shapes of Briarwatch people long dead, walking home up the lanes to houses that are empty tonight on purpose.

Then somebody on the watch line sees a light in an upstairs window of the last house on the mill lane. Somebody has gone back. The line starts to come apart, people going down into the white towards it.

crisis.text: That house is on my list. It's empty. It's on my list as empty.

oneOf.text: Nobody light it. Please. If we light it now, it's all for nothing.
Nobody ring. Please. If we ring now, it's all for nothing.

crisis.text: Someone's in there. I'm going. Don't—

peaceful.label: Hold the watch line, and bring whoever is in the last house up through the white

oneOf.narrate: {You have|@ has} heard the joined bells, and {you know|@ knows} every bound voice in the free wards is listening tonight to what one quiet night in Briarwatch costs. {You say|@ says} so along the watch line, so that nobody runs for the stream out of fear.

{You have|@ has} heard the joined bells, and {you know|@ knows} every bound voice in the free wards is listening tonight to what one quiet night in Briarwatch costs. {You say|@ says} so along the watch line, so that nobody rings out of fear.

success.narrate: The watch line is above the highest the white has ever come, with a lamp at every gate, and it holds where it was set.
{You walk|@ walks} the watch line in the dark, moving people up a hedge at a time, above where the white is coming.
Then {you go|@ goes} down the mill lane into the white with a lamp, slowly, on the hedge side, to the last house, and up its stair.

It is the old woman from the end of the lane, who would not sleep in the hall, because she has slept in her own bed every night for sixty years and the white has never once come up the mill lane past the stream. She is sitting on the bed with her shoes on, waiting to be fetched.
{You bring|@ brings} her up the lane on {their} arm, through the white to the waist, at the pace she walks, and the shapes in it walk home past {them} and do not stop.

oneOf.narrate: Nobody lights the fire. On the watch line Briarwatch stands in the dark with its lamps and lets the white lie in its lanes until the short night is over, and at dawn it goes back down over the stream into the wood, the way the tide goes out.

Nobody rings. On the watch line Briarwatch stands in the dark with its lamps and lets the white lie in its lanes until the short night is over, and at dawn it goes back down over the stream into the wood, the way the tide goes out.

success.narrate: Nobody on the Briarwood edge is lost. In the morning the old woman from the end of the lane cannot remember the name of the dog she had as a girl. She says she will ask her sister.

oneOf.narrate: {You start|@ starts} down the mill lane into the white with a lamp, but the shapes in it turn as {you come|@ comes}, all of them at once, and come up the lane towards the watch line, and the line breaks, and somebody runs for the stream with a light.

{You start|@ starts} down the mill lane into the white with a lamp, but the shapes in it turn as {you come|@ comes}, all of them at once, and come up the lane towards the watch line, and the line breaks, and somebody runs for the tower.

objective.name: The watch line
objective.label: Hold the watch line until dawn
objective.description: Four successful actions hold the shapes below the watch line, and bring the last house up, until the short night is over.
objective.failText: Dawn comes, and the white goes back into the wood, but the old woman from the end of the mill lane was brought up too late, and does not know Briarwatch, and asks everybody very politely where she is.
objective.successText: Dawn comes early, as it does at midsummer, and the watch line is where it was set, and nobody on it was taken.

b4-quietnight.foeName: The White on the Briarwood Edge

oneOf.narrate: Morning. The lanes on the Briarwood edge are wet and grey and empty, and the edge houses' people are coming down from the hall with their bedding to see whether their doors still open. They do.

Morning. The lanes on the Briarwood edge are wet, and torn up at the mill lane, where the fight was. In the small hours, with the shapes at the watch line, somebody lit the fire at the stream, and nobody has said who. Briarwatch's quiet night was half a night.

Morning. The lanes on the Briarwood edge are wet, and torn up at the mill lane, where the fight was. In the small hours, with the shapes at the watch line, somebody rang the bell, and nobody has said who. Briarwatch's quiet night was half a night.
Up in the tower, Tovin asks for you, and sits you on the bench under the window.
Up in the tower, Aster Vey asks for you.

oneOf.text: Nobody's in this bell but me, so I'm the one to ask. Ask me what Briarwatch's watch is for, now, and I'll tell you, and that'll be its answer. I've two answers in me. I'd like you to choose.

Last night I was asked not to ring. I was asked that last summer too, for a night a month, and I said yes. Nobody has ever asked me the rest. What I want rung through me. I want three things, and I can have one. Choose with me.

Last night I was asked not to ring. That's the first time anybody has asked me anything since I was put in here. I'd like to be asked the rest. What I want rung through me. I want three things, and I can have one. Choose with me.

after.text: She answered last night from Vell, at the evening hour. She said whatever Briarwatch chooses, she'll hear it.
She'd have answered for herself. She's at rest. I'll answer, and I'll say it was me.

decisions.label: It rings every night
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Briarwatch's watch is kept every night, by the bell's own answer, and the white goes north as it always has.

told.ballad: Briarwatch asked its bell what it wanted, and the bell said: every night, for the houses on the edge.
told.tally: Briarwatch. The bell was asked, and said: every night. Written: it was the bell's own answer.

oneOf.narrate: You ask Tovin for every night. He says yes before you have finished: the fire at the stream every night, and the hours on the bronze, and nobody on the Briarwood edge sleeping in the hall again because of a list.

You ask Aster for every night. She says yes before you have finished: for the houses on the Briarwood edge, and for the last house on the mill lane, and because she was put in this bell to keep Briarwatch, and she would rather keep it than be kept.

oneOf.text: Every night. That's the keeper's answer. Write that it was the keeper's, not the council's.
Every night. That's my answer. It's mine. I'd like it written that it's mine, if anybody comes to ring the bell from the Hall.

decisions.label: It keeps quiet nights
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Briarwatch's watch keeps quiet nights, by the bell's own answer, and Briarwatch takes its share of the white on them.

told.ballad: Briarwatch asked its bell what it wanted, and the bell said: some nights, let me be quiet.
told.tally: Briarwatch. The bell was asked, and said: quiet nights. Written: it chose them.

oneOf.narrate: You ask Tovin for quiet nights. He nods slowly, as if he had known what you would ask.
You ask Aster for quiet nights. She is quiet herself for a long time, which is how you know she is listening to the answer as well as giving it.

oneOf.text: Quiet nights. Pim's and mine, the fire not lit, and the Briarwood edge up in the hall. We know how now.
Quiet nights. Some of them. Ones I choose, with Pim. I've rung it north for so long. I'd like to be the bell that didn't, sometimes, on purpose.

decisions.label: Aster rests, and Briarwatch keeps a night watch
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Aster Vey goes to rest, by her own answer, and Briarwatch's bell is bronze only. The village keeps a night watch on the Briarwood edge, with a fire at the stream.

told.ballad: Briarwatch asked its bell what it wanted, and the voice in it said: rest, after the harvest.
told.tally: Briarwatch. The voice in the bell was asked, and said: let me stop. Written: she was let.

text.narrate: You ask Aster whether she would like to rest. She does not answer for so long that Tovin, on the stair below, looks up.

text.text: Yes. At the end of the summer. I'd like to hear one more harvest in, and then stop. Tell Pim he can keep the hours. He always could.

text.narrate: Aveline writes a new line at the top of her list: a fire at the stream, every night, from the first frost.

b4-gatehouse.name: Sable's Last Lesson
b4-gatehouse.region: Highpass Watch: the gatehouse, the cells under it, and the gatehouse yard
b4-gatehouse.threat: Ailith Strake's rope-men are coming up the lower road with a cart for the one man in the free wards who knows how the Parting Bell is rung, and he has written to say he will go.
b4-gatehouse.brief: Ailith Strake has sent a cart to Highpass for Sable, the man who once bound a bell's voice in secret to keep a village safe properly. He knows how the Parting Bell is rung, both ways. He has said he will go with her men. Before the cart comes, somebody should ask him why.

told.ballad: Under Highpass's gatehouse the old warden who once bound a bell alone was asked, at last, who he would give the last note to.
told.tally: Highpass. The south kept a prisoner who knew both notes. Written: they asked him who should have them.

opening.narrate: High summer at Highpass, a month after the quiet night. The pass is green to the snow-line, the north road is open to the top, and the gatehouse doors stand open all day for the air.

oneOf.narrate: In the gatehouse yard Highpass's bell stands in its frame with the sun on it: Sable, cast at his own asking in the first snow two winters ago. Sorrel's guard still reverse their pikes when they walk past it, and nobody has told them to.
Under the gatehouse, in the end cell, Sable has his brazier lit in high summer, and his books stacked to the ceiling, and a new pen.

opening.narrate: Sorrel sends for you. On her table there is a letter that came up the lower road from Cinder Fold, in a big round hand you last saw in the gate book, and a copy of the answer that went back down, made by the cell guard: every word Sable sends out of the gatehouse is copied first.

oneOf.text: Ailith Strake wants Highpass's bell lent to Cinder Fold until midwinter, with him in it, to read the founders' ledger for the casting hall. She's sending a cart. He's said yes. I didn't know a bell could say yes to anything. It turns out it can, in writing.

Ailith Strake wants my prisoner lent to Cinder Fold until midwinter, to read the founders' ledger for the casting hall. She's sending a cart. He's said yes. He can't go anywhere without the council's word, and the council's risen till the autumn, and she knows it.

opening.text: I'd like you to go down and ask him what he's doing. He won't tell me. He says I wouldn't follow the argument. He's right, and I'd like to hear it anyway.

oneOf.narrate: Cinder Fold answered the council's letter about the rope in the spring, in the same upright hand: the Parting Bell is in the casting hall, where it was cast, and it is safe, and the rope families will ring it at midwinter for the free wards, as they ring the Mother Bell. It does not say which way. The council read it out twice with the doors open, and still does not know.
Sloe has not asked the council about the bell once all summer. Every few days she asks you whether the promise at the end of the lower watch's street still stands. It does.
Nobody on the council has asked about the bell. Sorrel has her gate book locked in her office, and has not read the autumn page out, which is as near as she comes to forgetting it.
Sloe took the council's answer up to the Hall in the spring, and came down again after the quiet night, and has been on the bench outside the cells since, with her slate on her knee.
Sloe has been at Highpass all summer, on the bench outside the cells, with her slate on her knee.

opening.narrate: Hesk is in the cell next to Sable's. He has been there two years, and has heard everything said in the next cell, and has said nothing about any of it to anybody.

Davin has spent the summer on the gate with Sorrel's watch, learning their drill, and since you came back up from Briarwatch, Orin goes up most evenings to watch the boy get it wrong, and says nothing.
Davin has spent the summer on the gate with Sorrel's watch, learning their drill, and getting it wrong, and then less wrong.

oneOf.narrate: The Wold's door-bearers have cut and stacked the watch's winter wood along the inside of the gatehouse wall, up to the eaves, which is how Iona's bill was paid in the end. Iona has written 'Paid in wood' across it.
Iona's bill to the Wold hangs on the nail in her office, with 'Paid' across it in her own hand, and under that her own name.
Iona's bill to the Wold hangs on the nail in her office, crossed through, with 'Set against: nine hundred years' written under it.
Iona's bill to the Wold hangs on the nail in her office, unpaid, with 'Held to midwinter' on it in pencil.

talks.label: Go down to Sable, and ask him why he said yes

oneOf.narrate: You go out into the gatehouse yard and stand under the bell. It speaks before you have said anything, in Sable's voice, from inside the bronze.
You go down the cell stair to the end cell. Sable is at his table, writing. He does not get up, and he does not stop writing until he has finished the line.

lines.text: She came in the autumn, two days before she went up your road. She brought a page from her family's ledger, the founders' hand, and asked me to read it to her. I did. It was the Parting Bell's page: what the bell does, rung with the Mother Bell at midwinter, one way or the other. That is how she knows. I told her.
Then she asked me how it is rung forward. I said I would think about it. I have been thinking about it since the autumn.

Here is my case. She will ring it whether I help her or not. She is the best ringer alive, and she has the bell, and the rope families, and the nine, and midwinter will come whatever anybody votes. If she has to guess at the forward note she may guess it wrong, and a wrong note at Cinder Fold at midwinter is not nothing. Every bell in the free wards would answer it.

If I go, I am in the room. I am the only one living who knows both notes, and I would be standing beside her when she asks for one. I bound a bell's voice once, in secret, to keep a village safe properly. I know exactly what she is doing, and why. Who would you rather had her elbow?
You see. It is a good case. My cases always are. That has always been the trouble with them.
He means every word. That's the part I don't like.

talks.label: Ask Sable about Aster Vey

oneOf.narrate: You ask Sable about Aster Vey. Before he can answer, the bell in the yard answers instead, a breath late and very faint, from a long way off: Briarwatch's bell, under the ground, where the bells are joined.

You ask Sable about Aster Vey. Before he can answer, the bell in the yard answers instead, a breath late and fainter than you have ever heard her: Vell's great bell, from the far end of the free wards, where the bells are joined.

You ask Sable about Aster Vey. He has a letter from Briarwatch on his table, in Tovin's careful hand: what Aster said in the bell-room the night after the quiet night, when she asked Tovin to write it down and send it to Highpass.

You ask Sable about Aster Vey. He has a letter from Briarwatch on his table, in Tovin's careful hand: what Aster said through Briarwatch's bell, a breath late, from Vell's great bell, when she asked Tovin to write it down and send it to Highpass.
You ask Sable about Aster Vey. He does not answer for a long time.

oneOf.text: She is at rest. I bound her into Briarwatch's bell when I was the warden there, in secret, to keep the village safe properly, and she never once argued with me. Not that night, and not in all the years after.
Tell him Briarwatch asked its keeper at midsummer what its bell was for, and Tovin answered, and I heard it from here. Nobody asked me. Nobody has, since he put me in.
Tell him I was asked. Last summer, a night a month, and at midsummer for the rest. Tell him that's what it's like, being asked. He never did.
Tell him I was asked. At midsummer, in Briarwatch, for the first time since he put me in. Tell him that's what it's like, being asked. He never did.
If she were here she would ask me one thing: whether anybody has asked the bells. Nobody has. Then she would wait, and I would have nothing to say, and she would know it, and so would I.

If he goes to Cinder Fold, every one of us in a bell rings with whatever he gives Ailith. Him too. Me. Nobody's asked us. He asked to be put in a bell, and he was let. He knows the difference better than anybody. Tell him I said so.

If he goes to Cinder Fold, every one of us in a bell rings with whatever he gives Ailith. Me too. Nobody's asked us. He asked to be put in a bell once, and was told no, and lived with it. He knows the difference better than anybody. Tell him I said so.

lines.text: And tell him I'm going to rest after the harvest. I chose it. He can stop being sorry. I've decided to stop being angry.

oneOf.narrate: Sable does not say anything else while you are there.

oneOf.text: She has never once argued with me. She says what is so, and waits. I have never had an answer to it. I still have not.

talks.label: Sit with Sloe on the bench outside the cells

lines.narrate: Sloe moves along the bench to make room, and turns her slate face down on her knee.

lines.text: The founders' page says the Parting Bell can be rung two ways. It does not say how. I have the sum. I do not have the note. He has.

I want the other note from him. The quiet one. Its true form, not a guess at it. I have asked him every day since the quiet night. He says he is thinking. In the Wold we would write that on his door, and by now there would be no door left to write on.

oneOf.text: You told me who has the bell, at the end of the street, and asked me to wait. I am waiting. I am waiting here, where the note is.
Your council wrote to the rope families with the doors open. I liked that. Their answer says the bell is safe. Safe is a word that means whatever the person saying it needs.
Somebody in the south has the bell, and has not said so. Somebody in this gatehouse knows how it is rung. I can wait for one of them. I would rather not wait for both.

talks.label: Speak to Hesk in the next cell

lines.narrate: Hesk is at his table with his lamp, and the first winter of Iona's invoice still on his wall in charcoal.

oneOf.text: I've had his bell through my window for two years. It rings when it likes, and it likes to ring when I'm asleep.
I've had him through the wall for two years. He reads aloud. He reads aloud in his sleep, in the founders' spelling.

She came in the autumn, Ailith, with a lamp and a page, and stood under his bell in the yard for an evening, and I heard every word of it through my window. He told her what the bell does. She asked him how it's rung. He said he'd think. She thanked him. She's a polite woman. So was I, once.

She came down here in the autumn, Ailith, with a lamp and a page, and sat outside his bars for an evening, and I heard every word of it. He told her what the bell does. She asked him how it's rung. He said he'd think. She thanked him. She's a polite woman. So was I, once.

lines.text: I bought a ring of bells because I was sure. He bound one because he was sure. She's sure. Ask him which of the three of us he means to be at midwinter.

talks.label: Ask Rue what she learned from Sable

lines.narrate: Rue is on the cell stair with her book, copying something out of it into a second book, slowly.

lines.text: Last summer, while I was waiting for your council, I came down here every day, and he taught me the marks at the bottom of the founders' page. Not the letters. I have always had the letters. The marks under them, for notes. We never kept those in the Wold. Our ringers learn at the rope, by ear, and nobody writes a note down.
He said a note written down is a note anybody can ring. He showed me how the Parting Bell's would be written, and then he did not write it.
I have it in my book that he was kind to me. I am keeping that line, whatever he does.

b4-gatehouse.clue: Backward or forward, the Parting Bell's note is nothing on its own: either one needs the Parting Bell and the nine rung together, at Cinder Fold, at midwinter, when the Mother Bell is rung, and nowhere and at no time else.

investigate.label: Go through the Parting Bell's page with Sable, mark by mark

oneOf.narrate: {You sit|@ sits} under the bell in the yard with the clerk's copy of the page Ailith brought, the Parting Bell's page, and {read|reads} the marks under the founders' letters aloud one at a time, and the bell says what each one is.

{You sit|@ sits} outside the bars with Sable's tracing of the page Ailith brought, the Parting Bell's page, and {go|goes} through the marks under the founders' letters one at a time while he says what each one is.

success.narrate: It takes the afternoon. By the end {you have|@ has} all of them, and Sable has stopped correcting.

success.text: There. Backward or forward, the note is nothing on its own. It wants the Parting Bell and the nine, rung together, at Cinder Fold, at midwinter, when the Mother Bell is rung. Nowhere else, and no other night.

So nobody can ring it early, and nobody can ring it here. Not Ailith, and not Sloe. On the one night it can be rung, everybody who wants it rung will be in the same room. The founders made sure of that. I expect they meant to.

failure.narrate: {You go|@ goes} through the marks under the founders' letters with Sable, but they are a ringer's marks, not a scholar's, and by the end of the lamp {you know|@ knows} the names of a dozen of them and not what they say together.

route.label: Walk the gatehouse with the watch sergeant, and find the way a cart comes in

success.narrate: {You walk|@ walks} the gatehouse with the watch sergeant in the afternoon, and {find|finds} the one way a cart can come into the yard: up the lower road, through the yard gate, to the head of the cell stair. {You put|@ puts} a lamp on the yard gate, and two of the watch at the stair head, with nothing to do but stand there and be seen.

failure.narrate: {You walk|@ walks} the gatehouse with the watch sergeant, but in summer every gate in it stands open for the air, and {you come|@ comes} back with four ways a cart could come in and nobody to put on any of them.

direct.label: Wait in the gatehouse yard for the cart
direct.text: You wait in the gatehouse yard for the cart, with the doors open for the air and the watch up on the wall.

approach.narrate: The cart comes up the lower road at dusk, on the day the letter named: a long rope-families' cart with a hide over the bed and a hoist-frame lashed on top, and twelve of the rope families walking beside it.

The watch sergeant counts them in at the yard gate, out of habit, and looks at the gate book under his arm, and counts them again. They are the same twelve, by their names, who went up the north road with Ailith in the autumn and came down with a load.

oneOf.narrate: They draw up beside Highpass's bell in its frame. The rope-men's foreman looks at the bell, and at the cart, and at the hoist, the way a ringer looks at a weight.

They draw up at the head of the cell stair. The rope-men's foreman has a letter in Sable's hand, and gives it to the cell guard, who reads it twice and goes down for the keys, because Sable's letters have been obeyed at Highpass for two years, and nobody has told him this one should not be.

The rope-men have the hoist up over the bell's frame before the watch on the wall has come down the stair, and the bell off its beam and hanging over the cart's bed on four ropes, lowered slowly, the way the rope families lift a bell: as if it were somebody.

Sable comes up the cell stair between two of the rope-men with his books in a sack and his new pen behind his ear, and climbs up into the cart himself, and sits on the bench in the bed with his hands in his lap.

oneOf.text: I said yes. Let them do it properly. They know how to lift a bell.
I said yes. I should like it noted that nobody is carrying me.

crisis.narrate: Sorrel comes down off the wall with her watch behind her, pikes level, and the twelve stand round the cart with their hands on its ropes, and the yard gate is open behind them onto the lower road.

oneOf.text: That bell's Highpass's ward. It doesn't leave my yard on a letter.
That man's the council's prisoner. He doesn't leave my gatehouse on a letter he wrote himself.

crisis.text: Ailith said he'd come of his own will, and he has. We don't want a fight in your yard, Captain. We've a long road home, and we'd like to start it tonight.
Give me the word and I'll have a wheel off that cart. I'd rather you didn't give it.

peaceful.label: Go up to the cart, and talk Sable out of it

success.narrate: {You know|@ knows} what the founders' page says: the note can be rung nowhere but Cinder Fold, at midwinter, with the nine. {You say|@ says} so in the yard, loud enough for the foreman. Nothing is lost if Sable waits the summer where he is.
The lamp is on the yard gate, and the watch at the stair head, and the cart stands where everybody can see all of it.
{You put|@ puts} the watch between the cart and the yard gate, a pike at a time, without saying why.

oneOf.narrate: Then {you go|@ goes} up to the bell where it hangs over the cart on its ropes, and {ask|asks} it the one thing Sable's case leaves out: when Ailith asks him for the forward note at midwinter, with the rope in her hands, whether he means to give it to her, or the other one.

Then {you climb|@ climbs} up into the cart and {sit|sits} on the bench beside Sable, and {ask|asks} him the one thing his case leaves out: when Ailith asks him for the forward note at midwinter, with the rope in her hands, whether he means to give it to her, or the other one.

success.text: I have not decided. That is the truth. I was going to decide in the room.

success.narrate: {You tell|@ tells} him that is how a bell's voice was bound in Briarwatch once: by one man, in secret, who decided at the last moment, alone, what was safe for everybody else.

success.text: Yes. It is. Nobody has put it to me as plainly as that since the vault.

oneOf.narrate: The foreman looks at the bell, and at {you|@}, and has the hoist let down again, gently, rope by rope, until the bell is back on its beam in the frame.
Sable climbs down out of the cart, slowly, with his sack of books, and sits on the cell stair.

success.text: Ailith said he'd come of his own will. If his will's changed, we'll not carry him. She'll not thank me. She'll understand.

success.narrate: The twelve stand the cart in the yard for the night, and the watch brings them supper in the guardroom, and nobody draws anything.

failure.narrate: {You go|@ goes} up to the cart to talk Sable down, but the foreman has a long road and his orders, and before {you have|@ has} said three words he blows the rope families' horn, and the twelve take up the ropes, and the cart starts for the gate.

objective.name: The yard gate
objective.label: Hold the cart in the yard until the gate is shut
objective.description: Four successful actions hold the cart and the twelve in the gatehouse yard until the watch can get the yard gate shut and barred.
objective.failText: The yard gate is shut in the end, but the cart has been through it and back again first, with two of Sorrel's watch under its wheels, and both of them will be a month on their feet again.
objective.successText: The yard gate swings shut on its bar with the cart still inside it, and the twelve put down their ropes.

oneOf.narrate: Morning. The cart stands in the gatehouse yard where the twelve left it, with its hide folded and its hoist down, and Highpass's bell is on its beam in the frame with the dew on it.
Morning. The cart stands in the gatehouse yard where the twelve left it, with its hide folded, and Sable is still on the cell stair, where he sat all night with his sack of books.

Morning. The gatehouse yard is torn up from the bell's frame to the gate, where the fight was, and the cart is on its side by the gatepost with a wheel off. Highpass's bell is back on its beam, with a new bright scar on its lip where the hoist let it down too fast. The twelve are in the guardroom under Sorrel's watch, with their hurt.

Morning. The gatehouse yard is torn up from the cell stair to the gate, where the fight was, and the cart is on its side by the gatepost with a wheel off. The twelve are in the guardroom under Sorrel's watch, with their hurt. Sable is on the cell stair, where the watch put him.

after.text: I've sent to Cinder Fold to say the cart's here, and the twelve, and that they can have both back when somebody's decided what about. I'd like that to be you. He'll take it from you. He won't from me.

oneOf.narrate: The council has it from Sorrel by noon, with the doors open: the rope families came for Sable. After the rope on the clerk's table, nobody in the hall has to be told who sent them.
Sloe is on the bench by the cells with her slate on her knee. She has seen the cart and the twelve, and she does not ask you anything. You told her whose they would be, at the end of the street.
Sloe is on the bench by the cells with her slate on her knee. She has seen the cart and the twelve, and the knots on their ropes, and you can see her do the sum.

after.text: Ailith will have my answer by the next cart, whatever it is. I have three answers, and for the first time in my life I should like somebody else to choose between them. That is your doing. I have not decided whether to forgive you for it.

decisions.label: Let him go to Cinder Fold with Ailith's men
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Sable goes to Cinder Fold with the rope families, and will give Ailith the note she asks for. The forward ring will be ready at midwinter.

told.ballad: The hero let the old warden go to the rope families with the last note, because he had said he would.
told.tally: Highpass. The south let the man who knew the note go to the ones who had the bell. Written: they let him go.

oneOf.narrate: You tell him to go. In the afternoon the twelve lift the bell again, slowly, on four ropes, and lash it into the cart's bed under the hide, and take it down the lower road with the watch standing aside.
You tell him to go. In the afternoon he climbs back up into the cart with his sack of books, and the twelve take him down the lower road with the watch standing aside.

text.text: Then I will stand beside her, and give her what she asks for, because I said I would, and because I have never had a better answer than hers. I will write to you. You will not like the letters.
I'll put it in the gate book. 'Down. Twelve, and a load.' One fewer than last time.

decisions.label: Ask him to teach you both notes, and carry them yourself
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Sable teaches you the forward note and the backward one, in the founders' marks, and stays at Highpass. At midwinter you will be the one in the room who knows both.

told.ballad: The hero sat out the summer with the old warden at Highpass, and learned both notes of the Parting Bell, so that nobody would ring either one alone.
told.tally: Highpass. The south's prisoner taught the southerner both notes. Written: now there is somebody who can be asked.

text.text: Both, then. The one I would have given her, and the one Sloe wants. I will teach you them, and you will carry them, and at midwinter it will be you that is asked, and not me.

text.narrate: He teaches you through the rest of the summer, a mark at a time, in the evenings, until you can write both notes out under the founders' letters without the page, and say them, and know what each one would do.
The twelve take their cart home empty, with a letter for Ailith in Sable's hand. He does not tell you what it says.

text.text: Then at midwinter I will ask you for it, and not him. I would rather ask somebody who has to look at me.

decisions.label: Let him keep both notes to himself, and stay
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Sable keeps both notes to himself and stays at Highpass. Ailith will have to work the forward note out for herself.

told.ballad: The hero left the old warden at Highpass with both notes kept, and the rope families went home with an empty cart.
told.tally: Highpass. The man who knew the notes kept them. Written: the south has a secret again.

text.text: Then I keep them. I kept a bell's voice once, in secret, for everybody's good. I can keep two notes for nobody's in particular. I find that is easier.
Tell Ailith she will have to guess. She is the best ringer alive. She will guess well.

text.narrate: The twelve take their cart home empty, with Sorrel's letter and nothing from Sable.

text.text: Good. Let her guess. I'd rather nobody had it at all.

b4-ford.name: The Ford
b4-ford.region: Ashford Crossing: the old wall, the lower town, and the ford below the fulling mill
b4-ford.threat: The Wold's families have to cross Ashford's river by the old ford before the autumn, and Ashford's town meeting has said no to everything asked of it.
b4-ford.brief: A column of the Wold's people has to cross the river at Ashford, by the old ford, to reach the towns that will winter them. Ashford will not help. Sorrel has brought the council's watch down to see them over, and she wants somebody to command it who has been in a column before.

told.ballad: At Ashford's ford the soldier who never gave an order was asked to be a captain, with the river rising white behind him.
told.tally: Ashford. The south brought the Wold over its river at the old ford, in the white. Written: they were asked who would go in first.

opening.narrate: Late summer at Ashford. The barley is in, the ash trees along the river are going yellow at the top, and the board on the bridge with the town's no on it has been painted again, in the same words.

oneOf.narrate: Below the old wall, in the lower town, the scaffolding is mostly down. The streets are built again where they were, by the river, under the trees, and the new houses have the smell of lime about them still.
Below the old wall the lower town lies grey and empty, the way the winter before last left it. Grass has come up in its streets. Nobody has built there.
The lower town stands, every roof of it, and the fulling mill turns. In the gateway of the old wall Amos Wick rings the hours a little late, and people still touch the bronze as they go by.

The lower town stands, and the fulling mill turns, and in the market square a board lists the two hundred and forty children the council took up the road to Highpass two winters ago, and the day each one came home.

On the north bank, in the stubble below the old wall, the Wold's families have camped for three nights: the ones who came down from Highpass in the spring and have been a few to each town all summer, gathered up again now to go south together before the autumn, to the towns that will winter them.

On the north bank, in the stubble below the old wall, the first of the Wold's families from the Hall have camped for three nights. They came down the north road after the council's answer, and are going south to the towns that will winter them.

On the north bank, in the stubble below the old wall, the first of the Wold's families from Orme have camped for three nights. They came over the peaks after the council's answer, and are going south to the towns that will winter them.

With them, roped in a line with somebody at each end, are the walkers from the Hush, who walk as slowly as they did on the cairn road. Anwen Holt has written from Merrowgate that the harbour hospice has beds for every one of them.

With them, roped in a line with somebody at each end, are the walkers from the Hush who followed the marks. Anwen Holt has written from Merrowgate that the harbour hospice has beds for every one of them.

opening.narrate: There are a little over four hundred of them, with carts. The bridge takes one cart at a time and Ashford has shut it to them. The ford below the fulling mill takes a column, in late summer, when the river is low.
The council did not vote them a refuge. Fenmere and Saltwick have written that they will winter whoever comes, vote or no vote, and Briarwatch has made up its barns.
Ashford's town meeting sat last night, and voted: no camp on Ashford's fields, no carts over the bridge, no help at the ford. They may cross. They may not stop.

Captain Sorrel is in the stubble with forty of the council's watch, who came down the Highpass road with her a week ago. She has a paper in her coat with the council's seal on it, and she has been waiting for you.
Rue has come down from Highpass with Sorrel's watch, with her book, to write the crossing down.

oneOf.text: It's a commission. Captain of the council's watch, for the crossing and after it, as far as midwinter. I've a gate to keep at Highpass. I'd like it to be Orin. He's been in a column. I've only ever kept one out.

It's a commission. Captain of the council's watch, for the crossing and after it, as far as midwinter. I wanted the soldier who carried the back of your column over the peaks. He's not with you, and I've a gate to keep at Highpass. So I'm asking you.

opening.narrate: Orin reads the paper twice, standing up, the way he reads orders, and gives it back to her without saying anything.

talks.label: Ask Orin what he means to do with the commission

lines.narrate: Orin is down at the water's edge below the camp, looking at the ford, the way he looked at the switchbacks on the peaks: where the footing goes, and where it does not.

lines.text: Varn had a commission. Paper like that, with a seal on it. He kept it in his coat and took it out at night and read it, when he thought nobody was looking. I was always looking. I was the one at the back with the lantern.

oneOf.text: I gave an order at Sheddon. 'On.' Two hundred went on, and an old woman stayed in the white, and I asked her name after. That was one order. This is all of them. Every day till midwinter.
At Sheddon I didn't give the order. I went back, and gave you the front, and lost the name of Varn's company to the white. I went back because I couldn't say 'on'. A captain says 'on'.
At Sheddon you took the order off me. I'd have said it. I think I'd have said it. I'll never know now, and Sorrel's asking me to find out every day till midwinter.
I've never given an order. Not one. I've only ever done what I was told, or not.

lines.text: I'm good at carrying things. I'm good at being the one at the back. Somebody has to be good at that too. I don't know if I'm the man for the front. I know I'm the one she asked.

talks.label: Go up to the old wall and see Hollis Brede

lines.narrate: Hollis Brede is on the old wall above the north gate, where she stood the night the white came up the valley, with her arms folded on the parapet, watching the camp in the stubble.

oneOf.text: We said no, and we held, and we've built it all again under the trees. I'll not have that put in front of the white a second time for anybody. They may cross. They may not stop. That's the meeting's word, and it's mine.

We said no, and we held. The lower town's still down there under the grey. Ashford paid for its no. I'll not be told now that it has to pay for somebody else's yes. They may cross. They may not stop. That's the meeting's word, and it's mine.

The meeting voted it without me. I stood up to speak and sat down again. Amos is in the gateway, ringing. We said no to a price for a person once, and then a person paid it, and the white went down the valley. I don't tell anybody what this town may do any more. I just watch it.

The council took our children over our own vote. Now it wants our ford. It can have the ford. The meeting says they may cross and not stop, and I said it louder than anybody, and I'm not sorry. The council can learn what a no sounds like from the other side.

lines.text: Ashford's not cruel. Ashford's careful. There's a difference, and nobody up at Highpass has ever once troubled to learn it.
If the river comes up white while they're in it, they'll be on their own. You know that. I'd like you to know I know it.

talks.label: Find Davin among the watch

lines.narrate: Davin is in the grey coat of Sorrel's watch. It is too big for him across the shoulders and too short in the arms. He was seventeen at midsummer.

lines.text: I've done the whole summer on Sorrel's gate. Drill, and the stair, and the wall at night. I'm not bad. I was bad. I'm not now.

oneOf.text: If Orin takes it, I want to be in his company. Not Sorrel's. His. Don't tell him I said. I'll ask him myself. I've been going to all week.
I'd hoped it'd be his company. You know who I mean. The watch are all right. They're not him.
Gran sent me with him. She said he'd bring me back. She never said what I'd be when he did.
He said I'd do what I was told. That was the word. I've done it every day since. I'd like it to be him telling me.

talks.label: Speak to the old soldier at the end of the watch line

oneOf.narrate: At the end of the watch line, in an old coat with no badge on it, Odell Varn is sitting on his pack. He went back to Hesk's company with a message two years ago, and turned forty of Hesk's people back on the stair, and nobody in the free wards had seen him since. He looks older than sixty now.

At the end of the watch line, in an old coat with no badge on it, Odell Varn is cleaning a lamp-hook he has no use for, out of habit. He walked Saltwick's lamps for a season, as the roof council judged, and he has come down to Ashford on foot from the coast.

lines.text: I heard Sorrel had a paper. Word goes up and down the road. I've come to serve under him, if he'll have me. As a soldier. At the back, with a lantern. I know the place.
I gave the order at Saltwick and lived with it. I've been the one in front. I'd like to see what it's like to be told, by somebody who knows what it costs to tell.
Where's your soldier? The one who carried the back. I was told he'd be with you. I came all this way to stand behind him.
You'd take an order from me.
I'd take one from you. I don't know that you'd give one to me. That's for you.

talks.label: Ask Sorrel why she wants a captain for a ford

lines.text: Four hundred people and their carts, over a river, in a day, with a town on the bank that won't lift a hand. That's not a ford. That's a column. A column wants somebody at the front who'll say go, and mean it, and somebody at the back who'll see nobody falls off.

oneOf.text: I learned the north road off Rue last year. I kept the last fire lit all winter and left the bar off the gate for the Wold. I'm good at gates. I'm no good at rivers. I'd like somebody who is.
I've kept a gate twenty years. I keep people out. This is the other thing. I'd like somebody who's done it.

lines.text: And after the ford, midwinter. Cinder Fold. Whoever has this paper has the council's watch on the casting hall's doors, when the bell's rung. I'd sooner that was somebody who's been on a rope.

talks.label: Go to Sister Ilse in the archive

lines.narrate: Sister Ilse has the building rolls of the old wall out on the archive table again: six skins of parchment stitched together, three hundred years old, weighted at the corners with river stones.

lines.text: You read these the winter before last, by the wall's line. Read them again by the river's. Nobody ever does. The town only ever wanted to know where the wall went.

I've a question for you, since you're here. When the founders' people refused, three hundred years ago, and gave up the lower town to keep the wall, I wonder who had to walk through it on their way to somewhere else. Nobody writes that down. I would like to.

b4-ford.clue: Ashford's old wall was built the last time Ashford refused, three hundred years ago, by giving up the lower town. The old ford is below the line of what was given, and whenever the white comes up the river, it comes to that line and no further.

investigate.label: Read the building rolls again with Sister Ilse, by the river this time

success.narrate: {You go|@ goes} through the six skins of the building rolls with Ilse again, and this time {follow|follows} the line of the old wall down past the last house of the lower town to where the roll stops: at the river, at a stake marked on the bank, a little above the old ford.
Then {you walk|@ walks} it, with the roll in {their} hand, and {find|finds} the stake's stone at the water's edge, under the ash roots, with the founders' mark on it worn almost smooth.

The old ford is below the stone. Three hundred years ago Ashford gave everything below that line, the river with it, and whenever the white has come up the river since, it has come to that line and no further. Above the stone the river is deeper and slower, but it was never given.

success.text: So they drew the line through the water too. Of course they did. Nobody has ever needed to know that but somebody crossing.
