failure.narrate: {You go|@ goes} through the building rolls with Ilse again, but the line of the wall goes down through the lower town and then into a hand {you cannot|@ cannot} read, and {you come|@ comes} back to the ford with no more than {they} knew at noon.

route.label: Walk the ford with the watch, and stake the crossing

success.narrate: {You wade|@ wades} the ford at low water with a staff and a coil of rope, and {stake|stakes} it from bank to bank: a line of poles where the gravel is firm, a rope between them at waist height, and a lamp on every fourth pole for the carts to steer by.

failure.narrate: {You wade|@ wades} the ford with a staff, but the gravel shifts under every step, and the poles {you drive|@ drives} in at noon are leaning by dusk, and two have gone downstream.

direct.label: Take the column straight down to the ford
direct.text: You take the column straight down to the ford at first light, carts and all, with Sorrel's watch along the banks.

oneOf.narrate: At first light the column comes down out of the stubble to the north bank of the ford: the carts first, then the families on their ropes, then the walkers, with Sorrel's watch strung out along both banks.
At first light the column comes down out of the stubble to the north bank of the ford: the carts first, then the families on their ropes, with Sorrel's watch strung out along both banks.

approach.narrate: On the old wall above, all along the parapet, Ashford has come out to watch. Nobody calls out. Nobody comes down.

oneOf.narrate: Orin has not said whether he will take the commission. He is on the north bank at the head of the column, because somebody had to stand there.
You are on the north bank at the head of the column, because somebody had to stand there. Sorrel still has her paper.

crisis.narrate: The first carts are half over when the river changes. It goes quiet first, the way water does before a weir. Then it comes up white from downstream, against the current, over the gravel, the way the white came up Ashford's valley two winters ago.

There are shapes in it: the ford as it was before the wall, with a cart in it that is not there now, and people in old coats wading it with loads on their backs, three hundred years late for wherever they were going.

Half the column is in the water. The carts stop. Somebody's child starts to cry, and the families behind on the bank begin to push forward onto the ford, because the white is behind them too, and that is the way they have always gone from it.

crisis.text: Somebody give them a word. Now. Any word.
It's in the water. It's in the water with them. Don't let them turn round on the ford. If they turn round in that we lose half of them.

peaceful.label: Take the front and get the whole column over

success.narrate: {You know|@ knows} where the line is: the stake's stone under the ash roots, above the ford. Everything above it was never given. {You turn|@ turns} the front of the column upstream, across the current, to the deep water above the stone, where the white cannot follow.

oneOf.narrate: The watch pulls the poles up and drives them again above the stone, with the rope between them and the lamps lit, so that every cart has something to hold.
The poles are where they were driven, with the rope between them and the lamps lit, and every cart on the ford has something to hold.

success.narrate: {You get|@ gets} the watch into the water in a line, shoulder to shoulder downstream of the carts, to be the rope the ford does not have.

oneOf.narrate: Orin goes into the river first, to his chest, and stands at the head of the ford in the white, and gives the column its order: 'Eyes on me. Not on that. Walk.' And it walks.
{You go|@ goes} into the river first, to {their} chest, and {stand|stands} at the head of the ford in the white, and {give|gives} the column one word at a time: eyes front, walk, the next pole, walk.

Nobody turns round. The carts go over one behind another, slowly, in the deep water above the stone, and the families on their ropes after them, and below them on the old ford the white lies on the water and comes no further than the line.

Nobody turns round. The carts go over one behind another, slowly, and the families on their ropes after them, and the white comes up round their knees and their waists and finds nothing on the ford that will look at it.

success.narrate: The walkers come last, with somebody at each end of their rope, as slow as they have ever been.

success.text: Rear's over. All of it. Nobody fell off the back.

success.narrate: At dusk the white goes back down the river, the way the tide goes out, and the old ford is gravel and low water again, and the column is on the south bank, counting its ropes.
On the old wall, nobody calls out. But at dark a woman comes over the bridge with a basket of bread, and nobody on the wall stops her, and in a while two more come after her.

failure.narrate: {You try|@ tries} to take the front, but the families behind are already pushing out onto the ford, away from the white on the bank, and before {you have|@ has} said three words the carts are slewing sideways in the current, and the shapes in the white are among them.

objective.name: The ford
objective.label: Get the column over the ford before the white closes it
objective.description: Four successful actions get the carts and the families on their ropes over the ford to the south bank while the watch keeps the white off them.
objective.failText: The column gets over in the end, at dusk, but two carts went over in the white and were lost, and the families who had their goods on them have nothing now but their ropes, and a man from Lantry who went in after one of them came out not knowing whose cart it was.
objective.successText: The last of the families comes up out of the river onto the south bank with somebody at each end of the rope, and the column is over.

oneOf.narrate: Night on the south bank. The column is camped in the water-meadow below the ford, past Ashford's last field, with its fires lit, every rope counted, and nobody is hurt. Over the river the old wall is dark except for one lamp over the north gate, which somebody has left lit.

Night on the south bank. The column is camped in the water-meadow below the ford, past Ashford's last field, with its fires lit, and Sorrel's watch are binding each other's cuts by them. The ford behind is churned to mud where the fight was. Over the river the old wall is dark except for one lamp over the north gate.

oneOf.text: I came over the bridge to see you settled. That's all. The meeting didn't say I couldn't come and look.
Amos rang the hour while you were in the water, late, the way he does. Half the wall said he was ringing for them. I don't know. I never asked him.
I watched every one of them come up out of that water. Two hundred and forty, it was, the night you took ours. I counted those too.
Well. That was a column. My paper's still in my coat. I'd like to know tonight whose it is, before I go back up to my gate.
Well. That was a column. My paper's still in my coat. I'd like to know tonight whose it is, before I go back up to my gate.

decisions.label: Orin takes the commission
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Orin is captain of the council's watch until midwinter. At Cinder Fold, his company will hold the casting hall's doors.

told.ballad: At the ford Orin Stoneward took the paper with the seal on it, and was a captain, and found it weighed what Varn had said.
told.tally: Ashford. The southern soldier took the council's commission. Written: the one at the back is at the front now.

text.narrate: Orin holds out a hand for the paper, and Sorrel gives it over.
He reads it again by the fire, and folds it once, and puts it in his coat.

oneOf.text: All right. Till midwinter. I'll want the forty. I'll want them to know my name, and I'll want to know theirs, all of them, written down. And I'll want Varn at the back with a lantern, if he's still here.
All right. Till midwinter. I'll want the forty. I'll want them to know my name, and I'll want to know theirs, all of them, written down.

text.text: Captain Stoneward. Hm. It'll do.

text.narrate: He spends the rest of the night going down the watch's fires, one by one, learning forty names, and saying each one back.

decisions.label: Orin gives the paper back, and stays the man who carries things
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Orin refuses the commission. Sorrel's watch will hold the casting hall's doors at midwinter, with Sorrel's sergeant in command.

told.ballad: At the ford Orin Stoneward gave back the paper with the seal on it, and picked up the heaviest load on the bank instead.
told.tally: Ashford. The southern soldier gave back the commission. Written: he said somebody has to be good at the other thing.

text.narrate: When the paper is held out to him across the fire, Orin shakes his head.

text.text: Today, in the water, somebody had to give them the word. I'm glad I was there for it. I don't want to do it every day. I'm good at this. Carrying. The back. Let somebody else be good at that.
That's the most sense anybody's talked to me all week. My sergeant'll have it. He'll hate it.

text.narrate: Orin goes and helps the families from the last cart carry its load up the meadow, because somebody has to.

decisions.label: Orin takes it, and makes Davin his sergeant
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Orin is captain of the council's watch until midwinter, with Davin as his sergeant. At Cinder Fold, Davin will hold the casting hall's rear door, on Orin's order.

told.ballad: At the ford Orin Stoneward took the paper, and made a lamplighter's boy of seventeen his sergeant, and found out what it is to give the order you would rather not.
told.tally: Ashford. The southern soldier took the commission, and gave a boy the rear. Written: he will have to tell him to stay there.

text.narrate: Orin holds out a hand for the paper, and reads it again by the fire, and then looks across the fire at Davin, who is pretending not to listen.

text.text: Davin. Sergeant. The rear's yours. Every day till midwinter, and on the night. Nobody falls off the back. That's your order.
Yes. Yes, Captain.
Don't. Not yet. I'll get used to it, and then I'll be no good.

text.narrate: Later, when Davin has gone off to tell everybody, Orin sits by the fire with the paper on his knee for a long time.

text.text: I've just given a boy of seventeen the worst door in the hall, and I'll have to tell him to stay at it whatever comes through. That's what it is, being in front. Varn said nobody tells you. Nobody had to tell me. I knew the moment I said it.

decisions.label: Tell Sorrel to keep her paper: the watch is hers
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. You do not take the commission. Sorrel's watch will hold the casting hall's doors at midwinter, with Sorrel's sergeant in command.

told.ballad: At the ford the stranger from the south gave the column its word in the white, and gave the captain her paper back.
told.tally: Ashford. A southerner brought the Wold over the river, and would not be made captain for it.

text.narrate: You tell Sorrel to keep her paper. Somebody had to get the column over today, and the one she wanted for it is not here, and the watch is hers.

text.text: My sergeant'll have it, then. He'll hate it.
If you see him again, tell him I held the rear. Nobody told me to. I just did.

b4-hospice.name: The Hospice
b4-hospice.region: Merrowgate: the harbour hospice's long room, the tide steps, and the harbour steps under the Lantern Hall
b4-hospice.threat: Sloe has come to Merrowgate to ask the harbour council to stand with the Wold at midwinter, and the Lantern Hall has made Ailith Strake an offer that needs Sloe not to be heard.
b4-hospice.brief: Sloe of Orme has come down to Merrowgate to speak to the harbour council before midwinter. Nobody in the south can hear what she is asking them to believe. Maren has been where she comes from, and Sloe would like her to say so.

told.ballad: In Merrowgate's harbour a sister of the shrines was asked to stand up for a stranger, in front of a town that could not hear what the stranger heard.
told.tally: Merrowgate. The south's healer was asked to speak for the Reckoner. Written: what she said, and to whom.

opening.narrate: Autumn at Merrowgate. The fishing fleet is in, the quays smell of tar and herring, and the wind off the harbour has the first of the cold in it.

oneOf.narrate: In the harbour hospice's long room every bed is full. At the north end, in a row of their own, are the walkers from the Hush, who came down from Ashford on their rope with somebody at each end. They sit up in their beds and look at the door, as they looked at the white, and wait.

In the harbour hospice's long room every bed is full. At the north end are the harbour's white-touched: fishermen and dockers the white has taken too much from, over the years, who sit up in their beds and look at the door, and wait.

opening.narrate: Anwen Holt keeps the hospice: small and quick, greyer than she was, with her sleeves rolled up and a pack of cards in her apron pocket.

Sloe has been in Merrowgate a week. She has asked the harbour council to hear her before midwinter, and the council has said it will, tomorrow, on the harbour steps, in the open, because that is where Merrowgate hears anybody.

oneOf.narrate: Up at the top of the harbour the Lantern Hall's windows are lit late every night. Cass Ord has not forgiven the council for breaking her charter, and she has written to Ailith Strake at Cinder Fold.

Up at the top of the harbour the Lantern Hall's windows are lit late every night. The council has still not paid the Hall's bill for the relief convoy, and Cass Ord has written to Ailith Strake at Cinder Fold.
Up at the top of the harbour the Lantern Hall's windows are lit late every night. The Company's wagons are still in the Wold, and Cass Ord has written to Ailith Strake at Cinder Fold.

opening.narrate: Everybody on the quays knows what the letter says, because the Hall's clerks drink at the Tide Steps. The Hall has offered Ailith its foundries and its ledgers: rung forward at midwinter, every bell in the free wards rings louder for good, and the Hall will cast and sell a louder bell to every town that wants one, and pay the rope families a share of each.

opening.text: Sloe came asking this morning for your healer, the one who's been north. To stand up with her tomorrow on the steps, and tell them she's been there and seen it. I told her she's not here. She asked me what I'd seen instead. I said I'd think about it.

Sloe asked me this morning to stand up with her tomorrow. To tell them I've been there, and seen it, and that she's telling the truth. She believes every word she says. I know she does. I just don't know what I'd be vouching for.

talks.label: Sit with Maren on the tide steps

lines.narrate: Maren is on the tide steps below the hospice with her list of names on her knee, the old list from the year of the keepers, and a newer one under it.

lines.text: She wants me to say the free wards send the white north. I know the tally says so. I've read it. I've seen Orme's doors and Greve's room and the Hush. I believe her.

But tomorrow she'll stand on those steps and tell Merrowgate its bells have been burying people for nine hundred years, and there's nothing they can hear. No noise. No proof. A woman from a country they've never seen, with a slate. And they'll look at me, because they know me, and decide.

oneOf.text: At Greve I let the names stay. Yarrow's house stopped taking griefs, and the grieving kept theirs. I chose that for them. I'm tired of choosing what other people can carry.
At Greve I sent every name to Orme, to be written. I believed in writing it down. I still do. It's what Anwen taught me.
At Greve I let Yarrow's house go on as it always had. I didn't think I had the right to stop it. I'm not sure I've got the right to start anything here, either.

lines.text: If I vouch for her, I'm saying I'm sure. I'm not sure of anything except that she is.

talks.label: Help Anwen with the long room

lines.narrate: Anwen is going down the beds with a tray, and you take the other end of it.

oneOf.text: They came in a row, on a rope, and they've stayed in a row. I've stopped trying to move them about. They like to be able to see each other.
These are the harbour's. Every winter the white takes a little more off the men who work the outer quays, and some of them end up here with nothing left to take.

lines.text: I read them names. Every evening, the whole room, the way I did at the Sallows. Not their names. I don't know their names. Anybody's. The fishermen's, the nurses', mine.

oneOf.text: Maren does it too, when she's here. She reads them the list she keeps. She doesn't know I've noticed that she reads her own name on it last, and quickly.
Your healer used to do it with me, at the Sallows. She'd read her list and leave her own name till last. Tell her I said so, when she's back.

lines.text: Sloe came here first, before she went to the council. She sat with them all one evening and didn't say a word. Then she asked me if we'd always done this, in the south, or if somebody had to teach us. I said somebody taught me.

talks.label: Find Sloe on the harbour steps

lines.narrate: Sloe is sitting on the harbour steps where the council will hear her tomorrow, with her slate on her knee, looking at the boats.

lines.text: Here they hear people outside, on steps, where anybody may stand and listen. In Orme we hear people inside, in the Long Hall, under the oldest wall. I like this better. I would not tell Burdock so.

I have a sum and a tally and nine hundred years. They have their bells, which they love, and which have kept their children. I am going to stand here tomorrow and tell them what their bells do, and they will not hear anything when I say it, because there is nothing to hear. It is very quiet, being buried.

oneOf.text: Your sister of the shrines has been on our side of the peaks. She has read our doors. I have asked her to say so. If she says so, they will hear it. They do not know me. They know her.

I asked for your sister of the shrines. She is not here. I will ask the old woman with the cards instead. She has never been north. She has only been kind to the long room, for years. In Orme that would be enough.

lines.text: And the Hall would like me not to speak at all. I know this. I can do the sum.

talks.label: Go up to the Lantern Hall and see Cass Ord

lines.narrate: Cass Ord's office is at the top of the Hall, with the window over the whole harbour, where it always is. Ailith's answer is on her desk, under the inkwell, unopened.

oneOf.text: Your council broke my charter. Twelve hundred families who'd signed had to unsign. I kept a page for what was wrong with it, and now I keep a page for what it cost. Both pages are long.
Your council sent my wagons north with its seal on and grain in them, and hasn't paid for one of them yet. Iona has my bill. I'm told she's costing it.
My wagons are in the Wold. Forty of them, and the families, and the lamps. They write that the doors up there have everything on them but a price. They're learning. So am I.

lines.text: I'm not lying to you. I never have. Rung forward, every bell in the free wards is louder for good. Louder bells sell. Somebody's going to cast them. I'd rather it was the Hall, and that the rope families had a share, and that it was all written down where anybody can read it.
And the woman on the steps would rather it wasn't rung forward at all. I know. I've a page for her too.

talks.label: Go down to the north quay and find Bett Haddow

oneOf.narrate: Bett Haddow is on the north quay, a year taller, with tar on her hands. She went north on the coaster as ship's girl for one voyage, as her paper said, and came home, and has been asking about the next one ever since.
Bett Haddow is on the north quay with the mate's paper in her pocket, folded small. Last year was 'next year'. This year is next year.
Bett Haddow is up in the harbour's rope-loft over the harbour master's office, splicing, with her own marlinspike. The lines she makes go north on every ship that does.
Bett Haddow is on the north quay, watching the ships, the way she always did.
Bett Haddow is on the north quay, a year taller, coiling rope for anybody who will let her.
Her father is not with her. Coll went north with the Company's wagons, and has not come home. He writes at the end of every summer, from the empty land past Lantry, which is not empty.
Coll Haddow is home from the convoy, loading on his own quay again, at the far end where he can see her.
Coll Haddow is on a bollard at the far end of the quay with his arms folded, where he can see her.

lines.text: Is it true? What the woman with the slate says? That the bells push it all up there, on top of them?

lines.narrate: You tell her it is.

lines.text: Then why does everybody keep asking her to prove it? You don't ask somebody who's cold to prove it. You give them a coat.
Somebody give her a seat on that council.

talks.label: Find out what Elske Marrow makes of it

oneOf.narrate: Elske Marrow is in Merrowgate's chamber, with the Hall's letter to Ailith copied out in front of her, and a great many notes in its margins.
Elske Marrow is at the Sallows hospice, which the council sentenced her to keep open for five years, with the slate by the door wiped clean and a new column started.
Elske Marrow is in the long room at the harbour hospice, where she works now, with Anwen's cards on the table.

oneOf.text: I rang the Mother Bell myself, the night of the great note. I'd do it again. I thought I was sending it nowhere. Nobody ever asked where nowhere was.
I rang the Mother Bell, the night of the great note. I thought I was sending it nowhere. It's in their tally, that night, and I'm in it, without my name. I'd like my name put to it.
I'll be on the bench tomorrow, in my chair, and I'll vote. I don't know yet which way. That's the first time in my life I've said so.
I've no vote. I'll be on the steps anyway. Someone who rang that bell ought to have to stand there and listen.

b4-hospice.clue: The ones in the long room who have lost the most are saying names back. Not their own, which are gone, but new ones, learned from hearing names read aloud every evening, the way a child learns words: a name said aloud in a room is a person in the room, and the white cannot take it while it is being said.

investigate.label: Sit in the long room at the evening reading, and listen to the beds

success.narrate: {You sit|@ sits} at the north end of the long room through the evening reading, and {watch|watches} the beds while the names are read.

oneOf.narrate: At the end of the row a walker moves her lips with the names. Then, when the reading stops, she says one back, out loud, in a cracked voice that has not been used since the Hush: 'Anwen.' And then, after a while, the next one down the list.
At the end of the row an old docker moves his lips with the names. Then, when the reading stops, he says one back, out loud: 'Anwen.' And then, after a while, the next one down the list.
They are the names from Greve, the ones sent to Orme to be written: Maren has been reading the long room the Long Tally's newest page, every evening, and they have begun to say it back.
They are the names from Greve, of people whose families kept them. Maren has been reading the long room the names the grieving would not give, every evening, and they have begun to say them back.
They are anybody's names: the nurses', the fishermen's, Anwen's own. Nobody taught them. They have learned them the way a child learns words, from hearing them said.

success.text: That's new. That's this week. I wasn't going to tell anybody until I was sure. I'm sure.

failure.narrate: {You sit|@ sits} at the north end of the long room through the evening reading, but the beds are quiet, and by the end of the lamp all {you have|@ has} is that some of them move their lips, and {you cannot|@ cannot} tell if it means anything.

route.label: Walk the harbour steps and the lanes behind them before the hearing

success.narrate: {You walk|@ walks} the harbour steps and the lanes behind them at dawn, and {count|counts} the ways down from the Lantern Hall: the front stair, the clerks' lane, and the old rope-walk. {You put|@ puts} a word in with the dockers on the rope-walk, and with the fish-wives on the clerks' lane, to stand where they would stand anyway, and watch.

failure.narrate: {You walk|@ walks} the harbour steps at dawn, but the lanes behind them run every way between the warehouses, and {you come|@ comes} back with more ways down from the Hall than {you can|@ can} count.

direct.label: Go down to the harbour steps with Sloe for the hearing
direct.text: You go down to the harbour steps with Sloe in the morning, for the hearing, and stand where she stands.

approach.narrate: The harbour council sits on the steps at noon, on the benches that are carried out of the harbour master's office for it, with the town standing below on the quay and up the lanes, as many as can fit.

oneOf.narrate: Elske Marrow is in Merrowgate's chair, at the end of the front bench.
Elske Marrow stands at the back, with Anwen, and no chair.

approach.narrate: Sloe stands on the bottom step, facing up, with her slate, and the council looks down at her, and the town looks at both.

approach.text: I am Sloe of Orme. I keep the sum for the Wold. Every winter your bells ring back the white, and every winter it comes to us. I have nine hundred years of it written down. I have come to ask you to let it stop, for one winter, at midwinter, at Cinder Fold, and to share it.

approach.narrate: Nobody says anything. There is nothing to hear. The gulls go over.

crisis.narrate: The Hall's men come down the front stair from the Lantern Hall in a body, twenty of them in the Hall's blue, with staves, and a sergeant in front with a paper.

crisis.text: Sloe of Orme. The Hall has a complaint against you: that you are going about the free wards stirring up feeling against the casting trade. You're to come up to the Hall and answer it. There's a cart for Cinder Fold at the top of the stair. The rope families have asked to hear you too.

crisis.narrate: A cart for Cinder Fold. Everyone on the steps knows whose letter is on Cass Ord's desk.
The council half stands. The town below goes quiet the way a quay goes quiet before a fight. Sloe does not move off the bottom step.

crisis.text: In the Wold, when somebody comes to the door to be heard, nobody takes them away until they have been. I will go up to your Hall afterwards.
They'll have her in that cart before anyone on that bench decides anything. Somebody has to speak before they do.

peaceful.label: Stand up on the steps beside Sloe, and speak for her

success.narrate: {You know|@ knows} what the long room is doing: the ones who have lost the most have begun to say names back. {You send|@ sends} for them, and Anwen brings them down the tide steps, slowly, and stands them at the foot of the harbour steps beside Sloe, where everybody can see them.
On the rope-walk and the clerks' lane the dockers and the fish-wives are standing where they always stand, and every one of the Hall's men can see them.
{You step|@ steps} down between the Hall's sergeant and the bottom step, with nothing in {their} hands, so that he has to go round.

oneOf.narrate: Maren stands up on the bottom step beside Sloe, in her grey, in front of the whole harbour, which has known her since the winter of the Sallows. She does not say the white goes north. She says what she saw: Orme's doors, written top to bottom. Greve's room. The Hush. Somebody in the long room who said a name back to her this week. She says them one at a time, slowly, the way Anwen reads.

{You stand|@ stands} up on the bottom step beside Sloe and {say|says} what {they} saw on the other side of the peaks: Orme's doors, written top to bottom. Greve's room. The Hush. {You do|@ does} not say the white goes north. {You say|@ says} what {they} saw, one thing at a time, slowly, the way Anwen reads.

success.narrate: Nobody on the quay hears anything. They do not have to. They are watching somebody they know stand next to somebody they do not, and say so.

success.text: I've a paper.
You've a paper, and your mother heard me read your name, last on my list, for three winters at the Sallows, and you can put your paper in your coat and go home to her.

success.narrate: He looks at the council, and at the town on the quay, and at the twenty in blue behind him, who are looking at their boots. Then he puts the paper in his coat. The Hall's men go back up the front stair, slowly, and nobody on the quay gets out of their way.
The council sits down again. Sloe finishes what she came to say. It takes the afternoon.

failure.narrate: {You stand|@ stands} up to speak for Sloe, but the Hall's sergeant has his orders, and before {you have|@ has} said three words his men are down the steps with their staves out, and the quay below surges up to meet them.

objective.name: The harbour steps
objective.label: Keep the Hall's men off the bottom step until the council has heard her
objective.description: Four successful actions keep the Hall's men off Sloe and the bottom step until the harbour council has heard her out.
objective.failText: The Hall's men are driven back up the front stair in the end, but not before they had Sloe halfway up it, and her slate is broken on the steps, and the council has adjourned to the harbour master's office with its doors shut, and hears her there, without the town.
objective.successText: The last of the Hall's men goes back up the front stair, and Sloe is still on the bottom step, and the council sits down to hear her.

oneOf.narrate: Evening on the harbour steps. The benches have gone back into the harbour master's office, and the quay is emptying, and nobody is hurt. Sloe is still sitting on the bottom step with her slate, where she has been all day.

Evening on the harbour steps. The benches have gone back into the harbour master's office, and there is blood on the bottom step, and the hospice has six of the Hall's men in its long room and four dockers. Sloe is sitting on the step with her slate in her lap, and a cut over one eye that she has not let anybody look at.

after.narrate: The harbour council has heard her, and has said it will give its answer to the council at Highpass before midwinter, with the rest of the free wards. That is all Merrowgate ever says on the day.

after.text: They listened. Nobody heard anything, and they listened anyway. In Orme that is called a beginning.
Now I would like to know who in the south will say they believe me. Not that I believe it. They can see that. That they do. Before midwinter, I should like to know who.

decisions.label: Maren vouches for Sloe
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Maren gives her word for Sloe, to the council and to the free wards. At midwinter, Sloe will be given the casting hall's north door to keep.

told.ballad: On the harbour steps Sister Maren Vale gave her word for the Reckoner of the Wold, and was not sure, and gave it anyway.
told.tally: Merrowgate. The southern healer gave her word for the Reckoner. Written: she said she was not sure, and gave it.

text.text: I'll write it. To the council, and to Highpass, and to Cinder Fold. That I've been there, and seen it, and that I believe her. That I'm not sure of the sum and I'm sure of her. I'll sign it Maren Vale. Not Sister. Just my name.
Then at midwinter I will have something nobody in the Wold has ever had. A southerner's name on my side of the door.

text.narrate: She writes it that night at Anwen's table, three times, one for each, and reads each one aloud before she seals it.

decisions.label: Maren will not vouch: she is not sure
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Maren will not give her word for Sloe. The free wards will watch Sloe until midwinter, and Sloe will find her own way into the casting hall.

told.ballad: On the harbour steps Sister Maren Vale would not give her word for what she could not be sure of, and said so to the Reckoner's face.
told.tally: Merrowgate. The southern healer would not give her word for the Reckoner. Written: she said she was sorry. It is not the same.

text.text: I can't. I believe you. I've seen it. But if I put my name to it they'll stop asking, and somebody has to keep asking. I'm sorry. I am.
You are honest. I would rather you were honest than on my side. I did not know until now that those were different.

text.narrate: The council's clerk writes that night to Highpass that the Wold's Reckoner should be watched until midwinter, for her own safety. Sloe reads the letter over his shoulder, and says nothing about it.

decisions.label: Maren says nothing, and lets Sloe speak for herself
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Maren neither vouches for Sloe nor refuses her. Sloe will speak for herself, at midwinter, as she did on the steps.

told.ballad: On the harbour steps Sister Maren Vale said nothing, and let the Reckoner of the Wold be heard in her own voice.
told.tally: Merrowgate. The southern healer did not speak for the Reckoner. Written: she let her speak.

text.text: I'm not going to speak for you. Not for you, and not against you. You spoke today. They heard you, not me. I'd only get in the way of that.
In the Wold we would say that is what a door is for. I will try to think so too.

text.narrate: Maren goes back up to the long room, and sits at the end of the north row, and reads the names, and leaves her own till last.

decisions.label: Let Anwen speak for Sloe
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Anwen Holt gives the harbour her own word for Sloe. Sloe will speak for herself at midwinter.

told.ballad: On the harbour steps the old keeper with the cards stood up for the Reckoner of the Wold, and the harbour knew her.
told.tally: Merrowgate. The keeper of the harbour hospice spoke for the Reckoner. Written: she reads names aloud every night, anybody's.

text.text: I've never been north. I've had the long room for years, and this week it's saying names back. That's what I'll tell the council. That's all I know. I'll sign it.
That is more than most people know about anybody.

text.narrate: Anwen writes it at her table that night, on the back of a nurse's rota, and signs it, and puts the pack of cards on top of it so that it will not blow away.

b4-signal.name: The Signal
b4-signal.region: Cinder Fold: the forge-signal tower and the signal house, the town below it, and the casting hall's doors
b4-signal.threat: The rope families have the casting hall and the founders' hatch, a week before midwinter, and they mean to keep the forge-signal dark so that nobody in the deep workings comes up to see what is rung.
b4-signal.brief: A week before midwinter, Cinder Fold's forge-signal is the only light that can call the miners up out of the deep workings. The rope families would like it dark. And Rue has gone down to Sloe's ringers to ask for the rope herself.

told.ballad: At Cinder Fold, a week before midwinter, the girl who always went first went up the signal stair, with her friend gone down to the ringers below.
told.tally: Cinder Fold. The south lit its signal against its own rope families. Rue of Thrum went to the ringers. Written: who went with her.

opening.narrate: The edge of midwinter at Cinder Fold. Snow lies on the passes all round, and on the roofs, and melts off the streets as fast as it falls, because the ground here is warm, as it always is. The casting hall at the top of the town has its great doors shut.

oneOf.narrate: Wren has kept the forge-signal every night since the summer before last, from her chair at the top of the signal house stair. From up there she has watched the rope families carry things into the casting hall at night for a month, with no lamps, and has written down every load.

Ottilie Brand's committee has kept the forge-signal every night since the summer before last, on its rota. From the lamp-room the committee's people have watched the rope families carry things into the casting hall at night for a month, with no lamps, and Ottilie has had every load written in the minutes. The tenth bell on the lid rings a little ahead of the others, as it always does.

Hew has kept the forge-signal every night since the key was put round his neck, the summer before last, at midnight and again at four, and checked it twice each time. He has news, and nobody to tell it to.

The forge-signal has gone unkept since the summer the key left Cinder Fold on its cord. The lamp-room at the top of the town is dark, and nobody was watching the casting hall at night, and the rope families have it now. Its doors have been shut for a month, and rope-men stand at them.
Nessa still has the key on its cord round her neck. She has not taken it off since Cinder Fold gave it to her.
Nessa looks up at the lamp-room from the bottom of the town before she has put her pack down, to see that it is lit. It is. She looks twice.
Nobody has the key in Cinder Fold. It went north on its cord, and has not come back.

opening.narrate: Sloe's twenty ringers have come to Cinder Fold for midwinter, and the miners have lodged them in their own hall at the bottom of the town. They practise at a rope hung from the hall's roof-beam with nothing on the end of it, by ear, because that is how the Wold's ringers learn.
Rue is with them. She went down to the miners' hall two nights ago with her book under her arm, and has not come back up.

opening.text: Sloe means to ring it. Whoever rings it gives the bell everything they have. Sloe has the sum by heart, and nine hundred years of it, and the Wold needs her after. I have only a season to lose. So I am asking for the rope myself. I wanted you to hear it from me.

oneOf.text: She can't. She can't. Somebody tell her she can't.

oneOf.narrate: Nobody answers her.

talks.label: Go after Nessa

lines.narrate: Nessa is on the signal house stair, halfway up, sitting on a step with her knees drawn up, where the stair turns and you can see the whole of the town and the casting hall's shut doors.

lines.text: I went first. All my life. Up this stair, and over the peaks, and into the Hush. That's what I'm for. I said so. I said it to everybody.

And she's going first. Rue. Into the one thing I can't go into for her, because if I ring it, I'm gone, and if she rings it, she's gone, and she's got less to lose than me, and she knows it, and she's right.

oneOf.text: At Thrum she asked me what to do about her mother, because I was the one somebody went back for. I told her. She did it. I don't get to tell her this time. Do I.

She's been writing herself onto other people's doors since the day she walked out of the north. A line at a time, so she'd still be there in the morning. And now she wants to give the whole lot to a bell.

lines.text: I don't know whether to stand next to her or stand in front of her. I've always known. Every time. I don't know now.

talks.label: Go down to the miners' hall and find Rue

lines.narrate: Rue is in the miners' hall at the bottom of the town, sitting on a bench under the empty rope with her book open on her knee, watching the ringers practise.

oneOf.text: I gave my mother at Thrum. I have her written. I read her every morning, like somebody I have heard of, and I like her. There is nothing in me now that would miss her. That is why it should be me.

I kept my mother, at Thrum. All of it, and the hurt with it. If I ring, that goes too. It is the only thing I would lose that I would mind. I have it written. Somebody can read it to me after, and I will like her, the way you like somebody you have heard of.
My first book burned. You saw it. Ilse's copy has the winters in it, and not me. This one starts the summer of the fire. It is thin. It is mine. I would give it.
I have my book. Everything is in it, back to the first page. I would not lose any of it. I would only lose having read it. Somebody else can read it to me.

lines.text: Sloe said no. She said it three times. She is going to have to say it at midwinter, in front of everybody, at the rope. I am going to ask her there. In the Wold that is how it is done.

oneOf.text: Rue.

oneOf.narrate: She looks at the door as if somebody else might come through it, and turns a page.

lines.text: I know. I have written down that you will say that.

talks.label: Go up to the signal house, and ask what has been seen from it

oneOf.narrate: Hew is in the lamp-room at the top of the signal house, with the key round his neck on its cord and his hearth bell on the sill, writing in a book with every night in it, in a hand that has got better since the summer before last.
Ottilie Brand is in the lamp-room at the top of the signal house, with the committee's minutes book open on the sill and the key on its nail beside the rota.
Wren is in her chair at the top of the signal house stair, with a blanket over her knees and her stick across them, and a slate with a month of chalk marks on it.
Ottilie Brand meets you at the foot of the signal house, in the dark. The lamp-room door at the top of the stair has been shut since the summer, and the committee has no key to it.

oneOf.text: Thirty-one nights they've carried. I counted. Three nights ago they carried something heavy, on eight men, wrapped up, down the founders' stair under the lid. Not up. Down. I've never seen anything go down there.

Thirty nights of loads. The minutes have every one. Three nights ago they carried something heavy on eight men down under the lid, by the founders' stair, where nothing goes. The committee voted to ask Ailith what it was. She said bells are her families' business.

Thirty nights. I counted them, every load, the way I always count. Three nights ago, eight men carrying something heavy down under the lid, by the founders' stair. Nobody goes down there. I went down there once.
Nobody was up there to see. I'm the committee. I should have had somebody up there, key or no key. I didn't. Now they've the hall, and the hatch, and we've no light to call the miners up with.

oneOf.narrate: Nobody has told Hew to keep the signal lit this week. He is going to anyway.

oneOf.text: If the signal's lit at midnight, the deep workings come up. Every shift. That's what it's for. Ailith knows it. She'd like them down there till it's done.

oneOf.narrate: If the signal is lit at midnight, the deep workings come up, every shift. That is what it is for. Ailith knows it.

talks.label: Go up to the casting hall's doors and speak to Ailith Strake

lines.narrate: Ailith Strake comes out to you on the casting hall's step, and shuts the door behind her, so that you do not see in.

oneOf.text: A week. Then the rope families ring for the free wards, with the Parting Bell. Forward. Every bell louder, for good. The Mother Bell's rope is in your signal house under your lock, and I'll ask you for the key at midwinter, in front of everybody. Nobody in the free wards will ever have to go into the bronze again, or give at a floor, or be asked for anything. That is what I'm ringing for.

A week. Then the rope families ring for the free wards, as we have every midwinter since Elske's note. This time with the Parting Bell. Forward. Every bell louder, for good. Nobody in the free wards will ever have to go into the bronze again, or give at a floor, or be asked for anything. That is what I'm ringing for.

lines.text: Cass Ord wrote and offered me her foundries. I wrote back that the rope families don't sell bells. She won't have opened it. She'll know what it says.

oneOf.text: Highpass's bell is in the hall, on a frame by the first forge, where my twelve set it down. Sable. He hums when I'm wrong. When I ask him for the note, he'll give it. He said so.
Sable's here. He came of his own will. He stands by me in the hall and says nothing, and I hear him think. When I ask him for the note, he'll give it. He said so.

You have both notes. Sable taught you. I know he did; he wrote and told me. At midwinter I'll ask you for one of them, at the rope, in front of everybody. That's fair. I'd like you to think about which.
I've worked the forward note out for myself, since nobody would give it me. I'm the best ringer alive. I've guessed well. I've had a year.

lines.text: Whoever rings it gives the bell everything. I know. I'm ringing it myself. I'll not ask anybody else to.

b4-signal.clue: The rope families have opened the founders' hatch under the lid and carried the Parting Bell down through it. They mean to ring it from under the nine, at midwinter, with the Mother Bell rung over the first forge above.

investigate.label: Go round the casting hall in the snow, and find out where they have taken the bell

success.narrate: {You go|@ goes} round the outside of the casting hall in the snow after dark, the long way, by the slag heaps, and {find|finds} the founders' stair-house behind it, where the stair comes up from under the lid.

oneOf.narrate: The council's seal is off the hatch. It was lead, pressed with the council's bell, and somebody has cut it through with a chisel and pulled the two halves off and left them in the snow. The hatch stands open. Breaking that seal is a crime the committee can name.
The hatch stands open, and the frost on its lip has been broken by ropes, many times, going down.

success.narrate: In the snow round the hatch are the marks of eight men carrying, and the drag of something heavy on rollers. It went down. Whatever the rope families mean to ring at midwinter, they mean to ring it from under the nine.

oneOf.narrate: And in the snow by the signal house door, leading up from the hatch and back, are new boot-marks, two nights old, of somebody who tried the lock. The Mother Bell's rope is coiled in there, under the lock whose only key is yours. They cannot ring without it.
From the hatch {you can|@ can} see the lamp-room at the top of the signal house. From the lamp-room, anybody up there at midnight can see the hatch.

failure.narrate: {You go|@ goes} round the outside of the casting hall in the snow, but the rope families have men on every corner of it, and {you are|@ is} turned back at the slag heaps before {you have|@ has} seen anything but the backs of the stair-house.

route.label: Climb the signal house in the dark and learn every turn of the stair

success.narrate: {You climb|@ climbs} the signal house stair in the dark, twice, without a lamp, and {count|counts} it: a hundred and twelve steps, a turn every sixteen, and at the seventh turn a door to the signal house's store-room, with a bar on the inside.

failure.narrate: {You climb|@ climbs} the signal house stair in the dark, but it turns and turns again, and somewhere after the fifth turn {you lose|@ loses} count, and {come|comes} down not sure how many there are.

direct.label: Go straight up to the signal house at midnight
direct.text: You go straight up through the town to the signal house at midnight, with the snow coming down and melting on the street.

approach.narrate: Midnight. The snow is coming down thick over the casting hall and the town, and melting on the streets. At the top of the town the signal house stands up into it, with its lamp-room dark or lit, and its stair going up inside like a screw.

oneOf.narrate: Nessa goes up the stair first. She always has.
Hew goes up the stair first, with the key round his neck, and Nessa goes up behind him.
Hew goes up the stair first, with the key round his neck, and you go up behind him.
You go up the stair first.

crisis.narrate: At the fourth turn of the stair, below you, the door at the bottom opens, and rope-men come in out of the snow, a dozen of them, with ropes over their shoulders and no lamps.

crisis.text: Ailith says leave the lamp dark this week. Nobody's to be hurt. Come down, and nobody will be.

oneOf.text: And she'll have the key to the store-room. The rope's in there. She needs the rope.
The deep workings stay down till it's rung. Ailith's word. It's for them too.

crisis.narrate: They start up the stair. It is narrow enough for one at a time. Above, the lamp-room is three turns off, in the dark.

oneOf.text: Hew. Go up. Light it. I've got the stair.
I'll light it. Hold the turn. Don't let them past the turn.

peaceful.label: Get the signal lit before the rope-men reach the lamp-room

success.narrate: {You know|@ knows} where the bell went: down the founders' hatch, under the nine. If the miners come up tonight they will see the hatch, and the whole of Cinder Fold will know by morning what is being rung, and where. That is why the lamp must be lit tonight, and not tomorrow.
{You know|@ knows} the stair: a hundred and twelve steps, a turn every sixteen, and the store-room door at the seventh turn with its bar on the inside.
{You go|@ goes} up the stair two steps at a time in the dark, counting, and {lose|loses} count, and {go|goes} on anyway.

oneOf.narrate: Hew goes up to the lamp-room with the key, a step at a time, counting out loud, the way he has every night, and Nessa stands on the stair at the turn below him with her back to the wall and her hand out, and the first of the rope-men stops a step below her hand.
Nessa goes up the stair to the lamp-room without a lamp, two steps at a time, the way Wren taught her, and does not count, because she has never needed to.

Hew goes up to the lamp-room with the key, counting out loud, and {you stand|@ stands} on the stair at the turn below him, with {their} back to the wall, and the first of the rope-men stops a step below.
{You put|@ puts} {their} shoulder to the lamp-room door at the last turn until the old lock gives, and {find|finds} the wick and the flint by touch, where every keeper has kept them for twenty years.
{You go|@ goes} up the last turn to the lamp-room and {find|finds} the wick and the flint by touch, where every keeper has kept them for twenty years.

success.narrate: The lamp is lit. It goes up out of the lamp-room's high window over the snow, white and steady, and over the whole of Cinder Fold, and down the shafts, the way it is meant to every midnight.

success.text: That's done, then.

success.narrate: He says it to nobody, and stands on the stair a while with the others behind him. Then they go back down, slowly, one at a time, and out into the snow.
Within the hour the deep workings come up. Shift after shift, with their lamps, out of every shaft-head in the town, into the snow, to see what the signal wants. Then they see the hatch.

failure.narrate: {You go|@ goes} for the lamp-room, but the stair is narrow and dark and the rope-men are on it below, faster than anybody could be on a stair they do not know, and before {you are|@ is} at the sixth turn there are hands on the rope at {their} back.

objective.name: The lamp-room
objective.label: Hold the stair until the signal is lit
objective.description: Four successful actions hold the signal house stair against the rope-men until the lamp in the lamp-room is lit.
objective.failText: The lamp is lit in the end, an hour late, and the deep workings come up to it, but on the stair two of the rope-men went over the rail at the turn, and one of them is not getting up, and the miners carry him down to the hall past the ringers.
objective.successText: The lamp goes up in the lamp-room, white and steady over the snow, and the rope-men on the stair below it stop.

oneOf.narrate: Before dawn. The signal is lit over Cinder Fold. The miners stand round the founders' hatch in the snow with their lamps, a thousand of them, saying nothing, and the rope families stand at the casting hall's doors, and nobody is hurt.

Before dawn. The signal is lit over Cinder Fold. The miners stand round the founders' hatch in the snow with their lamps, a thousand of them, saying nothing, and the rope families stand at the casting hall's doors with their hurt, and the stair is dark with blood at the fourth turn.
The store-room is shut, and barred, and the Mother Bell's rope is still in it under your lock. Without it nobody rings the Mother Bell at midwinter.
The Mother Bell's rope is up in the casting hall, as it has been since the night of the great note. The rope families hold it.

after.narrate: Down in the miners' hall the ringers have heard the lamp go up. Rue has come out onto the step of the hall with her book, and stands in the snow looking up at the signal, and waits to see who will come down the hill to her.

after.text: The miners know now. Everybody does. Good. It should be rung in front of everybody. Now I would like to know who is coming with me, and who is stopping me, and who is staying up there with the lamp.

decisions.label: Nessa goes down to Rue, and stays with her among the ringers
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Nessa goes to Sloe's ringers with Rue. At midwinter she will be at Rue's side at the rope, whatever is rung.

told.ballad: At Cinder Fold Nessa Reed came down off the signal stair and stood beside her friend among the ringers, and did not go first.
told.tally: Cinder Fold. The southern girl went to the ringers with Rue of Thrum. Written: she will stand next to her.

text.narrate: Nessa comes down the hill in the snow, and stops on the step of the miners' hall in front of Rue, and does not say anything for a long time.

text.text: I'm not going to stop you. I'm not going to go first. I'm going to stand next to you. All the way to the rope. If you ring it, I'll be there when you've done. I'll tell you who you are. I'll tell you every day.
Write it down for me. Now. So it is written.

text.narrate: Nessa writes it in Rue's book, in capitals, under the last line: 'I WILL TELL YOU WHO YOU ARE. NESSA.'

decisions.label: Nessa tells Rue no, and stops her
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Nessa tells Rue no. Rue will not ring the Parting Bell at midwinter.

told.ballad: At Cinder Fold Nessa Reed told her friend no, for the first time, and her friend listened.
told.tally: Cinder Fold. The southern girl told Rue of Thrum no. Written: Rue did as she was asked. She wrote it down that she did not like it.

text.narrate: Nessa comes down the hill in the snow, fast, and takes Rue's book out of her hands on the step of the miners' hall, and holds it.

text.text: No. Not you. I don't care whose sum it is. I don't care that it's a season. It's your season. I was in it. I'm not having it rung out of you so everybody else can sleep. No.
Nobody has ever told me no for my own sake. In the Wold nobody would.
Then I will not ask for the rope. Give me the book. I want to write down that you said it.

text.narrate: She writes it, small, under the last line, and then shows Nessa, and Nessa reads it, and does not say anything.

decisions.label: Nessa lets Rue go, and keeps the signal
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Nessa stays in the lamp-room and keeps the signal lit. Rue goes to the ringers alone.

told.ballad: At Cinder Fold Nessa Reed kept the signal lit over the town, and let her friend go down the hill alone.
told.tally: Cinder Fold. The southern girl kept the forge-signal and let Rue of Thrum go. Written: somebody has to keep the lamp.

text.narrate: Nessa does not come down. She stands at the lamp-room's high window with the signal at her back and looks down at Rue on the step of the miners' hall, and Rue looks up.

text.text: Somebody's got to keep it lit. Till midwinter. Till it's done. So that whatever's rung, everybody sees. That's mine. That was always mine. She's got to go and do hers.

text.narrate: Rue lifts her book once, the way you lift a hand, and goes back into the miners' hall, and shuts the door.

text.text: She'll write it down that I didn't come. I'd like her to.

decisions.label: Let Rue go down to the ringers
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Rue goes to Sloe's ringers alone, to ask for the rope at midwinter.

told.ballad: At Cinder Fold the girl with the book went down to the ringers alone, under the signal.
told.tally: Cinder Fold. Rue of Thrum went to the ringers alone. Written: nobody stopped her, and nobody went with her.

text.narrate: You do not go down the hill. It is not yours to stop her, and the one who might have is not here.
Rue lifts her book once, the way you lift a hand, and goes back into the miners' hall, and shuts the door.

b4-ropes.name: The Rope Families
b4-ropes.region: Cinder Fold: the casting hall at the top of the town, the nine on the lid, and the Mother Bell over the first forge
b4-ropes.threat: Ailith Strake's rope families hold the casting hall on midwinter day, with the Parting Bell under the lid below them, and they mean to ring it forward at midnight.
b4-ropes.brief: Midwinter day at Cinder Fold. The rope families hold the casting hall, and the Parting Bell is under the lid below them. Ailith Strake means to ring it forward at midnight, for the free wards, for good. The hall has to be taken back before then.

told.ballad: On midwinter day at Cinder Fold the rope families shut the casting hall, and the bell was under their feet, and the founders had written them an answer.
told.tally: Cinder Fold, midwinter day. The rope families held the casting hall. Written: the founders were asked, nine hundred years ago, and said no.

opening.narrate: Midwinter day at Cinder Fold. The sun is up for six hours and does not get over the peaks for any of them. The whole town is out in the street below the casting hall, miners and committee and the council's people, and the snow melts on the cobbles as it falls.

The casting hall's great doors are shut. Inside, as everybody in Cinder Fold knows, the nine stand on the iron lid over the first forge, and the Mother Bell hangs over them all from its beam the size of a tree. Under the lid, at the foot of the founders' stair, is the Parting Bell, where the rope families carried it.

oneOf.narrate: The Mother Bell's rope is up, as it has been since the night of the great note, and the rope families have it. Every midwinter since Elske's note they have rung it for the free wards. Tonight they mean to ring it with the Parting Bell.

The Mother Bell hangs bare. Its rope is still coiled in the signal house's store-room, behind the bar, under your lock. Without it nobody rings the Mother Bell tonight, and without the Mother Bell the Parting Bell's note is nothing. Ailith knows it.

Orin's forty are across the street from the great doors, in the council's grey, with their captain in front of them. Davin has the rear door, round by the slag heaps, with six of them. Nobody has told him he may leave it.
Orin's forty are across the street from the great doors, in the council's grey, with their captain in front of them. He has learnt every name, and he says them under his breath as he walks the line.

The council's forty are across the street from the great doors, in grey. Their captain has gone up and down the line since dawn saying their names, and nobody has had to be told twice. Round by the slag heaps a boy of seventeen has the rear door, with six of them.
The council's forty are across the street from the great doors, in grey, under the captain Sorrel's paper made. They have their orders and their names, and nobody has had to be told twice.
Sorrel's watch is across the street from the great doors, forty of them in the council's grey, with Sorrel's sergeant in front of them hating every minute of it.

opening.narrate: Brannagh has come up from Highpass for the council. Elske Marrow has the chair this session, at Highpass; here, at Cinder Fold, Brannagh chairs.
At the top of the step, with the doors shut behind her, Ailith Strake stands and waits for the town to be quiet. When it is, she speaks to all of it.

opening.text: Once. That's all. The Parting Bell rung forward with the Mother Bell, once, at midnight, and every ward in the free wards is louder for good. No more floors. No more giving. No more asking a child what they'd miss. My families have rung for you for nine hundred years. Let us ring this.

oneOf.text: And don't let the council tell you it's not for one woman to say. The council took the rope off one woman three winters ago. Elske Marrow. Recalled her, in that hall, with the doors open. Now you'd take it off a town.
The rope's in your store-room, under your lock. Bring me the key by midnight, in front of everybody, or tell everybody why you didn't.
The rope's ours. It has been since the great note. We ring at midnight.

opening.narrate: Hesk stands beside her on the step. The free wards have called him their hero since the stair. He does not look as if he likes it any better than he did.

oneOf.narrate: Behind her, somewhere in the hall, a bell hums: low and patient, the hum of Highpass's bell when it is somewhere it would rather not be. Sable.
Behind her, in the doorway, stands a tall man in a scholar's coat with a sack of books at his feet. Sable, who came to Cinder Fold of his own will and has said nothing since.

opening.narrate: Then she goes back in, and the bar drops on the inside of the doors.

oneOf.text: Rue's in the miners' hall. Whatever happens in there, she's going to want to be at the rope for it. So am I.
She's the best ringer alive. She'll have it worked out to the breath. That's what scares me.

oneOf.narrate: Somewhere down the street a miner says it to the man next to him: she's the best ringer alive, and she will have it worked out to the breath.

talks.label: Knock on the small door in the great doors, and ask for Ailith Strake

lines.narrate: The small door in the great doors opens a hand's width, and then wider, and Ailith lets you in herself, and shuts it behind you. The casting hall is warm and enormous and full of rope. Her families are on every one of the nine, sitting on the lid with their ropes across their knees.

lines.text: My grandmother lost three of her five to the white in one winter. That's not a story. That's the line in our book above my mother's name. I'm the best ringer alive. I can stop it. I'm to be told I mayn't, because the north has a sum.

oneOf.text: Sable's taught you both notes. I know. He wrote and told me. I'll not ask you for the forward one; I've guessed it. I'm asking you not to stop me ringing it.
Sable gave me the note. He stands over there and hums it when I'm wrong. I'm not often wrong now.
Nobody would give me the note, so I worked it out. A year at it. I've guessed well. I'll know at midnight how well.

lines.text: Whoever rings it gives the bell everything. I'm ringing it. Not my son. Not a miner's boy. Me. That's the price, and I'm paying it, and I'd like it written down that I paid it.

talks.label: Find Ottilie Brand at the committee's table in the street

lines.narrate: Ottilie Brand has had the committee's table carried out into the street in front of the casting hall, with the minutes book on it under a stone so it does not blow, and she sits at it in her coat and writes down everything anybody says.

lines.text: The hall's the town's. Not the rope families'. Not the council's. The town's. The committee voted it this morning, eleven to none, with Ailith's own cousin voting. I've written to her that she's holding the town's hall against the town. She sent the letter back with 'yes' on it.

oneOf.text: Everybody knows now. The council said it out loud in Highpass, with the doors open, and half her families heard it from the inn yard and not from her. Some of them are in there because they're angry with her for not telling them. They're in there anyway.
She read the founders' page to her own families, the spring before last. Every one of them knows what the bell does. Some of them are in there because of it.
Half of them in there don't know what they're holding it for. They know Ailith asked.

lines.text: I don't want anybody hurt on that step. I'd like that in the minutes too.

talks.label: Go round to the hall's high windows and talk to whoever is on the ropes below them

lines.narrate: At the back of the casting hall the high windows are open for the heat, and below the nearest of them, on the first bell's rope, sits a young man with his mother's jaw, coiling and uncoiling the tail of the rope round his hand.

lines.text: Her son. Wystan. I'm on the first bell. I've been on the first bell since I was nine.
She says it's her that rings it. She says it every day, so that none of us offers. I offered. She said if I ever offered again she'd put me off the ropes for good. That's how I know she means it.

oneOf.narrate: Two bells along, on the ninth's rope, sits Garth Mott, the miner's son, fifteen now, with the rope across his knees the way the families sit. Nobody has taken it off him. Perrin Rowe's family is whoever Perrin says it is.
Two bells along, on the ninth's rope, sits Garth Mott, the miner's son, fifteen now, with the rope across his knees the way the families sit. Nobody has taken it off him.
Two bells along, on a spare rope beside the ninth, sits Garth Mott, the miner's son, in case anybody is short tonight. He has not been asked to leave.
Down through the lid, faint, from the miners' galleries, comes the gallery bell, rung in time against the nine. Garth Mott, below, keeping their time for them, as he does every shift.
Two bells along, on the ninth's rope, sits old Perrin Rowe, with his ruined hands bound to the rope with cloth so they will not slip.

lines.text: I don't know if she's right. I know she's never once been wrong on a rope.

talks.label: Go to the casting hall's north door, where Sloe is

lines.narrate: The casting hall's north door is small and iron and nobody uses it. Sloe sits on its step in the snow with her slate on her knee. The council gave her the door to keep at midwinter, on a southerner's word, and she is keeping it.

oneOf.text: Your healer wrote my name on three letters and signed hers under it. The council gave me this door because of it. It is the first door in the south that is mine to keep. I am not going to open it to go in. I am going to keep it.

Maren Vale wrote my name on three letters and signed hers under it. The council gave me this door because of it. It is the first door in the south that is mine to keep. I am not going to open it to go in. I am going to keep it.

lines.text: My ringers are in the miners' hall. Twenty of them. If Ailith rings forward, everything she pushes away from the south comes to the Wold at once, at midnight, with nobody on any rope there to stop it. I have done that sum. I do not need my slate for it.
I would like the hall taken back without anybody dying in it. In the Wold we would say that is the only way a hall is ever really taken back.

b4-ropes.clue: The founders cast nine bells on the lid, and drew a tenth, and did not pour it. Under the tenth mould, in their own hand, they wrote why: Not this way. Ask them all. The rope families have never been shown it.

investigate.label: Find what the founders wrote about the tenth bell, and bring it to the hall

oneOf.narrate: The tenth mould is not in Cinder Fold. Rafe and Tilda Coppin sold it to the Lantern Hall, and it has stood in the Hall's front hall at Merrowgate since the summer before last with its writing turned to the wall. But Cass Ord has had it carted back up the mountain this week, at the Hall's expense, with a note for the committee that Ottilie has pinned to her table: 'Since Cinder Fold does not sell.' {You find|@ finds} it on its cart in the street behind the committee's table, still roped down.

{You go|@ goes} to the tenth mould where it stands in the casting hall against the wall, by the small door, with its writing turned outwards, as Ottilie had it put. The rope families walk past it every day.

{You go|@ goes} down to the vault under the first forge, by the committee's key, and {find|finds} the founders' ledger in its iron box, and {turn|turns} to the last page, where the tenth mould is drawn and measured and never used.

success.narrate: Under it, in the founders' square hand, five words. Not this way. Ask them all.

{You copy|@ copies} them out large, on the back of a page of Ottilie's minutes, in letters a whole hall could read from the lid. The founders could have cast a tenth bell and rung the north quiet for good. They knew how. They wrote down that they would not, and why, and left it where the rope families would one day have to look at it.

failure.narrate: {You look|@ looks} for what the founders wrote, and {find|finds} the words, Not this way, Ask them all, but nobody in the street will take them on a southerner's word until they see the founders' own hand, and there is no time to fetch it before the light goes.

route.label: Learn every door into the casting hall, and who holds each one

success.narrate: {You go|@ goes} round the casting hall twice in the last of the light and {count|counts} its doors: the great doors, barred; the small door in them; the rear door by the slag heaps; the north door, iron, that nobody uses; and the high windows, open for the heat, with the ropes of the first bell hanging just inside the nearest of them.

failure.narrate: {You go|@ goes} round the casting hall in the last of the light, but the rope families have a man at every corner, and {you are|@ is} turned back twice, and by dark {you know|@ knows} only the great doors and the rear one.

direct.label: Walk up to the great doors and knock
direct.text: You walk up the step to the great doors in front of the whole town, and knock, and wait.

approach.narrate: Dusk. Every lamp in Cinder Fold is lit, and the forge-signal is lit over all of them. The town stands in the street below the casting hall and waits, and the snow comes down and melts.

oneOf.narrate: Orin takes his forty up onto the step, and puts them either side of the great doors in two lines, and stands at the end of one of them himself.
The council's forty go up onto the step, and stand either side of the great doors in two lines, the way they were told.
Sorrel's sergeant takes the watch up onto the step, and stands them either side of the great doors in two lines, and tells them, loudly, that nobody draws anything.

crisis.narrate: The great doors open from the inside, both of them, all the way, and the light of the hall comes out onto the step and the street. Inside, the rope families stand along the lid in their families, with their ropes in their hands, and in front of them stand their champions: the biggest of them, with the wedge-mauls the hall's doors are driven shut with.

crisis.text: Come in, then. All of you. You've a right to see it. But you'll not get past the lid while my families are on it.

crisis.narrate: Behind her, on its beam, the Mother Bell hangs over the hall. Under the lid, under all of them, something is waiting at the foot of the founders' stair.

oneOf.text: They'll fight. Not because they're sure. Because she asked, and they've never once said no to her. Somebody has to give them something else to listen to.

oneOf.narrate: The champions lift their mauls. Nobody on the step moves.

peaceful.label: Lay the founders' words before the rope families

easierWith.reason: The rope families already know what the bell does, and that the free wards know it too

harderWith.reason: Sable stands by Ailith in the hall, and every ringer there has heard him hum the note

success.narrate: {You have|@ has} the founders' five words, in their own hand, and a copy large enough for the lid to read.
{You know|@ knows} every door of the hall, and the council's people are at all of them, quietly, so that nobody in the hall can say they were shut in.
{You walk|@ walks} in at the great doors with nothing in {their} hands, past the champions, slowly, so that they have to decide whether to stop {them}.

oneOf.narrate: Ottilie's people bring the tenth mould in on its cart, through the great doors, and stand it at the edge of the lid with its writing turned to the families.
{You stand|@ stands} by the tenth mould, against the wall where it has always stood, and {put|puts} a hand on the band round its foot.
{You hold|@ holds} up the founders' ledger, open at the last page, where the whole lid can see the tenth mould drawn and measured and never poured.

success.narrate: {You read|@ reads} it out. Not this way. Ask them all. Then {you say|@ says} what it means, as plainly as it can be said: that the founders could have cast a tenth and stopped the white for the south for good, and chose not to, and wrote down why, and that the same hands wrote the lid's first rota.

oneOf.narrate: Nessa does not say anything. She goes up onto the lid, to the ninth bell, and sits down beside whoever is on its rope, and puts her hand flat on the iron the way the miners do.
Nobody says anything for a long time.

success.narrate: Then, on the first bell, Wystan Strake stands up, and puts his rope down on the lid, and steps back from it.

success.text: Ask them all. We never did. Not once in nine hundred years. We asked each other.

success.narrate: One by one, along the lid, the families put their ropes down. Not all of them. Enough. The champions look at Ailith, and she looks at the five words for a long time, and does not tell them anything, and they lower their mauls.

failure.narrate: {You read|@ reads} the founders' words out across the lid, but the champions are already coming, and in the noise of the hall nobody on the ropes can hear a word of it.

objective.name: The lid
objective.label: Hold the lid's edge until the families put their ropes down
objective.description: Four successful actions hold the edge of the lid against the rope families' champions, without taking a rope from anybody, until the families put them down of their own will.
objective.failText: The families put their ropes down in the end, when there is nobody left standing to hold them, and two of the champions do not get up off the lid.
objective.successText: Along the lid, one by one, the rope families put their ropes down, and their champions lower their mauls.

oneOf.narrate: Late on midwinter day, in the casting hall. The ropes lie where the families put them down, across the lid, and the champions sit with their backs to the wall and their mauls across their knees, and nobody is hurt.

Late on midwinter day, in the casting hall. The ropes lie across the lid where they were dropped, and there is blood on the iron by the third bell, and Cinder Fold's physicians are on their knees beside two of the champions. The rest sit with their backs to the wall.

after.narrate: Ailith Strake stands at the head of the founders' stair, with the hatch open below her and the warm coming up out of it, and does not go down, and does not come away.

after.text: I'll not run. I'm the best ringer alive. Somebody's going to need me on a rope before tonight's out. I can hear it.

oneOf.text: The committee will have her, if the council lets it. It's our hall she held, and our town.
The committee will have her, if the council lets it. The council recalled one woman from that rope three winters ago. I'd like the town to do this one.

after.text: The council will have her. It's every town's bell she meant to ring.

decisions.label: Give Ailith to the council's judgement
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Ailith Strake answers to the council for holding the casting hall and the Parting Bell. She is held under the council's guard until she is judged.

told.ballad: At Cinder Fold the best ringer alive put down her rope and gave herself to the council, and was led out under guard.
told.tally: Cinder Fold. Ailith Strake was given to the council to be judged. Written: she did not run.

text.narrate: You give her to the council. Brannagh says it in front of everybody, so that it is said: Ailith Strake will answer to the council of the free wards, in the open, in the spring session.

text.text: Good. In the open. I'll say it all again, and they can write it down.

text.narrate: Two of the council's people take her to the door of the hall, and stop there, and stand either side of her, because she has asked to see it rung, whatever is rung, and nobody can think of a reason why not.

decisions.label: Give her to Cinder Fold's committee
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Ailith Strake answers to Cinder Fold, whose hall she held. Ottilie Brand's committee will judge her, in the casting hall.

told.ballad: At Cinder Fold the town took its own ringer home, and judged her in its own hall.
told.tally: Cinder Fold. Ailith Strake was given to the committee of her own town. Written: Cinder Fold asked for her.

text.narrate: You give her to the town. Ottilie writes it in the minutes first, and then says it, and Brannagh lets her.

text.text: In the casting hall, after the thaw, with every family in it. I'll chair it. Nobody else wants to.

text.narrate: Two of the committee's miners take Ailith to the door of the hall, and stand either side of her there, because she has asked to see it rung, and Cinder Fold has never in its life refused a ringer that.

decisions.label: Leave her on the ropes, under watch: she is the best ringer they have
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Ailith Strake stays on the ropes, under watch, because whatever is rung tonight will need the best ringer alive. She rings in whatever comes next.

told.ballad: At Cinder Fold they left the best ringer alive on her rope, with a guard at her back, because the night was not over.
told.tally: Cinder Fold. Ailith Strake kept her rope, under watch. Written: she was needed.

text.narrate: You leave her on the ropes. Brannagh does not like it, and says so, and then puts two of the council's people at her back, and says that too.

text.text: Under watch. Fine. Watch, then. You'll see how it's done.

text.narrate: She goes back up onto the lid, to the first bell, and picks up her son's rope where he put it down, and puts it back in his hands, and stands beside him.

b4-ropes.ledgeLabel: Rest, then go back to the lid
b4-ropes.climbLabel: Go back out into Cinder Fold
b4-ropes.climbText: The party goes out of the casting hall into Cinder Fold. The lid waits where you left it: depart again to go back to the same encounter.

ledge.narrate: You wake on the casting floor, by the committee's table that someone has carried in out of the snow, with a miner's coat over you and the warm of the first forge coming up through the iron.
Above you the nine stand on the lid, and the Mother Bell hangs over them from its beam. Below, the hatch at the head of the founders' stair is open, and something under the lid is humming.

b4-lid.name: The Lid
b4-lid.region: Cinder Fold: under the lid, at the foot of the founders' stair, where the Parting Bell is
b4-lid.threat: Half a note of the Parting Bell has been struck under the lid, and the white of both countries, rung back from both sides of the peaks, is meeting under Cinder Fold.
b4-lid.brief: Midwinter night. Somebody has struck the Parting Bell half a note under the lid, and it has not stopped. The white of the south and the white of the Wold are coming up under Cinder Fold together, and the lid is heaving.

told.ballad: Under the lid at Cinder Fold, on midwinter night, the two winters met, and the miners and the Wold's ringers rang the nine together.
told.tally: Cinder Fold, midwinter night. Both winters under the lid. Written: who held the bell until midnight.

opening.narrate: Midwinter night. The first you know of it is the floor. The iron lid under the nine lifts under your boots, a finger's breadth, and settles, and lifts again, and every bell standing on it rings a little, by itself, out of time.
