Then the sound comes up the founders' stair: one note, or half of one, from the Parting Bell at the foot of it, going on and on, as if it had been struck and nobody had told it to stop.

oneOf.text: That was me. In the last hour of the day, before the doors opened, I went down and struck it half a note. To hear it. I'd only guessed the note. I guessed wrong. It's not stopping.
That was me. In the last hour of the day, before the doors opened, I went down and struck it half a note. To hear it. I wanted to know I had it right. I had. It's not stopping.

opening.narrate: Under the lid the white is coming. Not from the north, or not only: from both sides of the peaks at once: the south's white, that the wards ring north every winter, and the white that has lain on the Wold for nine hundred years and been rung back at it every winter since, meeting under Cinder Fold at the one bell that can turn them.

oneOf.narrate: The Mother Bell hangs over the hall on its beam, its rope up, humming with the half note.
The Mother Bell hangs over the hall on its beam, bare, its rope still in the signal house, humming with the half note anyway.

oneOf.text: The council recalled that bell three winters ago, and I'll not have anybody ring it tonight without the council's say. I'll say it again at midnight, if we get there.

oneOf.narrate: Out in the street, the town has heard it, and nobody has gone home.
Sloe comes in by the north door, the door she was given to keep, with her twenty ringers behind her in single file, and shuts it behind them.
Sloe comes in by the north door with her twenty ringers behind her. Nobody gave it to her. She came because it was you who told her where the bell was, and she tried the door, and it was open.

Sloe does not come in by any door. She comes up through the lid, by the hatch at the foot of the marked way, with her twenty ringers behind her on a rope, out of the dark under Cinder Fold, the way the founders went.
Sloe comes in at the great doors with her twenty ringers behind her, and asks at them to be let in, as anybody may, and is.
Maren watches her come in. Maren would not vouch for her, at the harbour. She does not say anything now either.
At Merrowgate the harbour's clerk wrote that she should be watched. She trusted your word over his.

opening.text: Two winters. Both of them, under one town. I did not have that in my sum. I should have.

oneOf.text: Then we hold it. Whatever's coming up those stairs. That's all there is to do.

oneOf.narrate: Nobody says what to do.

talks.label: Talk to Sloe at the head of the founders' stair

lines.narrate: Sloe stands at the head of the founders' stair with her slate, and looks down it, and does a sum.

lines.text: If the half note goes on until midnight, both winters come up through this floor at once, into the nine, and the nine cannot hold one of them out of time. Cinder Fold first. Then whatever is nearest.
If the nine are rung in time, the lid settles, and the bell stops, and at midnight we are where we were this morning, and somebody has to choose. I would rather be where we were this morning.

oneOf.text: Your council gave me a door. I am in the south's hall, by the south's door. I would like to keep it until midnight. After that I do not know what is mine.
I came up the marked way because I was not sure any door in the south would open to me. It was cold. It was my choice. I would make it again.
You trusted me with where the bell was. I came here because of it. Nobody has written it on your door. You know it is there.
I asked at your doors like anybody. It was strange, being let in for asking. I would like the Wold to try it.

talks.label: Find Rue among Sloe's ringers

oneOf.narrate: Rue is with the ringers, on the lid, with her book under her arm and Nessa beside her. Neither of them is talking.
Rue is with the ringers, on the lid, with her book under her arm. Somebody wrote in it, in capitals, that they would tell her who she is. She keeps her thumb on that page.
Rue is with the ringers, on the lid, with her book. She is not asking for a rope. She said she would not, and she has written down that she does not like it.
Rue is with the ringers, on the lid, with her book under her arm. She came down to them alone, and she has stayed.

lines.text: I can hear it in the floor. Both of them. The Wold's white, and yours. They are the same white. I always thought it would be different. It is only the same thing, going both ways, and meeting.
I am writing it down. Whatever happens at midnight, somebody will want to read that tonight the two winters met, and what the floor did.

oneOf.text: Somebody told me no. I am writing that down too. Again. In case I forget I minded.
Sloe will say no again at midnight. I will ask again. That is how it is done.

talks.label: Put a hand on the nearest of the nine, and listen

lines.narrate: You put your hand flat on the third bell, where it stands on the lid, the way the miners do. Under the half note, through the bronze, the joined bells are all ringing at once, every bell in the free wards with somebody in it.

oneOf.text: Can you hear this? It's Tovin, at Briarwatch. I've got my hand on our bell, and it's shaking, and Pim says yours must be shaking worse. She's not in it to ask. So I'm asking. Whatever you do down there, do it in time.

Can you hear this? It's Tovin, at Briarwatch. I've got my hand on our bell, and it's shaking, and Pim says yours must be shaking worse. She's not in it to ask. So I'm asking. Whatever you do down there, do it in time.
It's in every one of us. Every bell with somebody in it, from Vell to Briarwatch. Half a note, and we're all half out of ourselves.
It's in every one of us. Every bell with somebody in it. Half a note, and we're all half out of ourselves. Pim's holding the rope. He won't let go.

oneOf.narrate: Then the bells carry nothing but the half note.
Then the bells carry nothing but the half note.

oneOf.text: Ring them in time. The nine. That's all it wants. Something in time, to stand on.

talks.label: Find Burdock, who came south with the tally

lines.narrate: Burdock sits on the casting floor with his back to the wall and the book of winters on his knees, open at a page he has not written on yet.

lines.text: Nine hundred years. I have read every line of it, and in every one of them the white comes from the south. I never once asked where the south had it from. From us. It is the same white, going both ways. I will have to go back and write that in, at the beginning.
Tonight I am going to write down what happened. Exactly. Whoever holds the bell, and how they held it. It is the only thing I can do that nobody else here can.

b4-lid.clue: The half note has put the nine out of time. Ring the nine in time, all of them, together, and the lid will settle, and the Parting Bell will stop.

investigate.label: Listen to the nine, and find what the half note has done to them

success.narrate: {You stand|@ stands} on the lid among the nine and {listen|listens}, bell by bell, the way the rope families teach their children to, with an ear to each.

oneOf.narrate: The nine are only bronze now. They rested, when the free wards voted it, and nobody in them answers. But bronze can be out of time too, and they are: every one of them shaken off its beat by the half note under the lid. Rung by hand, in time, together, they would give the floor something to stand on.

The nine are out of time. Every one of them, shaken off its beat by the half note, ringing a little by itself, and the voices in them are pulling against each other. Rung by hand, in time, together, they would give the floor something to stand on, and the voices something to hold.

success.narrate: {You tell|@ tells} Sloe, and the rope families, and the miners at the door. In time, all nine, together, from the first rope to the ninth, and keep it.

failure.narrate: {You listen|@ listens} to the nine, but the half note is in everything, the lid and the bronze and the floor, and {you can|@ can} hear that something is wrong with the beat, and not what.

route.label: Go down the founders' stair to the Parting Bell, and learn the way back up

success.narrate: {You go|@ goes} down the founders' stair under the lid, into the warm and the dark, and {count|counts} it: forty steps cut in the rock, and then the vault, and the Parting Bell on its frame in the middle of it, humming, small as a bucket and black with age.
{You come|@ comes} back up it twice, until {you know|@ knows} it in the dark.

failure.narrate: {You go|@ goes} down the founders' stair, but the lid heaves overhead, and dust and grit come down, and {you come|@ comes} back up not sure how many steps there were.

direct.label: Go straight down the founders' stair to the bell
direct.text: You go straight down the founders' stair to the Parting Bell, with the lid heaving over your head.

approach.narrate: Under the lid. The vault at the foot of the founders' stair is round and warm, cut out of the rock, with the first forge's heat in its walls. The Parting Bell hangs in the middle of it on a frame of new timber, humming, small and black.
Round the walls, and up through the cracks in the floor, comes the white: grey and slow and very cold, from two sides at once.

crisis.narrate: The white comes up out of the floor in two shapes, from two sides of the vault, and they turn to face each other across the Parting Bell: one the south's, the colour of a free-wards winter, and one the Wold's, the colour of Orme's doors. Two winters, each the size of a country, folded small into a room.
They come for the bell. They do not want it rung. They want it to go on humming until midnight, so that they can come up through the lid together.

crisis.text: Up there. Every rope. In time. Now.

oneOf.text: Ringers to the ropes! Miners too! Everybody who's ever pulled a rope, get on one!

oneOf.narrate: Somebody up on the lid is shouting for every rope to be manned.

peaceful.label: Get every rope on the nine manned, miners and the Wold's ringers together, and call the time down the stair

success.narrate: {You know|@ knows} what the nine need: in time, all nine, together, and kept.
{You know|@ knows} the founders' stair in the dark, every step, and the vault at the foot of it.
{You go|@ goes} up and down the founders' stair in the dark with the lid heaving, and {miss|misses} a step, and {go|goes} on.
{You stand|@ stands} at the head of the stair, halfway between the bell and the nine, and {call|calls} the time: down to the vault, and up to the lid.

oneOf.narrate: On the lid the miners take ropes beside the rope families, and the Wold's ringers beside them, a miner and a ringer to a bell, and Ailith on the first with her son, calling the families in, and for the first time in nine hundred years nobody asks whose rope is whose.

On the lid the miners take ropes beside the rope families, and the Wold's ringers beside them, a miner and a ringer to a bell, and from the door, under guard, Ailith calls the families in, and for the first time in nine hundred years nobody asks whose rope is whose.
Orin goes down the stair to the vault and stands with his back against the Parting Bell's frame, holding it still with both arms, while the white comes round him.
Somebody's arms are round the Parting Bell's frame in the vault, holding it still.

success.narrate: They ring. Ragged, then less ragged, then in time: nine bells, a southerner and a northerner on every rope, and Sloe on the ninth, and the beat goes down through the lid like a hand laid flat on it.

The lid settles. The half note goes thin, and thinner, and stops. In the vault the two winters stand a moment longer, facing each other across the silent bell, and then there is nothing to stand on, and they go down into the floor.

failure.narrate: {You call|@ calls} the time, but the ringers on the lid cannot hear it over the half note, and the nine stay out of time, and the white comes up round the Parting Bell in two shapes and does not stop.

objective.name: The nine
objective.label: Hold the vault until the nine are rung in time
objective.description: Four successful actions hold the Parting Bell and the vault against the two winters until the nine above are rung in time and the lid settles.
objective.failText: The nine come into time in the end, and the lid settles, but the white got up through the floor first, and the miners carry four of the ringers out of the hall stiff with it, and one of them does not wake.
objective.successText: Above, the nine come into time, all together, and the lid settles, and the Parting Bell goes quiet.

oneOf.narrate: An hour before midnight. The lid is still. The nine stand on it in time and silent, with their ropes hanging, and a southerner and a northerner sitting under every one, and nobody is hurt.

An hour before midnight. The lid is still. The vault below is scored white across its floor where the fight was, and the cold has not gone out of the rock, and the physicians are with the ringers by the north wall.

after.narrate: The Parting Bell is carried up the founders' stair on its frame, by eight people, slowly, and set down on the casting floor under the Mother Bell. Somebody has to hold it until midnight. Everybody looks at it, and then at everybody else.

after.text: It should not be the one who rings it, if anybody rings it. It should be somebody who will give it up.
The council's here. All of it that matters. We can hold a bell for an hour.

decisions.label: Sloe holds the Parting Bell until midnight
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. The Wold's Reckoner holds the Parting Bell until midnight.

told.ballad: On midwinter night the Reckoner of the Wold sat with the Parting Bell in her lap, in the south's own hall, and nobody took it from her.
told.tally: Cinder Fold. Sloe of Orme held the bell until midnight. Written: the south let her.

text.narrate: You ask Sloe. She looks at the bell a long time before she sits down on the casting floor beside it, and puts one hand on its frame, the way you would put a hand on a door.

text.text: Until midnight. Then it is everybody's, and I will give it to whoever everybody says.

decisions.label: The council holds it, in Brannagh's hands
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. The council of the free wards holds the Parting Bell until midnight, in Brannagh's hands.

told.ballad: On midwinter night old Brannagh of Fenmere held the Parting Bell for the council, and said she was too old to drop it.
told.tally: Cinder Fold. The council held the bell until midnight. Written: in Brannagh's hands.

text.narrate: You give it to the council. Brannagh takes the frame's handle herself and has a stool brought, and sits on it with the bell beside her knee.

text.text: An hour. I've sat through worse sessions. Nobody touches it unless the council says so, and the council's me, for an hour.

decisions.label: Hold it yourself
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. You hold the Parting Bell until midnight.

told.ballad: On midwinter night the hero of the south held the Parting Bell in two hands, and both countries watched them do it.
told.tally: Cinder Fold. The southerner held the bell until midnight. Written: nobody asked them to give it up.

text.narrate: You hold it yourself. You sit down on the casting floor with the Parting Bell's frame against your knee and your hand on it, and every face in the hall turns to you, and stays turned.

text.text: Then it is yours to give up, at midnight. I hope you do.

b4-lid.ledgeLabel: Rest, then go back to the bell
b4-lid.climbLabel: Go back out into Cinder Fold
b4-lid.climbText: The party goes out of the casting hall into Cinder Fold. The Parting Bell waits where you left it: depart again to go back to the same encounter.

ledge.narrate: You wake at the head of the founders' stair, on the casting floor, with somebody's coat under your head and the nine standing in time above you.
The Parting Bell is on its frame under the Mother Bell, where it was set down, and somebody's hand is still on it. It is not quite midnight.

b4-parting.name: The Parting Bell
b4-parting.region: Cinder Fold: the casting hall at midwinter midnight, under the Mother Bell
b4-parting.threat: At midnight the Mother Bell's midwinter note is due, and the Parting Bell can turn it. When the Parting Bell is touched, something that was waiting under the lid will come up to stop it.
b4-parting.brief: Midwinter midnight at Cinder Fold. The Mother Bell's note is due, every bell in the free wards is listening, and the Parting Bell is on the casting floor beneath it. How the winter is shared is decided tonight.

told.ballad: At midnight on midwinter at Cinder Fold, with every bell in the south listening, the hero of the song decided how the winter would be shared.
told.tally: Cinder Fold, midwinter midnight. The winter was decided. Written: how.

opening.narrate: Midwinter, a quarter before midnight. The casting hall is as full as it has ever been: the council on the casting floor, the committee by the wall, the rope families on the lid with the miners beside them, and the Wold's ringers in among them all, a southerner and a northerner to every rope.

Every bell in the free wards is listening. You can feel it through the iron of the lid: Highpass and Merrowgate and Briarwatch and every hearth bell in every town, quiet, waiting for the Mother Bell's note.

oneOf.narrate: Away north, over the peaks, Campion is standing under Dunnet's pot-bell in an empty valley with the clapper-rope in her hand, listening too.

Away north, on the boundary stones between Dunnet and Wem, the pot-bell stands in its frame with the rota chalked on it, and nobody to ring it tonight. Whoever comes back will read whose night it was.
Away north, in Dunnet, the pots are back on their hooks, and nothing in the Wold rings at all.
The Parting Bell is on its frame on the casting floor under the Mother Bell, with Sloe sitting beside it and one hand on its frame, the way you would put a hand on a door.
The Parting Bell is on its frame on the casting floor under the Mother Bell, with Brannagh on a stool beside it and the frame's handle in her fist.
The Parting Bell is on its frame on the casting floor under the Mother Bell, with your hand on it. Every face in the hall has been turned to you for an hour.

The Mother Bell's rope is in your hands. You went up to the signal house at eleven, and unbarred the store-room with the only key, and carried it down through the town on your shoulder with the whole of Cinder Fold watching. Whether the Mother Bell rings its midwinter note tonight is yours to allow. Nobody here can take it from you.

oneOf.text: The council asks for the midwinter note. In the council's name, and in mine, since I'm what's left of it in this hall. We recalled that rope three winters ago, and we're asking for it tonight, out loud, as it should have been asked for every year.

oneOf.narrate: The towns have asked for the Mother Bell's note, as they have every midwinter since the night of the great note: Ottilie has the letters on the committee's table, one from every town, and reads out their names.

opening.text: There are three things that can be done with the Parting Bell tonight. Ring it backward with the Mother Bell. Ring it forward with the Mother Bell. Or not at all. I have done the sum for all three. I am not going to do it again. Somebody else has to choose.

talks.label: Talk to Sloe

lines.text: Backward, and every ward in the free wards goes quiet for a winter, and the Wold has its first clear winter since the founders. Your worst. Towns I have never seen will fall, and I will have to write their names. Whoever rings it gives the bell everything they are.

Not at all, and the south gives at the floor and keeps quiet nights, town by town, and the Wold gives too, and every generation somebody has to ask again. Nobody is spared. Everybody pays a little, and has to keep paying.
Or the Wold leaves. Comes south, everyone, and gives the Wold to the white. I will not come. Somebody has to stay and be the Wold, even if it is only me.
Forward I will not talk about. Nobody in this hall is going to ring it forward. You will see to that.

talks.label: Talk to Ailith Strake

oneOf.narrate: Ailith is on the lid, on the first bell's rope, with her son on the rope beside her and two of the council's people at her back.
Ailith stands at the door of the hall, under guard, where she asked to stand, so that she can see whatever is rung.

lines.text: I'll not ask you for forward. I've read the five words. I don't like them. I'll not pretend I didn't read them.

oneOf.text: Whatever you ring, I'll ring it. Properly. Nobody will say a Strake let a note go out of time on a night like this.
Whatever you ring, I'll be stood here, listening for who's out of time. Somebody will be. Tell my son to watch the third.

talks.label: Find Rue

oneOf.narrate: Rue is on the lid, by the Parting Bell's side of it, with her book under her arm and Nessa beside her, close enough that their shoulders touch.
Rue is on the lid with her book under her arm, with nobody beside her. She keeps her thumb on the page where somebody once wrote in capitals that they would tell her who she is.
Rue is sitting on the edge of the lid with her book shut on her knees. She has not asked for a rope. She has written down, again, that she minds.

Rue is on the lid with her book under her arm, alone, near the Parting Bell. Up above the town the forge-signal is lit. Nessa lit it at dusk and came down for the midnight, and she stands at the back of the hall by the doors, where she can see Rue and the signal both.
Rue is on the lid with her book under her arm, alone, near the Parting Bell. Up above the town, the forge-signal is lit. Somebody is keeping it.

oneOf.text: I asked Sloe for the rope again, at eleven. She said no again. I said that I would ask once more, at midnight, in front of everybody. That is how it is done.
I am not going to ask. I said so. If Sloe rings it, I will hold her book for her, and read it to her after. Every day.
If she rings it, I'm the first thing she sees after. I'll tell her. I said I would.

oneOf.narrate: Rue writes the time at the top of a clean page, and the date, and nothing under it yet.

talks.label: Find Burdock

lines.narrate: Burdock has a place against the wall by the committee's table, with the book of winters open on his knees at tonight's page and a pen ready.

lines.text: One line. Every winter gets one line. Nine hundred of them. I have never in my life wanted so much to know what a line will say before I write it.
Whatever you choose, I will write it exactly. And then I will write who chose it. That is the part nobody ever reads, and it is the part I mind most.

talks.label: Put a hand on the nearest of the nine, and listen to the joined bells

lines.narrate: You put your hand on the third bell where it stands on the lid. Through the bronze, every bell in the free wards with somebody in it is listening.

oneOf.narrate: Among them, far off, Briarwatch's bell is listening too, rung by hand at the top of its tower. It does not answer. Nobody is in it to answer.
Among them, far off, Briarwatch's bell is listening too, rung by hand at the top of its tower. It does not answer. Nobody is in it to answer.

oneOf.text: I'm here. In Vell's bell, still. I can hear all of you. Whatever you ring, tell me after. I'd like to have been told.
I'm here. Pim's got the rope. I can hear every one of us, all the way to you. Whatever you ring, I'd like to have been asked. You did ask. Thank you.

b4-parting.clue: The Parting Bell only turns the Mother Bell's note. Rung with it, backward or forward, it sends the note one way or the other; left alone, the Mother Bell rings its note as it always has. The Mother Bell rings either way.

investigate.label: Read the Parting Bell's founders' marks, and learn what it can do to the Mother Bell's note

success.narrate: {You kneel|@ kneels} by the Parting Bell's frame and {read|reads} the marks round its lip, in the founders' letters, by lamplight: what it does, and when, and with what.

It does nothing by itself. It turns the Mother Bell's note, that is all. Rung backward with it at midwinter, every ward in the south goes quiet for a winter, and the white stays where it is. Rung forward, every ward is louder for good, and all of it goes north. Left alone, the Mother Bell rings its note as it always has, and the Parting Bell is only a small black bell.
Under the marks for forward, very small, somebody long ago has scratched a line through them. Not this way.

failure.narrate: {You kneel|@ kneels} by the Parting Bell and {try|tries} to read its marks, but the founders' letters are worn almost flat round the lip, and by lamplight {you can|@ can} read only that it turns the Mother Bell's note, and not how far.

route.label: Find a place on the lid where you can see every rope and the Parting Bell at once

success.narrate: {You find|@ finds} the place: on the lid by the fifth bell, in the middle, where every rope and every ringer's hands are in sight, and the Parting Bell below, and the Mother Bell above.

failure.narrate: {You look|@ looks} for a place on the lid where all of it can be seen at once, but there are too many people, and the lid is crowded to its edges, and {you end|@ ends} up at the side of it, by the ninth.

direct.label: Walk out into the middle of the casting floor, to the Parting Bell
direct.text: You walk out into the middle of the casting floor, through everybody, to the Parting Bell under the Mother Bell, and stand by it.

approach.narrate: Five minutes to midnight. The casting hall goes quiet, the way the street did this morning, from the doors inwards.
Somebody has to touch the Parting Bell first, whatever is to be done with it: to ring it, or to lift it off the floor and carry it away so that it is not.

crisis.narrate: When the Parting Bell is touched, the lid answers. Up through the iron, between the nine, through the ringers' feet and the ropes, comes something that has been waiting under Cinder Fold since the bell was cast.

The Founders' Shade: nine shapes in the white, as tall as the bells, with the faces the free wards' songs give them. The ones on the coins and the gatehouse arch and the broadsheets. The legends. Not the people who drew the tenth mould and wrote under it; the people the songs made out of them.
They have come for the bell. They want it rung forward, the way the songs say the founders would have wanted, and they mean to have it.

oneOf.text: That's not them. That's what we said about them. The real ones wrote five words and left them for us. Don't let the songs have it.

oneOf.narrate: Somebody on the lid says it out loud: that is not them. That is what the songs made of them.

peaceful.label: Ring the nine in time, with both countries on the ropes, and give the Shade nothing to stand on

easierWith.reason: Both countries have shared a bell before, the council has stood together, or you know both notes and can call the true time

success.narrate: {You know|@ knows} what the Parting Bell does and does not do, and that forward is not in it any more except in songs.
{You can|@ can} see every rope from the middle of the lid, and every pair of hands on them.
{You push|@ pushes} through the crowd on the lid to the middle of it, and {see|sees} as many ropes as {you can|@ can}.
{You call|@ calls} the time. The same time as under the lid, an hour ago, that the nine already know.

oneOf.narrate: Ailith takes it up on the first bell, and calls the families in after it, and her son beside her.
From the door, under guard, Ailith calls it too, for her families, louder than anybody.

success.narrate: The nine ring in time. A southerner and a northerner on every rope, miners and rope families and the Wold's ringers, nine bells and one beat, and the beat goes out through the lid and the floor and up the walls.

The Founders' Shade stands among the bells and has nothing to stand on. The songs that made it are being sung by nobody. Its faces go one by one, the way breath goes off a cold window, and the nine shapes are white, and then grey, and then nothing.

failure.narrate: {You call|@ calls} the time, but the Shade is among the ropes already, and the ringers falter at the faces they have known from coins and broadsheets all their lives, and the beat breaks.

objective.name: The Parting Bell
objective.label: Hold the Parting Bell until the nine are rung in time
objective.description: Four successful actions hold the Parting Bell on the casting floor against the Founders' Shade until the nine are rung in time.
objective.failText: The nine come into time in the end and the Shade goes down through the lid, but it went through the ringers on the lid first, and the physicians are at the ropes of the second and the seventh, and one of the rope families' oldest is carried out of the hall.
objective.successText: The nine ring in time, and the Founders' Shade goes out like breath off a window, and the Parting Bell is still on the floor.

oneOf.narrate: Midnight. The nine have stopped. The casting hall stands in the silence after them, and the Parting Bell is on the floor under the Mother Bell where it was, and nobody is hurt.

Midnight. The nine have stopped. The lid is scored white between the bells where the Shade went through it, and the physicians are still on their knees by the ropes, and the Parting Bell is on the floor under the Mother Bell where it was.

after.narrate: The Mother Bell's note is due. Everybody in the hall is looking at the same small black bell, and then at you.

after.text: Choose. I will hold you to it. So will the tally.

decisions.label: Share it: nobody rings the Parting Bell, and both countries give
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. Nobody rings the Parting Bell. It goes back to the Hall of Legends, silent. The Mother Bell is rung softer, by the rota, and both countries keep quiet nights and give at the floor, and must keep doing it, every generation.

told.ballad: At midnight on midwinter the hero of the song left the Parting Bell on the floor, and the Mother Bell was rung soft, and both countries took a share of the winter, and must take it again.
told.tally: Midwinter. The bell was not rung. The winter is shared: quiet nights in the south, giving at the floor in both countries. Written: it must be asked again.

text.narrate: You lift the Parting Bell off the floor, frame and all, and hand it to the nearest pair of hands that will carry it out of the hall. It is not rung. It is going back to the Hall of Legends, to its hook, to hang there silent.

oneOf.narrate: You go up the lid to the Mother Bell's rope with the rope from the signal house on your shoulder, and hang it, yourself. You allow the note.
The Mother Bell's rope comes down off its cleat.

text.narrate: The Mother Bell rings its midwinter note, softer than it has ever been rung, by the rota: four ringers, a southerner and a northerner and two more, a quarter-pull each, so that less goes north than any winter since the great note.

text.text: Less. It is not nothing. It is less, every year, if you keep it. I will write that down myself.

decisions.label: Bring them south: the Parting Bell stays silent, and the Wold comes over the peaks to live
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. The Parting Bell stays silent. The Wold's people come over the peaks to live in the free wards, and the Wold is left to the white for good.

told.ballad: At midnight on midwinter the hero of the song left the bell unrung and opened the south to the whole of the Wold, and the Wold came over the peaks, all but one.
told.tally: Midwinter. The bell was not rung. The Wold is to come south. Written: the Wold is given to the white. Written: Sloe of Orme stays.

text.narrate: You leave the Parting Bell where it is, on the floor, and say it in front of everybody: the Wold comes south. All of it that will come. The free wards will take them in.

oneOf.narrate: You go up the lid to the Mother Bell's rope with the rope from the signal house on your shoulder, and hang it, yourself. You allow the note, as it has always been rung.
The Mother Bell rings its midwinter note, as it has every midwinter since the great note, and everything it pushes goes north, to a country that will be empty by the spring.

oneOf.text: I've costed it. I costed it at ten thousand, the autumn before last, and the council voted it in the spring with its eyes open. It's three thousand. It holds. Just. Don't anybody have a child for a year.
I've costed it. It holds. Just. Ask me again in the spring and I'll tell you how just.

text.text: I will not come. Somebody has to stay and be the Wold, even if it is only me. I will keep the last door. Write that I chose it.

decisions.label: Sloe's note: the Parting Bell rung backward with the Mother Bell
decisions.description: This decision is permanent. The Parting Bell is rung backward with the Mother Bell. Every ward in the free wards goes quiet for one winter: the Wold's first clear winter in nine hundred years, and the free wards' worst. Whoever rings it gives the bell everything they are.

told.ballad: At midnight on midwinter the Parting Bell was rung backward, once, and every ward in the south went quiet, and somebody gave everything they were to ring it.
told.tally: Midwinter. The bell was rung backward. The Wold's first clear winter since the founders. Written: the south's worst. Written: who rang it.

text.narrate: You say it: backward. Sloe's note. Once.

oneOf.narrate: Rue comes across the lid to the Parting Bell with Nessa beside her, and asks for the rope in front of everybody, and Sloe says no, and Rue asks again, and Sloe looks at her a long time and gives it to her.
Rue comes across the lid to the Parting Bell, and asks for the rope in front of everybody, and Sloe says no, and Rue asks again, and Sloe looks at her a long time and gives it to her.
Sloe takes the Parting Bell's rope herself. Nobody asks for it. Rue holds her book.
You go up the lid to the Mother Bell's rope with the rope from the signal house on your shoulder, and hang it, yourself. You allow the note.
The Mother Bell's rope comes down off its cleat.

text.narrate: The Mother Bell rings its midwinter note, and under it, once, backward, the Parting Bell.

Every ward in the free wards goes quiet. You can hear it go: through the lid, through the floor, through every bell with somebody in it, one after another, Highpass and Merrowgate and Briarwatch and every hearth bell in every town, like lamps going out down a street.

oneOf.narrate: Rue lets go of the rope. She looks at the bell, and at her hands, and at the hall full of people, and at Nessa, and does not know any of it.
Rue lets go of the rope. She looks at the bell, and at her hands, and at the hall full of people, and does not know any of it. Her book is on the lid by her feet. She does not know it is hers.
Sloe lets go of the rope. She looks at the bell, and at her slate, and at the sum on it, and cannot read it. Rue picks up the slate and holds it for her.

oneOf.text: Hello. I'm Nessa. You're Rue. You wrote it down. I'll show you.

oneOf.narrate: Somebody picks up the book and gives it to her, open at the first page.
Rue sits down beside her on the lid, and begins to read her the slate, from the top, slowly.
